fr-alsace-grand-cru-pfersigberg.name: Alsace grand cru Pfersigberg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-pfersigberg.summary: Pfersigberg, the peach hill, is a large grand cru of about 71 ha above Eguisheim and Wettolsheim, on warm limestone and marl facing southeast. It gives aromatic Gewurztraminer and broad, peachy Riesling and Pinot Gris, with Kuentz-Bas, Paul Ginglinger, Bruno Sorg and Léon Beyer among its leading growers.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-pfersigberg.terroir: Limestone and marl on a long southeast slope. Communes: Eguisheim, Wettolsheim (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-pfersigberg.nerd_note: Peach trees once grew among the vines, giving the hill its name.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-pfingstberg.name: Alsace grand cru Pfingstberg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-pfingstberg.summary: Pfingstberg, Pentecost hill, rises above Orschwihr in the southern Haut-Rhin on a steep southeast slope of sandstone, limestone and marl. It gives fine, racy Riesling and aromatic Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer, and the biodynamic Zusslin family and Lucien Albrecht are its best-known producers.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-pfingstberg.terroir: Sandstone and limestone on a steep southeast slope. Communes: Orschwihr (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-pfingstberg.nerd_note: Zusslin, a biodynamic estate, also owns the Clos Liebenberg monopole nearby.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-praelatenberg.name: Alsace grand cru Praelatenberg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-praelatenberg.summary: Praelatenberg, the prelates' hill, was owned by the monks of Ebersmunster abbey. Its granite and gneiss slopes below the Haut-Koenigsbourg castle give fresh, mineral Riesling and fine Pinot Gris.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-praelatenberg.terroir: Granite and gneiss below the castle of Haut-Koenigsbourg. Communes: Kintzheim (Bas-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-praelatenberg.nerd_note: Praelatenberg is the only grand cru of the Bas-Rhin on the Haut-Koenigsbourg massif.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-rangen.name: Alsace grand cru Rangen
fr-alsace-grand-cru-rangen.summary: Rangen is the southernmost grand cru and one of the most extraordinary vineyards in France: a very steep, south-facing wall of volcanic rock above the Thur river at Thann. Its wines, smoky, powerful and deeply mineral, were famous in the sixteenth century. Zind-Humbrecht's Clos Saint-Urbain, around the chapel of Saint-Urbain, and Schoffit's Clos Saint-Théobald are its references.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-rangen.terroir: Volcanic rock (andesite, tuffs and greywacke) on an extremely steep south-facing slope. Communes: Thann, Vieux-Thann (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-rangen.nerd_note: Thanks to its volcanic soil and steepness, the Rangen ripens late despite its south-facing slope; local lore says its wine 'makes your head spin'.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-rosacker.name: Alsace grand cru Rosacker
fr-alsace-grand-cru-rosacker.summary: Rosacker, the field of roses, above Hunawihr and its fortified church, gives taut, mineral, long-lived Riesling. Trimbach's Clos Sainte Hune, a 1.67 ha parcel owned for more than 200 years, lies entirely within it but is sold without the grand cru name.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-rosacker.terroir: Dolomitic limestone and marl on an east-facing slope. Communes: Hunawihr (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-rosacker.nerd_note: Clos Sainte Hune, often called Alsace's greatest Riesling, has never carried the Rosacker name on its label.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-saering.name: Alsace grand cru Saering
fr-alsace-grand-cru-saering.summary: Saering is the most northerly of Guebwiller's four grands crus, on terraced slopes of limestone, marl and sandstone facing east and southeast. It gives fine, citrusy, early-approachable Riesling and aromatic Gewurztraminer and Muscat; Domaine Schlumberger and Dirler-Cadé are the main owners.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-saering.terroir: Limestone and marl with sandstone on terraced slopes. Communes: Guebwiller (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-saering.nerd_note: Saering, Kessler, Kitterlé and Spiegel make Guebwiller the commune with the most grands crus.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-schlossberg.name: Alsace grand cru Schlossberg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-schlossberg.summary: Schlossberg, castle hill, was the first Alsace grand cru, created by decree in 1975. Its steep granite terraces below the ruined castle of Kaysersberg give some of the most elegant, floral and mineral Rieslings of Alsace. It covers about 80 ha.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-schlossberg.terroir: Granite with sand on steep terraces. Communes: Kientzheim, Kaysersberg (Kaysersberg Vignoble).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-schlossberg.nerd_note: Schlossberg's terraces were rebuilt after the war; its first grand cru vintage was 1975.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-schoenenbourg.name: Alsace grand cru Schoenenbourg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-schoenenbourg.summary: Schoenenbourg, the beautiful castle, rises behind the medieval walls of Riquewihr and was famous across Europe in the sixteenth century. Its gypsum-rich marl gives rich, long-lived Riesling, and its Vendanges Tardives and Sélections de Grains Nobles are among Alsace's greatest. Hugel, Dopff au Moulin, Marcel Deiss and Bott-Geyl own parcels.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-schoenenbourg.terroir: Keuper marl with gypsum, sandstone and dolomite on a north and northeast-facing amphitheatre above Riquewihr. Communes: Riquewihr, Zellenberg (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-schoenenbourg.nerd_note: Hugel long refused to use grand cru names on its labels; it now marks wines from its best sites, including Schoenenbourg, as Grossi Laüe, Alsatian for great growths.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-sommerberg.name: Alsace grand cru Sommerberg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-sommerberg.summary: Sommerberg, summer hill, is a steep granite slope above Niedermorschwihr that gives some of the most precise, mineral Rieslings in Alsace, notably from Albert Boxler.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-sommerberg.terroir: Granite on extremely steep terraces. Communes: Niedermorschwihr, Katzenthal (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-sommerberg.nerd_note: Boxler bottles separate Sommerberg cuvées from different parts of the hill.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-sonnenglanz.name: Alsace grand cru Sonnenglanz
fr-alsace-grand-cru-sonnenglanz.summary: Sonnenglanz, sunshine glow, is a warm, sheltered slope above Beblenheim known for rich Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and for botrytised sweet wines. It was among the first sites in Alsace to be marketed by name.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-sonnenglanz.terroir: Limestone and marl on a gentle southeast slope. Communes: Beblenheim (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-sonnenglanz.nerd_note: Beblenheim is home to the Bott-Geyl family, one of the biodynamic leaders of the central Haut-Rhin.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-spiegel.name: Alsace grand cru Spiegel
fr-alsace-grand-cru-spiegel.summary: Spiegel, the mirror, lies between Bergholtz and Guebwiller on sandstone and marl facing east and southeast. It gives fine, spicy Riesling and supple Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, and it shares the village of Bergholtz with Domaine Eugène Meyer, the first wine estate in France to farm biodynamically (1969).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-spiegel.terroir: Sandstone and marl on a southeast slope. Communes: Bergholtz, Guebwiller (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-spiegel.nerd_note: Bergholtz is home to Domaine Eugène Meyer, France's first biodynamic wine estate (1969).

fr-alsace-grand-cru-sporen.name: Alsace grand cru Sporen
fr-alsace-grand-cru-sporen.summary: Sporen, next to Schoenenbourg, is traditionally planted with Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and was once used for a famous field blend (Gentil). Its clay gives rich, powerful wines.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-sporen.terroir: Clay and marl with stones on a gentle slope east of Riquewihr. Communes: Riquewihr (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-sporen.nerd_note: Hugel's Gewurztraminer Grossi Laüe comes largely from Sporen.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-steinert.name: Alsace grand cru Steinert
fr-alsace-grand-cru-steinert.summary: Steinert, the stony one, is a hot, steep limestone slope above Pfaffenheim and Westhalten, so stony that the soil warms quickly in spring. It gives powerful, smoky Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer and fine, mineral Riesling, and the biodynamic pioneer Pierre Frick makes some of its most distinctive wines.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-steinert.terroir: Limestone on a steep, stony slope. Communes: Pfaffenheim, Westhalten (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-steinert.nerd_note: Pierre Frick, a biodynamic pioneer since 1981, is known for sulphur-free wines from Steinert.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-steingrubler.name: Alsace grand cru Steingrubler
fr-alsace-grand-cru-steingrubler.summary: Steingrubler, the stone quarry, lies above Wettolsheim on a mixed soil of limestone, sandstone and granite, a reflection of the faulting that shattered the Vosges foothills here. It gives spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and fine Riesling; Albert Mann and Barmès-Buecher are its best-known growers.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-steingrubler.terroir: Limestone, sandstone and granite in a mixed soil. Communes: Wettolsheim (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-steingrubler.nerd_note: Its name refers to old stone quarries on the hill.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-steinklotz.name: Alsace grand cru Steinklotz
fr-alsace-grand-cru-steinklotz.summary: Steinklotz, block of stone, is the northernmost grand cru, above Marlenheim, where the Merovingian kings had a royal estate. Its limestone gives powerful Pinot Gris and Riesling; Pinot Noir from here is renowned locally.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-steinklotz.terroir: Limestone with marl at the northern gateway of the Route des Vins. Communes: Marlenheim (Bas-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-steinklotz.nerd_note: Marlenheim's Merovingian royal villa is mentioned by Gregory of Tours in the sixth century.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-vorbourg.name: Alsace grand cru Vorbourg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-vorbourg.grapes: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat; Pinot Noir for red (since 2022)
fr-alsace-grand-cru-vorbourg.summary: Vorbourg is a large, warm grand cru between Rouffach and Westhalten. Its limestone gives rich Pinot Gris, Gewurztraminer and Riesling, and since 2022 it may also make Pinot Noir. René Muré's Clos Saint Landelin, a walled monopole within it, is its best-known wine.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-vorbourg.terroir: Limestone and sandstone on a sunny, south-facing hill. Communes: Rouffach, Westhalten (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-vorbourg.nerd_note: Clos Saint Landelin belonged to the bishops of Strasbourg before the Revolution.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-wiebelsberg.name: Alsace grand cru Wiebelsberg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-wiebelsberg.summary: Wiebelsberg rises above Andlau on light, quartz-rich sandstone facing southeast, in contrast to neighbouring Kastelberg's black schist. It gives delicate, floral and saline Riesling that is approachable younger than Kastelberg's, from growers such as Marc Kreydenweiss and Guy Wach.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-wiebelsberg.terroir: Quartz-rich sandstone on a southeast slope above Andlau. Communes: Andlau (Bas-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-wiebelsberg.nerd_note: Andlau has three grands crus: Kastelberg, Moenchberg and Wiebelsberg.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-wineck-schlossberg.name: Alsace grand cru Wineck-Schlossberg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-wineck-schlossberg.summary: Wineck-Schlossberg lies below the ruined tower of the Wineck castle at Katzenthal and Ammerschwihr, on a steep granite slope in a side valley west of Colmar. Its granite gives precise, floral, finely mineral Riesling and delicate Gewurztraminer, with Meyer-Fonné and Klur among its growers.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-wineck-schlossberg.terroir: Granite below the ruined castle of Wineck. Communes: Katzenthal, Ammerschwihr (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-wineck-schlossberg.nerd_note: The Wineck castle tower stands among the vines above Katzenthal.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-winzenberg.name: Alsace grand cru Winzenberg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-winzenberg.summary: Winzenberg, the winegrowers' hill, rises above Blienschwiller in the Bas-Rhin on two-mica granite facing south. Its light, quick-draining soils give fresh, floral Riesling and Gewurztraminer with a fine mineral edge, and the village is also one of Alsace's 13 dénominations géographiques complémentaires.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-winzenberg.terroir: Granite on a south-facing slope. Communes: Blienschwiller (Bas-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-winzenberg.nerd_note: Blienschwiller is one of Alsace's 13 dénominations géographiques complémentaires.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-zinnkoepfle.name: Alsace grand cru Zinnkoepflé
fr-alsace-grand-cru-zinnkoepfle.summary: Zinnkoepflé is one of the highest and driest grands crus, a steep south-facing hill above the Vallée Noble where wild orchids and Mediterranean plants grow. It gives powerful, spicy Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris and taut Riesling.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-zinnkoepfle.terroir: Limestone and sandstone on a high, hot, south-facing slope up to about 420 m. Communes: Soultzmatt, Westhalten (Haut-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-zinnkoepfle.nerd_note: Its microclimate is so dry that a protected steppe-like flora, unusual in northern France, grows on the hillside.

fr-alsace-grand-cru-zotzenberg.name: Alsace grand cru Zotzenberg
fr-alsace-grand-cru-zotzenberg.grapes: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat, Sylvaner
fr-alsace-grand-cru-zotzenberg.summary: Zotzenberg, above Mittelbergheim, is the only grand cru allowed to make Sylvaner (since 2006), a tribute to a local grape long prized here. Its limestone also gives fine Riesling and Gewurztraminer.
fr-alsace-grand-cru-zotzenberg.terroir: Limestone and marl on a southeast slope above Mittelbergheim. Communes: Mittelbergheim (Bas-Rhin).
fr-alsace-grand-cru-zotzenberg.nerd_note: Albert Seltz led the campaign that won Sylvaner grand cru status in Zotzenberg.

fr-alsace-klevener-de-heiligenstein.name: Alsace Klevener de Heiligenstein
fr-alsace-klevener-de-heiligenstein.summary: A unique name for wine from Savagnin Rose (Klevener), a non-aromatic relative of Gewurztraminer, planted at Heiligenstein in the eighteenth century by mayor Ehret Wantz; also grown in four neighbouring communes. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

fr-alsace-ottrott.name: Alsace Ottrott
fr-alsace-ottrott.summary: A red-wine enclave below Mont Sainte-Odile, where Pinot Noir (the Rouge d'Ottrott) has been made for centuries; the name is reserved for Pinot Noir. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

fr-alsace-rodern.name: Alsace Rodern
fr-alsace-rodern.summary: A village between Ribeauvillé and Saint-Hippolyte on granite and sandstone, with a long tradition of Pinot Noir; the name is used for red wine. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

fr-alsace-saint-hippolyte.name: Alsace Saint-Hippolyte
fr-alsace-saint-hippolyte.summary: The village below the Haut-Koenigsbourg, known for Pinot Noir on granite and sandstone; the name is used for red wine. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

fr-alsace-scherwiller.name: Alsace Scherwiller
fr-alsace-scherwiller.summary: A Bas-Rhin village on granite and alluvial soils at the mouth of the Val de Villé, known for Riesling. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

fr-alsace-val-saint-gregoire.name: Alsace Val Saint Grégoire
fr-alsace-val-saint-gregoire.summary: The Munster valley villages around Turckheim, Ingersheim and Wintzenheim, on granite and sandstone; the name applies to Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois and Pinot Gris. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

fr-alsace-vallee-noble.name: Alsace Vallée Noble
fr-alsace-vallee-noble.summary: A side valley above Soultzmatt in the Haut-Rhin with limestone and sandstone, known for Riesling, Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris; the Zinnkoepflé grand cru lies here. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

fr-alsace-wolxheim.name: Alsace Wolxheim
fr-alsace-wolxheim.summary: A village west of Strasbourg on limestone and marl, famed for Riesling; Napoleon is said to have favoured its wine. It is a dénomination géographique complémentaire of AOC Alsace, recognised in the 2011 rules.

fr-anjou.name: Anjou
fr-anjou.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc; Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Gamay, Pineau d'Aunis, Grolleau
fr-anjou.summary: Anjou is the regional appellation for the department of Maine-et-Loire and neighbouring parts of Deux-Sèvres and Vienne. Anjou Blanc, made from Chenin, is the star: a group of growers on the dark schists since the 1990s (Richard Leroy, Mark Angeli, Thibaud Boudignon, Patrick Baudouin, Stéphane Bernaudeau) has made some of the world's most sought-after dry Chenin under this humble name. Anjou Rouge and Anjou Gamay are juicy and light; Anjou Mousseux is sparkling.
fr-anjou.terroir: The 'Anjou Noir' schist and volcanic rock to the west, the 'Anjou Blanc' tuffeau to the east.
producers: Mark Angeli (La Ferme de la Sansonnière)
fr-anjou.nerd_note: Several of the best Anjou Blancs are labelled as Vin de France because their makers refused to follow appellation rules, so the most famous Anjou is sometimes not legally Anjou.

fr-anjou-brissac.name: Anjou Villages Brissac
fr-anjou-brissac.summary: A red appellation for ten communes around Brissac-Quincé, between the Aubance and the Loire. Firm, dark Cabernet with a mineral finish; Domaine de Montgilet and Domaine de Bablut are leading names. The Château de Brissac, the tallest château in France at seven storeys, presides.
fr-anjou-brissac.terroir: Schist and sandstone, with some limestone at the border with the Saumurois.
fr-anjou-brissac.nerd_note: Brissac sits right on the boundary between the dark schists of the Armorican Massif and the pale limestone of the Paris Basin.

fr-anjou-coteaux-de-la-loire.name: Anjou-Coteaux de la Loire
fr-anjou-coteaux-de-la-loire.summary: A small appellation for sweet Chenin from slopes along the Loire west of Angers, around Montjean and Ingrandes. The wines are lighter and more mineral than the Layon.
fr-anjou-coteaux-de-la-loire.terroir: Schist and limestone slopes above the river.
fr-anjou-coteaux-de-la-loire.nerd_note: Its limestone patches, rare in Anjou Noir, once supplied lime kilns along the river.

fr-anjou-villages.name: Anjou Villages
fr-anjou-villages.summary: A red-only appellation for the best Cabernet sites in 46 communes of Anjou, created in 1987. The wines are deeper and more structured than Anjou Rouge, and Cabernet Sauvignon ripens unusually well on the warm schist.
fr-anjou-villages.terroir: Schist and volcanic soils in the Layon and Aubance valleys.
fr-anjou-villages.nerd_note: Anjou is one of the few places in the Loire where Cabernet Sauvignon can ripen fully, thanks to dark, heat-retaining schist.

fr-arbois.name: Arbois
fr-arbois.grapes: Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard, Trousseau, Pinot Noir
fr-arbois.summary:
Arbois was among the very first AOCs decreed in France, on 15 May 1936, and it is the Jura's most important appellation by name, covering about 800 ha in production around the town of Arbois and 12 surrounding communes. It makes every Jura style: Trousseau and Poulsard reds (it is the heartland of Trousseau), Chardonnay and Savagnin whites, ouillé and sous voile, vin jaune and vin de paille. The village of Pupillin, the 'world capital of Ploussard', may add its name (Arbois-Pupillin).

Arbois is also the town where Louis Pasteur grew up and did much of his research on wine fermentation; his family house is a museum. Producers range from the Fruitière Vinicole d'Arbois, founded in 1906 as one of France's first wine co-operatives, to Stéphane Tissot, Jacques Puffeney (retired 2014), Domaine de la Tournelle, Domaine Rolet and Lucien Aviet.
fr-arbois.terroir: Triassic red and grey marls and Liassic marls, with limestone scree; vines at 250 to 450 m around the Cuisance valley.
fr-arbois.nerd_note: Arbois's AOC decree is dated 15 May 1936, in the first batch of French appellations; Arbois-Pupillin is the only village name allowed on an Arbois label.

fr-arbois-pupillin.name: Arbois Pupillin
fr-arbois-pupillin.summary: Pupillin is a village on a plateau above Arbois that calls itself the world capital of Ploussard (Poulsard), the pale, delicate red grape of the Jura. It is also the home of Pierre Overnoy and Emmanuel Houillon, pioneers of sulphur-free natural wine.
fr-arbois-pupillin.terroir: Blue and grey Liassic and Triassic marls on slopes around the village.
fr-arbois-pupillin.nerd_note: Pupillin's wines carry Arbois Pupillin, the only village name allowed within Arbois.

fr-auxey-duresses.name: Auxey-Duresses
fr-auxey-duresses.summary: Auxey-Duresses lies in the valley that runs west from Meursault toward Saint-Romain, and it makes both reds and whites. The reds come mostly from the southeast-facing slope opposite Monthélie, including the premier crus Les Duresses and Climat du Val; the whites from the cooler slopes facing Meursault. Both are leaner and fresher than their famous neighbours' wines. Lalou Bize-Leroy's Maison Leroy has its headquarters in the village.
fr-auxey-duresses.terroir: Marl and limestone in a narrow valley; the Montagne du Bourdon faces southeast and holds the premier crus.
fr-auxey-duresses.nerd_note: Leroy's cellars in Auxey hold one of the largest stocks of old Burgundy in the world, much of it from the négociant era.

fr-bandol.name: Bandol
fr-bandol.grapes: Mourvèdre (at least 50% of reds), Grenache, Cinsault; Clairette, Ugni Blanc, Bourboulenc
fr-bandol.summary:
Bandol is the great red wine of Provence, from a natural amphitheatre of terraced hills (restanques) above the fishing port of Bandol, between Marseille and Toulon. Its grape is Mourvèdre, which needs heat to ripen, and the sun-baked south-facing slopes, sheltered from the mistral, provide it. The rules require at least 50% Mourvèdre in the red (top wines often use 75 to 95%) and at least 18 months of ageing in wood before release. The wines are dark, structured and long-lived, with notes of black fruit, garrigue, liquorice, leather and game. Bandol rosé, also built on Mourvèdre, is one of the most serious rosés in France.

Bandol was a famous wine in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, exported through its port. After phylloxera it almost disappeared. Lucien Peyraud of Domaine Tempier, who married into the family in 1936, led the fight for the appellation (1941) and the return of Mourvèdre. Tempier, Château de Pibarnon, Château Pradeaux, Domaine de la Bégude and Château Vannières are among the leading estates.
fr-bandol.terroir: Terraces (restanques) of limestone, marl and sandstone facing south toward the sea, sheltered by the Sainte-Baume massif; the sea moderates temperatures.
fr-bandol.nerd_note: Lucien Peyraud is called the 'father of Bandol'; his friend Richard Olney, the American food writer, made Tempier famous in the United States through Kermit Lynch and Alice Waters.

fr-banyuls.name: Banyuls
fr-banyuls.grapes: Grenache Noir (at least 50%), Grenache Gris, Grenache Blanc, Carignan, Macabeu, Malvoisie, Muscat
fr-banyuls.summary:
Banyuls is France's great fortified red, made on the steep schist terraces of four communes (Banyuls-sur-Mer, Collioure, Port-Vendres and Cerbère) where the Pyrenees fall into the Mediterranean. It is a vin doux naturel: the fermentation of very ripe Grenache is stopped by adding neutral grape spirit (mutage), which keeps natural sugar and lifts alcohol to about 16%. Banyuls winemakers often add the spirit *sur grains*, onto the skins, and macerate for weeks, which extracts colour and tannin, much like Port.

What happens next defines the style. In the *oxidative* tradition, the wine ages for years in old barrels or in glass demijohns called *bonbonnes* left outdoors in the sun, where it oxidises, concentrates and develops a nutty, maderised character: flavours of walnut, coffee, prune, cocoa and dried fig, and the prized *rancio* note. Some houses age wine in large barrels for decades, refreshing old wine with younger, like a solera. In the *reductive* tradition, called *rimage* (Catalan for 'vintage'), the wine is bottled young to keep its fresh red and black fruit, and it is closer to a vintage Port. There are also white and rosé Banyuls, and *hors d'âge* wines aged at least five years.

The Cellier des Templiers cooperative makes most Banyuls and keeps a huge collection of old barrels; Domaine de la Rectorie, Domaine du Mas Blanc (whose founder, Dr André Parcé, led the campaign for the appellation) and Coume del Mas are leading estates. Banyuls is one of the few wines that can match chocolate.
fr-banyuls.terroir: Steep terraces of Cambrian schist with very thin soil, often under a few centimetres of topsoil, facing the sea; tiny yields (often under 20 hl/ha); extreme wind and drought.
fr-banyuls.nerd_note: Arnau de Vilanova, a physician at Montpellier in the 1280s, described adding spirit to fermenting grape must to stop fermentation; tradition holds that the King of Majorca granted him a patent for it in 1299.

fr-banyuls-grand-cru.name: Banyuls grand cru
fr-banyuls-grand-cru.summary: Banyuls Grand Cru is the top tier of Banyuls, with at least 75% Grenache Noir, a maceration of at least five days on the skins, and at least 30 months of ageing in oak before release. The wines are deep, complex and oxidative, with notes of dried fruit, walnut, coffee and rancio, and they last for decades.
fr-banyuls-grand-cru.terroir: The same schist terraces as Banyuls; the best old-vine plots.
fr-banyuls-grand-cru.nerd_note: Grand Cru Banyuls is one of the very few French appellations that requires a specific period of oak ageing.

fr-barsac.name: Barsac
fr-barsac.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris, Muscadelle
fr-barsac.summary:
Barsac is the largest of the five Sauternais communes, on the north bank of the Ciron where it flows into the Garonne. It has its own appellation, but by a historic right its estates may label their wines either Barsac or Sauternes; most top estates use Barsac on the label to stress their identity. Ten classed growths of 1855 are here, including two Premiers Crus, Climens and Coutet, plus Doisy-Daëne, Doisy-Védrines, Doisy-Dubroca, Nairac, Caillou, Broustet, Suau and de Myrat.

The difference is geology. Barsac is a low limestone plateau (the *calcaire à astéries*) covered by a thin layer of red, iron-rich sand and clay, unlike the gravel of Sauternes and Bommes. The soils drain fast but the limestone keeps vines supplied in drought, and the wines tend to be a touch lighter, fresher and more citrus-driven, with a mineral, almost saline finish. Climens, made from 100% Sémillon and farmed biodynamically since 2010, is the benchmark, and the estate's ability to make elegant wine even in hot years shows what limestone brings.

The village is also known for its stone walls: many vineyards are enclosed by walls of local limestone, a reminder that the Barsac quarries supplied building stone for Bordeaux.
fr-barsac.terroir: Flat to gently rolling limestone plateau at 10 to 20 m altitude, with shallow red sand (*sables rouges*) over fissured limestone; lower-lying vineyards towards the Garonne have more alluvium.
fr-barsac.nerd_note: Château Coutet's Cuvée Madame, made only in exceptional years from a few of the oldest parcels and the richest tries, is one of the rarest wines of the Sauternais.

fr-batard-montrachet.name: Bâtard-Montrachet
fr-batard-montrachet.summary: Bâtard-Montrachet, about 11.9 ha directly below Le Montrachet and divided between Puligny and Chassagne, is the richest and most opulent of the Montrachet family: broad, honeyed and powerful, with more weight than Chevalier and less finesse than Montrachet. Its name means bastard, and folklore spins tales of a medieval knight's illegitimate son, though it more likely refers to a lesser piece of land. Leflaive, Ramonet, Pierre-Yves Colin-Morey, Jean-Noël Gagnard, Bernard Morey and the Hospices de Beaune make it.
fr-batard-montrachet.terroir: Deeper brown soils with more clay on the lower slope below the Route des Grands Crus, at 240 to 255 m.
fr-batard-montrachet.nerd_note: Bâtard is the largest of the five Montrachet grand crus.

fr-bearn.name: Béarn
fr-bearn.grapes: Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Fer Servadou; Gros Manseng, Petit Manseng, Raffiat de Moncade, Petit Courbu
fr-bearn.summary: Béarn covers scattered vineyards in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques around Jurançon, Madiran and Salies-de-Béarn, mostly for rosés and reds built on Tannat and the Cabernets. Béarn-Bellocq is a small sub-zone around the village of Bellocq, where the cooperative makes most of the wine. The appellation is a useful outlet for red grapes in an area best known for white Jurançon.
fr-bearn.terroir: Clay-limestone and pebbles in the Gave valleys.
fr-bearn.nerd_note: Raffiat de Moncade, a white grape found almost only here, is named after the Moncade tower in Orthez.

fr-beaujolais.name: Beaujolais
fr-beaujolais.summary: Beaujolais AOC is the regional appellation, covering about 40,000 ha delimited (though far less is planted today) across 88 communes, mostly in the south of the region on limestone and clay around the golden-stone villages of the Pierres Dorées. It is the source of most Beaujolais Nouveau, released on the third Thursday of November, a few weeks after harvest, and of light, fruity reds for drinking within a year or two. Beaujolais blanc from Chardonnay is a growing niche. Some 38 communes in the north may add their name to Beaujolais or sell as Beaujolais-Villages.
fr-beaujolais.terroir: Limestone, clay and sandstone in the south (Pierres Dorées), granite in the north.
fr-beaujolais.nerd_note: Jean-Paul Brun of Domaine des Terres Dorées makes his reds with indigenous yeasts and destemming, Burgundy-style, rather than carbonic maceration, and was sometimes refused the appellation in tastings for being atypical.

fr-beaujolais-villages.name: Beaujolais-Villages
fr-beaujolais-villages.summary: Beaujolais-Villages covers 38 communes in the northern hills of the region, between and around the ten crus. On granite and schist soils, its Gamay is deeper and more structured than plain Beaujolais, though still fresh and fruity, and it can be made as Nouveau. Villages such as Lantignié, Quincié and Lancié are well known to fans for their quality.
fr-beaujolais-villages.terroir: Granite and schist slopes of the northern Beaujolais at 200 to 450 m.
fr-beaujolais-villages.nerd_note: Many cru growers bottle their younger vines as Beaujolais-Villages, which makes it one of the best bargains in French red wine.

fr-beaumes-de-venise.name: Beaumes de Venise
fr-beaumes-de-venise.summary: Beaumes de Venise became a cru for its red wines in 2005, separate from the older Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise. Its 738 ha (2025) of Grenache and Syrah grow at the southern foot of the Dentelles de Montmirail on unusually diverse soils, and the reds are fresh and spicy with a firm line. The name refers to the caves (baumes) in the hillside and to the Comtat Venaissin, the papal territory.
fr-beaumes-de-venise.terroir: Triassic gypsum and marl, Jurassic limestone and sandy soils, sometimes within a single estate; vineyards up to 400 m.
fr-beaumes-de-venise.nerd_note: Venise has nothing to do with Venice: it derives from the Comtat Venaissin.

fr-beaune.name: Beaune
fr-beaune.summary:
Beaune is both Burgundy's wine capital and one of its largest village appellations, and it has more premier crus by area than any other commune: about 320 ha of the roughly 410 ha in production are premier cru, and there are no grand crus. Much of the slope is owned by the big négociants of the town, and their premier crus are flagship wines: Bouchard Père et Fils's Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus (in Les Grèves), Louis Jadot's Clos des Ursules (in Les Vignes Franches) and Joseph Drouhin's Clos des Mouches.

Beaune's reds are medium-bodied, fragrant and red-fruited, softer and earlier-maturing than Côte de Nuits wines. The best premier crus run in a continuous band along the slope: Les Marconnets and Clos du Roi near Savigny, Les Bressandes, Les Grèves, Les Teurons and Les Cents Vignes in the middle, and Les Avaux, Clos des Mouches and Les Vignes Franches to the south toward Pommard. Some climats, notably Clos des Mouches and Les Aigrots, also make excellent whites.
fr-beaune.terroir: Limestone with marl and gravel; the middle slope has stony soils (Les Grèves takes its name from gravel), while the southern end has more clay.
fr-beaune.nerd_note: Bouchard Père et Fils's L'Enfant Jésus, a 4 ha parcel in Les Grèves once owned by Carmelite nuns, takes its name from the order's devotion to the Infant Jesus of Beaune.

fr-bellet.name: Bellet
fr-bellet.grapes: Vermentino (Rolle), Chardonnay; Braquet, Folle Noire, Grenache, Cinsault
fr-bellet.summary: Bellet is a tiny appellation in the hills above Nice, one of the few vineyards inside a large French city. Only a few dozen hectares survive among the villas. It uses grapes found almost nowhere else in France: Braquet (Brachetto) and Folle Noire (Fuella) for reds and rosés, and Rolle (Vermentino) for whites. The whites are fresh and aromatic. Château de Bellet, Château de Crémat and Clos Saint-Vincent are the main producers.
fr-bellet.terroir: Steep terraces of poudingue (conglomerate) and sand above the Var river, at 200 to 400 m.
fr-bellet.nerd_note: Bellet's history reflects that Nice was part of the Kingdom of Sardinia until 1860, which explains its Italian grapes.

fr-bergerac.name: Bergerac
fr-bergerac.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Fer Servadou, Mérille; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle, Ondenc, Chenin Blanc
fr-bergerac.summary: Bergerac is the regional appellation for the vineyards around the town of Bergerac on the Dordogne, east of Bordeaux. It uses Bordeaux grapes on similar soils, which long made it a cheaper Bordeaux substitute. Reds are Merlot-led and supple; Bergerac Sec whites are fresh Sauvignon and Sémillon; rosés are growing. A small number of growers showed that Bergerac can be much more: Luc de Conti at Château Tour des Gendres, Château de Tiregand in Pécharmant, and Claudie and Bruno Bilancini at Tirecul la Gravière.
fr-bergerac.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes and molasse on both banks of the Dordogne, river gravels, and sandy terraces.
fr-bergerac.nerd_note: Bergerac's Protestant growers exported their wine to Holland after the 1685 revocation of the Edict of Nantes, and Dutch buyers favoured them over Bordeaux for a century.

fr-bienvenues-batard-montrachet.name: Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet
fr-bienvenues-batard-montrachet.summary: Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet, about 3.7 ha in the northeast corner of Bâtard-Montrachet entirely in Puligny, gives a slightly lighter, more elegant and earlier-approachable wine than Bâtard. The name, 'welcome', may refer to a gift of land. Domaine Leflaive is the largest owner (about 1.15 ha), followed by Ramonet, Paul Pernot, Faiveley and Vincent Girardin.
fr-bienvenues-batard-montrachet.terroir: Brown limestone soil at the lowest, most northerly part of the Bâtard slope.
fr-bienvenues-batard-montrachet.nerd_note: Wine from Bienvenues may legally be sold as Bâtard-Montrachet.

fr-blagny.name: Blagny
fr-blagny.summary: Blagny is a hamlet high on the hill between Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet, and its appellation is one of Burgundy's oddities: the Blagny AOC is for red wine only. Its whites, from the same slopes, are sold as Meursault premier cru Blagny or Puligny-Montrachet premier cru. The reds are firm, rustic and earthy, and only a handful of growers still make them, as the whites are more profitable.
fr-blagny.terroir: Marl and limestone at about 350 m, high above Meursault and Puligny, cooler than the slope below.
fr-blagny.nerd_note: The hamlet once belonged to the Cistercians of Maizières, whose wine house is now owned by Domaine Martelet de Cherisey.

fr-blaye.name: Blaye
fr-blaye.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Petit Verdot
fr-blaye.summary: Blaye AOC is a stricter red appellation for the Blayais, with lower yields, higher planting density and longer ageing than Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux. It is used by a minority of ambitious estates for their top cuvées.
fr-blaye.terroir: Clay-limestone hills around the citadel of Blaye.
fr-blaye.nerd_note: Blaye AOC demands denser planting and lower yields than Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux, so only a handful of estates claim it, usually for their top cuvée.

fr-bonnes-mares.name: Bonnes-Mares
fr-bonnes-mares.summary:
Bonnes-Mares, about 15 ha, straddles the Morey-Chambolle border, with most of it (about 13.5 ha) in Chambolle-Musigny. Its name may come from marer, to plough, or from the 'good mothers', the nuns of Tart who owned it. A diagonal line divides it: the northern terres rouges on iron-rich clay give firm, structured wine; the southern terres blanches on white marl give a more aromatic, mineral style. Most growers blend both.

Bonnes-Mares is the most powerful wine of Chambolle, darker and more tannic than Musigny, and ages for decades. Comte Georges de Vogüé (2.7 ha), Georges Roumier, Domaine Dujac, Robert Groffier, Drouhin-Laroze and Fougeray de Beauclair make it.
fr-bonnes-mares.terroir: Two soils: red clay over limestone in the north (terres rouges) and white Bathonian marl in the south (terres blanches).
fr-bonnes-mares.nerd_note: The Morey part (about 1.5 ha) is mostly owned by Clos de Tart, which bottles a Morey Bonnes-Mares.

fr-bonnezeaux.name: Bonnezeaux
fr-bonnezeaux.summary: Bonnezeaux is a small appellation on three steep schist hillsides above the Layon in the commune of Thouarcé, and with Quarts de Chaume it is the best sweet-wine site of the Layon. The wines are rich, honeyed and long-lived. Château de Fesles, Domaine de Petit Val and Mark Angeli (La Ferme de la Sansonnière) are names to know.
fr-bonnezeaux.terroir: South-facing schist hillsides with quartz, warm and dry.
fr-bonnezeaux.nerd_note: Mark Angeli's Bonnezeaux, made without chaptalisation and with long ageing, helped inspire the natural wine scene in Anjou.

fr-bordeaux.name: Bordeaux
fr-bordeaux.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Petit Verdot, Carmenère, plus small shares of Marselan, Touriga Nacional, Castets, Arinarnoa; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle, Colombard, Ugni Blanc, Alvarinho, Liliorila
fr-bordeaux.summary:
Bordeaux AOC is the regional appellation that can be used anywhere in the Gironde's delimited vineyard, and it is where the region's crisis has been most visible. In good times it supplied supermarket claret, rosé and dry white to the world; when demand for red Bordeaux collapsed after 2018, prices for bulk Bordeaux fell below production costs and much of the land pulled up in 2023 to 2026 was regional AOC vineyard.

The appellation still makes excellent everyday wine. Juicy Merlot-based reds, crisp Sauvignon whites and a growing amount of rosé come from estates and cooperatives across the Entre-Deux-Mers, Blaye and the Libournais. Many top châteaux sell white wines as Bordeaux because their communal AOCs are red-only (Pavillon Blanc de Château Margaux, Aile d'Argent from Mouton). Bordeaux Clairet, a deep pink wine with a short maceration, keeps alive the colour of the medieval claret that England once drank.

In 2019 the INAO approved six climate-adaptation varieties for Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur: the reds Arinarnoa, Castets, Marselan and Touriga Nacional and the whites Alvarinho and Liliorila, limited to 5% of a property's vineyard and 10% of a blend.
fr-bordeaux.terroir: Any of the region's soils, though most regional AOC wine comes from the clay-limestone and sandy-gravel soils of the Entre-Deux-Mers and the outer Libournais.
fr-bordeaux.nerd_note: Castets is a near-extinct Gironde red variety rediscovered in the 2000s; its inclusion among the 2019 climate varieties is a rare case of an old local grape returning through climate policy.

fr-bordeaux-haut-benauge.name: Bordeaux Haut-Benauge
fr-bordeaux-haut-benauge.summary: Bordeaux Haut-Benauge is a seldom-used name, attached to AOC Bordeaux, for white wines from the Haut-Benauge, a hilly area in the south of the Entre-Deux-Mers around the castle of Benauge. The wines, dry to medium-sweet, must come from Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle; most growers in the zone prefer to sell under the better-known Entre-deux-Mers-Haut-Benauge name for dry wine.
fr-bordeaux-haut-benauge.terroir: Clay-limestone hills, among the highest in the Entre-Deux-Mers.
fr-bordeaux-haut-benauge.nerd_note: The medieval Château de Benauge, a stronghold of the counts of Benauge, still stands over the vineyards that give the appellation its name.

fr-bordeaux-superieur.name: Bordeaux Supérieur
fr-bordeaux-superieur.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Petit Verdot, Carmenère
fr-bordeaux-superieur.summary: Bordeaux Supérieur covers the same area as Bordeaux with stricter rules: lower yields, higher minimum alcohol, denser plantings, and red wines aged until at least the June after the harvest. It is the home of many serious family estates outside the famous districts, such as Château Reignac, Château Penin and Château de Parenchère, and its best wines outperform many cheaper communal labels. Whites under the name must be medium-sweet; Y d'Yquem is sold as Bordeaux (dry white), not Supérieur.
fr-bordeaux-superieur.terroir: Mostly clay-limestone and gravel of the Entre-Deux-Mers and the outer Libournais.
fr-bordeaux-superieur.nerd_note: Bordeaux Supérieur was briefly the home of 'Bordeaux garage' wines in the 2000s, when ambitious growers made tiny, extracted cuvées that challenged the hierarchy.

fr-bourgogne.name: Bourgogne
fr-bourgogne.grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay; also Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, César (Yonne), Gamay in the Beaujolais crus
fr-bourgogne.summary:
Bourgogne is the regional appellation of Burgundy, covering about 40,000 ha across 264 communes in four departments, from the Yonne to the Beaujolais crus. Red Bourgogne is mostly Pinot Noir and white mostly Chardonnay. Many good domaines make their Bourgogne from village-quality vines just below the appellation line, which makes it one of the best introductions to their style.

Fourteen named zones (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) may follow the name: Côte d'Or (created 2017), Hautes Côtes de Nuits, Hautes Côtes de Beaune, Côte Chalonnaise, Côtes du Couchois, Chitry, Coulanges-la-Vineuse, Côtes d'Auxerre, Épineuil, Tonnerre, Côte Saint-Jacques, La Chapelle Notre-Dame, Le Chapitre and Montrecul. Since 2011 the crus of Beaujolais have also been allowed to declare Pinot Noir and Gamay as Bourgogne rouge, a controversial rule.
fr-bourgogne.terroir: From Kimmeridgian marl in the Yonne to the limestones of the Côte d'Or and the granite of the Beaujolais crus.
fr-bourgogne.nerd_note: Bourgogne Côte d'Or, created in 2017, can be used only for wines from the 40 communes of the Côte d'Or slope, letting growers distinguish their regional wine from that of the wider region.

fr-bourgogne-aligote.name: Bourgogne aligoté
fr-bourgogne-aligote.grapes: Aligoté (up to 15% Chardonnay historically, now 100% Aligoté)
fr-bourgogne-aligote.summary: Bourgogne Aligoté is the regional appellation for Aligoté, Burgundy's second white grape, a natural cross of Pinot and Gouais Blanc. Long dismissed as a sharp wine to mix with crème de cassis (the kir, named after Canon Félix Kir, mayor of Dijon), it is now taken seriously by growers who plant it on good slopes and keep old vines: Ponsot, d'Auvenay, de Villaine, Sylvain Pataille and Roulot. A movement called Les Aligoteurs promotes it.
fr-bourgogne-aligote.terroir: Grown across Burgundy, best on limestone slopes of the Côte d'Or and Hautes-Côtes.
producers: Domaine A. et P. de Villaine
fr-bourgogne-aligote.nerd_note: The kir was popularised by Canon Kir after the Second World War; the original mix used Bourgogne Aligoté and crème de cassis from Dijon.

fr-bourgogne-chitry.name: Bourgogne Chitry
fr-bourgogne-chitry.summary: Bourgogne Chitry, next to Chablis, gives mostly crisp Chardonnay and some Pinot Noir from the village of Chitry-le-Fort, with its fortified church. Chitry is one of the Yonne villages that sell as both Chablis and Bourgogne, depending on where each parcel lies. The Grand Auxerrois was once one of France's largest vineyards, shipping wine to Paris down the Yonne; phylloxera and the railways shrank it to a few hundred hectares around Chablis.

fr-bourgogne-cote-chalonnaise.name: Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise
fr-bourgogne-cote-chalonnaise.summary: Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise is the regional Bourgogne zone for the 44 communes of the Côte Chalonnaise, used for wines from outside the village appellations or from young vines. It is light, fresh and easy, often excellent value from good village growers.
fr-bourgogne-cote-chalonnaise.terroir: Limestone and marl hills west of Chalon-sur-Saône.
producers: Domaine A. et P. de Villaine

fr-bourgogne-cote-d-or.name: Bourgogne Côte d'Or
fr-bourgogne-cote-d-or.summary: Bourgogne Côte d'Or is a regional appellation created in 2017 for red Pinot Noir and white Chardonnay grown within the Côte d'Or communes of the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune. It lets growers distinguish generic Bourgogne from the famous slope from wine made elsewhere in the region, and often offers village-like quality at a regional price.
fr-bourgogne-cote-d-or.terroir: Limestone and marl of the Côte d'Or escarpment and the foot of its slopes.

fr-bourgogne-cote-saint-jacques.name: Bourgogne Côte Saint-Jacques
fr-bourgogne-cote-saint-jacques.summary: Bourgogne Côte Saint-Jacques is a tiny slope above Joigny on the Yonne, famous for its pale 'vin gris' from Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris, and for reds. Joigny's vineyard is the northernmost of Burgundy and was revived in the 1970s.
fr-bourgogne-cote-saint-jacques.terroir: Limestone on a south-facing slope above the town.

fr-bourgogne-cotes-d-auxerre.name: Bourgogne Côtes d'Auxerre
fr-bourgogne-cotes-d-auxerre.summary: Bourgogne Côtes d'Auxerre covers hillsides around Auxerre, Vaux, Champs-sur-Yonne, Augy, Quenne and Saint-Bris in the Yonne, giving fresh Chardonnay and light, fragrant Pinot Noir. The Goisot family of Saint-Bris is the reference grower.
fr-bourgogne-cotes-d-auxerre.terroir: Kimmeridgian limestone and marl, as in Chablis, on south-facing slopes above the Yonne.
fr-bourgogne-cotes-d-auxerre.nerd_note: Auxerre's vineyards supplied Paris by river for centuries before the railway brought cheaper southern wine and phylloxera finished the trade.

fr-bourgogne-cotes-du-couchois.name: Bourgogne Côtes du Couchois
fr-bourgogne-cotes-du-couchois.summary: The Côtes du Couchois is a small, red-only Bourgogne zone around Couches, west of the Maranges, on granite and sandstone hills that are unusual for Burgundy. Light, peppery reds are its speciality.
fr-bourgogne-cotes-du-couchois.terroir: Triassic sandstone, granite and marl on hills around Couches.

fr-bourgogne-coulanges-la-vineuse.name: Bourgogne Coulanges-la-Vineuse
fr-bourgogne-coulanges-la-vineuse.summary: Bourgogne Coulanges-la-Vineuse, south of Auxerre, is known above all for light, cherry-scented Pinot Noir; its 'vineuse' name shows how central wine was to the village. Coulanges was once famous for its 'vin de Coulanges', shipped to Paris, and it remains the Yonne's red-wine village. The Grand Auxerrois was once one of France's largest vineyards, shipping wine to Paris down the Yonne; phylloxera and the railways shrank it to a few hundred hectares around Chablis.
fr-bourgogne-coulanges-la-vineuse.terroir: Limestone and marl on gentle slopes.

fr-bourgogne-epineuil.name: Bourgogne Epineuil
fr-bourgogne-epineuil.summary: Bourgogne Épineuil, near Tonnerre, is a small red and rosé zone for Pinot Noir, revived after phylloxera and the First World War had almost wiped it out. The Grand Auxerrois was once one of France's largest vineyards, shipping wine to Paris down the Yonne; phylloxera and the railways shrank it to a few hundred hectares around Chablis.
fr-bourgogne-epineuil.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl on south-facing slopes of the Armançon valley.

fr-bourgogne-hautes-cotes-de-beaune.name: Bourgogne Hautes Côtes de Beaune
fr-bourgogne-hautes-cotes-de-beaune.summary: The Hautes-Côtes de Beaune is the hill country behind the Côte de Beaune, from Échevronne to the Couchois, with vineyards at 300 to 450 m among woods and pastures. Like its Nuits counterpart it is a named zone of the Bourgogne AOC. Its fresh reds and crisp whites have become far more consistent with warmer summers, and the village of La Rochepot with its castle is the area's landmark.
fr-bourgogne-hautes-cotes-de-beaune.terroir: Limestone and marl plateaus and valleys; cooler and windier than the côte below.
fr-bourgogne-hautes-cotes-de-beaune.nerd_note: Many Côte d'Or domaines source Aligoté and Bourgogne blanc from the Hautes-Côtes.

fr-bourgogne-hautes-cotes-de-nuits.name: Bourgogne Hautes Côtes de Nuits
fr-bourgogne-hautes-cotes-de-nuits.summary: The Hautes-Côtes de Nuits is the high country behind the Côte de Nuits: a plateau of combes, woods and hamlets at 300 to 450 m, where vines alternate with blackcurrant fields for crème de cassis. It is a named zone (dénomination géographique) of the Bourgogne AOC, not an AOC of its own. Long considered too cold for good ripening, it has become one of the winners of climate change: its Pinot Noir and Chardonnay are fresh, aromatic and increasingly sought out, and several Côte d'Or domaines have bought land here.
fr-bourgogne-hautes-cotes-de-nuits.terroir: Limestone and marl plateaus and combes at altitude; later ripening and cooler nights than the main slope.
fr-bourgogne-hautes-cotes-de-nuits.nerd_note: The Hautes-Côtes were replanted after the 1950s, encouraged by the founding of the Caves des Hautes-Côtes co-operative in 1968.

fr-bourgogne-la-chapelle-notre-dame.name: Bourgogne La Chapelle Notre-Dame
fr-bourgogne-la-chapelle-notre-dame.summary: Bourgogne La Chapelle Notre-Dame is a tiny regional name around a chapel at Serrigny in Ladoix, for red, white and rosé. It is one of several 'dénominations géographiques complémentaires' that let regional Bourgogne name a small area with its own rules, and one of the smallest of them.
fr-bourgogne-la-chapelle-notre-dame.terroir: Limestone and marl at the foot of the Corton hill.

fr-bourgogne-le-chapitre.name: Bourgogne Le Chapitre
fr-bourgogne-le-chapitre.summary: Bourgogne Le Chapitre is a small walled vineyard at Chenôve, south of Dijon, said to have belonged to the canons (the cathedral chapter) of Autun, giving red and white Bourgogne.
fr-bourgogne-le-chapitre.terroir: Limestone slope at the northern tip of the Côte de Nuits.

fr-bourgogne-montrecul.name: Bourgogne Montrecul
fr-bourgogne-montrecul.summary: Bourgogne Montrecul (also written Montre-Cul) is one of the last vineyards of Dijon, a tiny slope whose cheeky name, roughly 'show your backside', is said to refer to its steepness. Dijon once had extensive vineyards of its own; Montrecul is a survivor of that urban wine culture.
fr-bourgogne-montrecul.terroir: Limestone on the edge of the city.

fr-bourgogne-mousseux.name: Bourgogne mousseux
fr-bourgogne-mousseux.summary: Bourgogne mousseux is now reserved for sparkling red Burgundy, a nineteenth-century speciality once popular in Britain and America. Since Crémant de Bourgogne was created in 1975, white and rosé sparkling wines go under that name instead, leaving Bourgogne mousseux as a tiny, almost forgotten red style.
fr-bourgogne-mousseux.nerd_note: Sparkling red Burgundy was a Victorian fashion; a few houses still make it for curiosity.

fr-bourgogne-passe-tout-grains.name: Bourgogne Passe-tout-grains
fr-bourgogne-passe-tout-grains.grapes: Gamay with at least 30% Pinot Noir
fr-bourgogne-passe-tout-grains.summary: Bourgogne Passe-tout-grains is Burgundy's traditional field blend of Pinot Noir and Gamay, co-fermented, with at least 30 percent Pinot Noir and 15 percent Gamay. Once the growers' everyday red, it has been shrinking as Coteaux Bourguignons replaced it, but a few domaines such as Lafarge, Rossignol and Henri Jayer's heirs keep it as a light, joyful, cherry-fruited wine.
fr-bourgogne-passe-tout-grains.terroir: Grown across Burgundy, mostly on plain and plateau sites.
fr-bourgogne-passe-tout-grains.nerd_note: Its name means 'all grapes go in', a reminder that most old Burgundian vineyards were mixed plantings.

fr-bourgogne-tonnerre.name: Bourgogne Tonnerre
fr-bourgogne-tonnerre.summary: Bourgogne Tonnerre, east of Chablis, is a white-only regional name (since 2006) for Chardonnay from the slopes around Tonnerre, Épineuil and Dannemoine, giving crisp, mineral wines in the Chablis mould. It is one of several 'dénominations géographiques complémentaires' that let regional Bourgogne name a smaller area with its own rules. The Grand Auxerrois was once one of France's largest vineyards, shipping wine to Paris down the Yonne; phylloxera and the railways shrank it to a few hundred hectares around Chablis.
fr-bourgogne-tonnerre.terroir: Kimmeridgian and Portlandian limestone and marl.

fr-bourgueil.name: Bourgueil
fr-bourgueil.grapes: Cabernet Franc, up to 10% Cabernet Sauvignon
fr-bourgueil.summary: Bourgueil faces Chinon across the Loire on the north bank, and its Cabernet Franc is a touch firmer and more tannic, especially from the tuffeau slopes. The Benedictine abbey founded at Bourgueil in 990 is traditionally credited with bringing Cabernet Franc (Breton) to the area. Pierre-Jacques Druet, Domaine de la Butte (Jacky Blot), Catherine and Pierre Breton and Yannick Amirault are leading producers.
fr-bourgueil.terroir: Sand and gravel terraces by the Loire give lighter wines; clay-limestone and tuffeau on the slopes give structure.
fr-bourgueil.nerd_note: The local name Breton for Cabernet Franc may come from Abbot Baudry of Bourgueil, who is said to have brought it from Brittany via the Nantes trade, but the evidence is thin.

fr-boutenac.name: Corbières-Boutenac
fr-boutenac.summary: Corbières-Boutenac is the first cru of Corbières, created in 2005, covering ten communes around Boutenac in the north-east. Its rules give old Carignan a leading role in the blend, a deliberate statement that this once-despised grape can make great wine. The reds are deep and long-lived.
fr-boutenac.terroir: Sandstone, clay-limestone and gravel on a natural basin around the Pinada hills.
fr-boutenac.nerd_note: Boutenac was the first part of Corbières promoted to its own appellation, a model for the cru tier the Languedoc has built since.

fr-bouzeron.name: Bouzeron
fr-bouzeron.summary: Bouzeron is the only village appellation in Burgundy dedicated to Aligoté, the region's other white grape. Promoted from Bourgogne Aligoté Bouzeron in 1997, it requires the golden-berried Aligoté doré rather than the more productive green Aligoté vert. The wines are fresher and more floral than Chardonnay, with lemon, white flowers and a salty bite, and age better than most people expect. Domaine A. et P. de Villaine, founded by Aubert de Villaine of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti in 1973 and now run by his nephew Pierre de Benoist, is the appellation's ambassador.
fr-bouzeron.terroir: Limestone and marl slopes at 270 to 350 m in a narrow valley just north of Rully.
producers: Domaine A. et P. de Villaine
fr-bouzeron.nerd_note: Bouzeron's red and Chardonnay wines are sold as Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise; only Aligoté may carry the village name.

fr-brouilly.name: Brouilly
fr-brouilly.summary: Brouilly is the largest and southernmost cru, encircling Mont Brouilly across six communes (Odenas, Saint-Lager, Cercié, Charentay, Quincié and Saint-Étienne-la-Varenne). Its wines are generous, fruity and approachable, the most typical of easy-drinking cru Beaujolais, with Pierreux and Les Brouilly among its best lieux-dits. Every September the Fête des Vins de Brouilly ends with a pilgrimage to the hilltop chapel.
fr-brouilly.terroir: Pink granite, sand and alluvial soils on the lower slopes and plains around Mont Brouilly.
fr-brouilly.nerd_note: Château de la Chaize, built from 1676 for the brother of Louis XIV's confessor Père La Chaize, was long the largest single estate in Brouilly.

fr-brulhois.name: Brulhois
fr-brulhois.grapes: Tannat, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec, Fer Servadou
fr-brulhois.summary: A small area on both banks of the Garonne around Agen, known for its 'vin noir', a dark, tannic red from Tannat blended with Bordeaux grapes. Most wine comes from the Vignerons du Brulhois cooperative at Donzac. It was promoted from VDQS to AOC in 2011.
fr-brulhois.terroir: Gravel and clay terraces along the Garonne.
fr-brulhois.nerd_note: Brulhois markets its 'vin noir' as a tribute to the dark wines that the Haut-Pays sent to England in the Middle Ages.

fr-bugey.name: Bugey
fr-bugey.grapes: Gamay, Poulsard, Pinot Noir, Mondeuse; Chardonnay, Jacquère, Altesse
fr-bugey.summary: Bugey became an AOC in 2009 after decades as a VDQS. It makes still whites (at least half Chardonnay), reds and rosés, traditional-method sparkling, and three named crus. Bugey Cerdon is a pink, off-dry ancestral-method sparkler from Gamay and Poulsard, with strawberry and raspberry fruit and only about 8 percent alcohol: the fermentation starts in tank and finishes in bottle, without added sugar. Bugey Manicle (Chardonnay white or Pinot Noir red) and Bugey Montagnieu (Mondeuse red or Altesse-based sparkling) are smaller crus.
fr-bugey.terroir: Limestone scree and marl in valleys of the southern Jura massif; Cerdon in the Ain valley in the north, Montagnieu and Manicle along the Rhône in the south.
fr-bugey.nerd_note: Raphaël Bartucci's Cerdon was one of the first natural wines from Bugey to reach Paris wine bars in the early 2000s.

fr-bugey-cerdon.name: Bugey Cerdon
fr-bugey-cerdon.summary: Bugey Cerdon is a pink, off-dry, low-alcohol sparkling wine made by the ancestral method from Gamay and Poulsard in the Cerdon valley and nine other communes. Fermentation stops partway in tank (by chilling and filtering) and finishes in bottle, so the bubbles and sweetness come only from the grapes. It is fresh, fruity and about 8 percent alcohol.
fr-bugey-cerdon.terroir: Limestone scree and marl in the Ain valley.

fr-bugey-manicle.name: Bugey Manicle
fr-bugey-manicle.summary: A steep, south-facing limestone lieu-dit at Cheignieu-la-Balme and Pugieu near Belley, about 24 ha delimited, reserved for Chardonnay whites and Pinot Noir reds. It is the most Burgundian of Bugey's crus, giving taut, mineral whites and light, fragrant reds.

fr-bugey-montagnieu.name: Bugey Montagnieu
fr-bugey-montagnieu.summary: Steep limestone slopes above the Rhône at Montagnieu, Briord and Seillonnaz, about 124 ha delimited. The cru is known for dark, peppery Mondeuse reds and for traditional-method sparkling wine based on Altesse, Chardonnay and Mondeuse; Altesse whites are sold as Roussette du Bugey Montagnieu.

fr-buzet.name: Buzet
fr-buzet.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
fr-buzet.summary: Buzet, in the Lot-et-Garonne between the Garonne and the Landes forest, makes Bordeaux-style reds. The cooperative Vignerons de Buzet, founded in 1953, makes most of the wine and has its own cooperage, one of the first French cooperatives to do so.
fr-buzet.terroir: Gravel terraces, clay-limestone hills and sand.
fr-buzet.nerd_note: Buzet was called Côtes de Buzet until 1986.

fr-cabardes.name: Cabardès
fr-cabardes.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Grenache, Syrah, Fer Servadou
fr-cabardes.summary: Cabardès, north of Carcassonne, is unique in France: it is the meeting point of the Atlantic and Mediterranean climates, and its rules require a blend of Bordeaux grapes (at least 40% of Merlot, Cabernets, Malbec) and Mediterranean grapes (at least 40% of Grenache, Syrah). The wines are fresh and balanced. Château de Pennautier, owned by the Lorgeril family since 1620, is the reference.
fr-cabardes.terroir: Limestone, schist and gravel on the southern slopes of the Montagne Noire.
fr-cabardes.nerd_note: Cabardès's blending rule, half Atlantic and half Mediterranean grapes, makes it the only French AOC that requires both families.

fr-cabernet-d-anjou.name: Cabernet d'Anjou
fr-cabernet-d-anjou.summary: Cabernet d'Anjou is a medium-sweet rosé made from the two Cabernets, richer and fuller than Rosé d'Anjou, and one of the biggest-selling wines of the Loire. Good examples age surprisingly well; old Cabernet d'Anjou can develop notes of dried fruit and tea.
fr-cabernet-d-anjou.nerd_note: Many Anjou rosés are made by direct pressing and stopping fermentation by chilling, which keeps the natural sweetness.

fr-cabernet-de-saumur.name: Cabernet de Saumur
fr-cabernet-de-saumur.summary: A small appellation for dry or off-dry rosé from Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon grown on the Saumur tuffeau. It is drier and lighter than Cabernet d'Anjou. Volumes are small and the wine is rarely seen outside the region.
fr-cabernet-de-saumur.nerd_note: Cabernet de Saumur is drier and lighter than Cabernet d'Anjou.

fr-cadillac.name: Cadillac
fr-cadillac.summary: Cadillac AOC is for sweet white wine from 22 communes on the right bank of the Garonne around the walled town of Cadillac. Since 2008 the name has also been used for the separate red appellation Cadillac Côtes de Bordeaux, which confuses everyone. The sweet wines, from botrytised or late-picked Sémillon, are soft and honeyed and usually drunk within 10 years. The town's Château des Ducs d'Épernon, built in the 1600s, houses an interpretation of the area's wine heritage.
fr-cadillac.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes facing the river, warmer than the Sauternais but with less consistent botrytis.
fr-cadillac.nerd_note: The town's Château des Ducs d'Épernon, begun in 1599 for the Duc d'Épernon, served as a women's prison from the nineteenth century until the 1950s before becoming a monument open to visitors.

fr-cahors.name: Cahors
fr-cahors.grapes: Malbec (Côt, Auxerrois) at least 70%, Merlot, Tannat
fr-cahors.summary:
Cahors is the homeland of Malbec, here called Côt or Auxerrois. Its 'black wine' was famous in the Middle Ages: the grapes' dark colour, sometimes intensified by heating part of the must, gave wines so deep that they were used to colour paler Bordeaux. English merchants shipped it through Bordeaux, and the Russian Orthodox Church adopted it as communion wine. The vineyard almost disappeared after phylloxera and the February 1956 frost; replanted from the 1960s, Cahors became AOC in 1971.

Its rules require at least 70% Malbec, completed with Merlot and Tannat, and many top wines are pure Malbec. Two terroirs give two styles: the gravel and clay terraces along the Lot make supple, fruity wines; the limestone causse plateau, at about 300 m, gives tight, mineral, long-lived wines. The success of Argentine Malbec from the 1990s prompted Cahors to rebrand itself as the 'birthplace of Malbec', and a new generation, alongside established estates such as Château du Cèdre, Clos Triguedina and Château Lagrézette, has made fresher, less extracted wines.
fr-cahors.terroir: The meandering Lot valley: three alluvial terraces of gravel and clay, and the causse, a Jurassic limestone plateau with red clay (*terres rouges*) and siderolithic deposits.
fr-cahors.nerd_note: Clos Triguedina's 'The New Black Wine' revives the old technique of heating the grapes before fermentation to make an inky, concentrated wine.

fr-cairanne.name: Cairanne
fr-cairanne.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre; whites from Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne
fr-cairanne.summary: Cairanne, on a hill north of Rasteau, was promoted from Côtes du Rhône Villages to cru in 2015 after a long campaign by its growers. With 886 ha (2025), it makes sumptuous, spicy reds and a small amount of rich white. Rosé is not allowed under the cru. Marcel Richaud, Oratoire Saint-Martin and the Cave de Cairanne are its leading producers.
fr-cairanne.terroir: Ancient terraces with pebbles, red clay and limestone (Garrigues des Plateaux), and sandy-clay soils on the slopes.
fr-cairanne.nerd_note: Marcel Richaud pioneered estate bottling in Cairanne in the 1970s and campaigned for decades for its promotion.

fr-canon-fronsac.name: Canon-Fronsac
fr-canon-fronsac.summary: Canon-Fronsac is a small enclave within Fronsac on the steepest limestone slopes in Fronsac and Saint-Michel-de-Fronsac, facing south over the Dordogne. Its wines are deeper and more structured than Fronsac, often compared to the côtes of Saint-Émilion. Château Canon de Brem, Moulin Pey-Labrie and Vrai Canon Bouché are the references.
fr-canon-fronsac.terroir: Steep south-facing limestone slopes with thin clay soils over the calcaire à astéries.
fr-canon-fronsac.nerd_note: In the nineteenth century the wines of 'Canon' hill were shipped and priced separately from other Fronsac wines, which is how a village slope became an appellation.

fr-cassis.name: Cassis
fr-cassis.grapes: Marsanne, Clairette, Ugni Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Bourboulenc; Grenache, Cinsault, Mourvèdre
fr-cassis.summary: Cassis, a small fishing town east of Marseille, was one of the first French AOCs (1936) and is one of the few in Provence known for white wine. Its vines grow on terraces between the sea and Cap Canaille, among the highest sea cliffs in Europe. The whites, from Marsanne and Clairette, are fresh and saline, the classic partner for bouillabaisse. Urban growth and land prices put constant pressure on its small vineyard of around 200 ha. Clos Sainte-Magdeleine, on a promontory above the sea, Domaine du Bagnol and Clos Val Bruyère are references.
fr-cassis.terroir: Limestone and marl terraces between the sea and the Cap Canaille cliffs.
fr-cassis.nerd_note: The Provençal poet Frédéric Mistral praised Cassis wine in his 1859 epic *Mirèio* as shining like a clear diamond and smelling of the rosemary, heather and myrtle of its hills.

fr-cerons.name: Cérons
fr-cerons.summary: Cérons is a tiny sweet-wine appellation in the Graves, covering the communes of Cérons, Illats and Podensac just north of Barsac. It is the forgotten sibling of Sauternes: the same Garonne climate and botrytis, lighter and cheaper wines, and only a few dozen hectares now declared as sweet each year because most growers find dry Graves easier to sell. Château de Cérons and Grand Enclos du Château de Cérons keep the flame alive, and old vintages are among the best bargains in sweet wine.
fr-cerons.terroir: Gravel and sand over limestone, close to the Garonne and the Ciron's mouth.
producers: Grand Enclos du Château de Cérons
fr-cerons.nerd_note: Growers in Cérons can declare the same vines as Cérons (sweet) or Graves (dry or red) depending on the year, so the appellation's size changes with each vintage's weather.

fr-chablis.name: Chablis
fr-chablis.summary:
Chablis is one of the most imitated wine names in the world and one of the most distinctive white wines in France. The AOC covers about 3,800 ha of Chardonnay across Chablis and 19 surrounding communes along the Serein valley, and includes the premier cru climats, which carry the village name followed by their own: Chablis premier cru Montée de Tonnerre, Chablis premier cru Vaillons.

Village Chablis is pale, dry and taut, with green apple, lemon and a chalky, sometimes saline finish often compared with oyster shell. It is usually fermented and aged in stainless steel, which keeps the focus on acidity and stone, though many good growers use some old oak. Premier crus add depth and a longer life: Montée de Tonnerre and Mont de Milieu on the warmer right bank give fuller, more structured wines, while left-bank Vaillons, Montmains and Les Forêts are finer and more mineral. Good premier crus improve for 10 years or more and develop notes of hazelnut, honey and wet stone.
fr-chablis.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl and limestone on both banks of the Serein, 130 to 300 m; the premier crus mostly face southeast or southwest on the side valleys. Cold winters and spring frost; harvests in mid-September.
fr-chablis.nerd_note: INAO's parcel file registers only some premier cru names (Fourchaume, Mont de Milieu, Vosgros, Vaucoupin and others) as separate denominations; famous names such as Montée de Tonnerre, Vaillons and Montmains are grouping names that can legally cover several smaller climats, such as Chapelot and Pied d'Aloup under Montée de Tonnerre.

fr-chablis-grand-cru.name: Chablis Grand Cru
fr-chablis-grand-cru.summary:
Chablis Grand Cru is a single appellation of about 107 ha on one southwest-facing hillside across the Serein from the town of Chablis, divided into seven climats that appear on the label: Bougros, Preuses, Vaudésir, Grenouilles, Valmur, Les Clos and Blanchot. It is the 33rd grand cru of Burgundy and the only one outside the Côte d'Or.

The wines are richer, riper and far longer-lived than other Chablis, but still keep the region's nervy acidity and chalk. Many growers ferment or age them partly in oak, and the best need five to ten years to show their depth of honey, smoke, citrus peel and iodine. Les Clos, the largest, is the most powerful and slow-developing; Blanchot, facing southeast, is the most floral and delicate; Valmur and Vaudésir sit in a fold of the hill and show both power and finesse; Preuses is round and open; Bougros, at the western end, is the most rustic and earthy; Grenouilles, the smallest at the foot of the slope by the river, is dominated by the La Chablisienne co-op's Château Grenouilles.
fr-chablis-grand-cru.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl, steep slopes between about 130 and 250 m, sheltered and facing the afternoon sun; the warmest site in Chablis, which is why it ripens fully every year.
fr-chablis-grand-cru.nerd_note: La Moutonne, a 2.35 ha monopole of Domaine Long-Depaquit lying mostly in Vaudésir with a strip in Preuses, is often called the eighth grand cru. It is not a separate climat in law but may appear on the label alongside the grand cru name.

fr-chablis-grand-cru-blanchot.name: Chablis Grand Cru Blanchot
fr-chablis-grand-cru-blanchot.summary: Blanchot is the easternmost grand cru, about 12.7 ha facing south-east rather than south-west, which gives the most delicate, floral and refined Chablis of the seven. Raveneau, Vocoret and Laroche are known for it.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-blanchot.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl with white, chalky topsoil, the name possibly from 'blanc' for its pale earth.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-blanchot.nerd_note: All seven grand cru climats share one AOC, Chablis Grand Cru (1938), on a single south-west-facing slope above the Serein, about 100 ha in all.

fr-chablis-grand-cru-bougros.name: Chablis Grand Cru Bougros
fr-chablis-grand-cru-bougros.summary: Bougros is the westernmost grand cru, about 12.5 ha on the lower slope near the river, giving broad, powerful Chablis. William Fèvre's Côte de Bouguerots, from the steepest part, is its most famous wine.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-bougros.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl with heavier, deeper soils on the lower slope.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-bougros.nerd_note: All seven grand cru climats share one AOC, Chablis Grand Cru (1938), on a single south-west-facing slope above the Serein, about 100 ha in all.

fr-chablis-grand-cru-grenouilles.name: Chablis Grand Cru Grenouilles
fr-chablis-grand-cru-grenouilles.summary: Grenouilles ('frogs') is the smallest grand cru, about 9.4 ha at the foot of the slope beside the Serein, and the most lavish in fruit. La Chablisienne's Château Grenouilles owns the largest share.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-grenouilles.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl at the bottom of the slope, warmed by reflection from the river.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-grenouilles.nerd_note: All seven grand cru climats share one AOC, Chablis Grand Cru (1938), on a single south-west-facing slope above the Serein, about 100 ha in all.

fr-chablis-grand-cru-les-clos.name: Chablis Grand Cru Les Clos
fr-chablis-grand-cru-les-clos.summary: Les Clos is the largest and most powerful of the seven Chablis grands crus, about 26 ha in the middle of the great slope facing the town across the Serein. Its name recalls the enclosed vineyard of the Cistercian monks of Pontigny, who planted vines here in the twelfth century. The wines are the most structured and long-lived of Chablis: tight and saline in youth, opening over ten to twenty years into flavours of citrus, smoke, hazelnut and oyster shell. Raveneau, Vincent Dauvissat, William Fèvre, Droin, Christian Moreau and Pinson are reference names.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-les-clos.terroir: Kimmeridgian limestone and marl full of tiny fossil oysters (Exogyra virgula), with a rocky, stony topsoil on the upper slope and deeper marl below; south-west exposure at about 150 to 250 m.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-les-clos.nerd_note: All seven grand cru climats share one AOC, Chablis Grand Cru (1938), on a single south-west-facing slope above the Serein, about 100 ha in all.

fr-chablis-grand-cru-preuses.name: Chablis Grand Cru Preuses
fr-chablis-grand-cru-preuses.summary: Preuses is the highest and most north-westerly of the main grand crus, about 11 ha, giving rounder, generous yet elegant Chablis that is often approachable earlier. Vincent Dauvissat and William Fèvre make classic versions.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-preuses.terroir: Kimmeridgian limestone with a stonier topsoil high on the slope, south-west facing.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-preuses.nerd_note: All seven grand cru climats share one AOC, Chablis Grand Cru (1938), on a single south-west-facing slope above the Serein, about 100 ha in all.

fr-chablis-grand-cru-valmur.name: Chablis Grand Cru Valmur
fr-chablis-grand-cru-valmur.summary: Valmur lies in a fold of the slope between Les Clos and Vaudésir, about 13 ha whose two faces (one turned south-east, one south-west) give rich, exotic yet mineral Chablis with great ageing power. Raveneau's Valmur is legendary; Moreau-Naudet and William Fèvre also excel.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-valmur.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl and limestone in a small combe that shelters the vines.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-valmur.nerd_note: All seven grand cru climats share one AOC, Chablis Grand Cru (1938), on a single south-west-facing slope above the Serein, about 100 ha in all.

fr-chablis-grand-cru-vaudesir.name: Chablis Grand Cru Vaudésir
fr-chablis-grand-cru-vaudesir.summary: Vaudésir is a steep, south-facing bowl of about 14.5 ha in the centre of the grand cru slope, giving perfumed, floral and finely chiselled Chablis. Part of the La Moutonne vineyard, a monopole of Domaine Long-Depaquit, straddles Vaudésir and Preuses.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-vaudesir.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl on a steep, sheltered amphitheatre that warms quickly.
fr-chablis-grand-cru-vaudesir.nerd_note: All seven grand cru climats share one AOC, Chablis Grand Cru (1938), on a single south-west-facing slope above the Serein, about 100 ha in all.

fr-chambertin.name: Chambertin
fr-chambertin.summary:
Chambertin is the king of Gevrey and one of the two or three most famous red vineyards in Burgundy. About 12.9 ha of gentle east-facing slope above the Route des Grands Crus, it takes its name from the field of a man called Bertin, who, legend says, planted it to copy his neighbours the monks of Bèze. Napoleon drank it diluted with water on campaign, and it was Burgundy's most celebrated red through the nineteenth century.

Great Chambertin combines power and depth with polish: black cherry, liquorice, game and earth, firm but fine tannin, and a long life of 20 to 40 years. Ownership is divided among about 25 producers, and quality has varied, but Armand Rousseau (2.15 ha), Trapet, Rossignol-Trapet, Denis Mortet, Leroy, Dugat-Py and Bouchard set the standard.
fr-chambertin.terroir: Brown limestone soils with marl and clay over Bathonian and Bajocian limestone, at about 275 to 300 m; a wood above protects it from cold air and erosion.
fr-chambertin.nerd_note: Wine from Chambertin-Clos de Bèze may be sold as Chambertin, but never the reverse; INAO's parcel file therefore draws the Chambertin AOC at 28.2 ha, enclosing both vineyards.

fr-chambertin-clos-de-beze.name: Chambertin-Clos de Bèze
fr-chambertin-clos-de-beze.summary:
Clos de Bèze is the oldest documented great vineyard of Burgundy. In 630 Duke Amalgaire gave land here to the abbey of Bèze, whose monks cleared and enclosed it; their walled vineyard became the model for Chambertin next door. Today about 15.4 ha, it lies just north of Chambertin, and the two are rivals for the title of Gevrey's finest wine.

Clos de Bèze tends to be slightly more aromatic and refined than Chambertin, with silky, sometimes spicy black fruit and great length. The wine may also be labelled Chambertin, but most owners prefer the older name. About 18 producers share it, including Armand Rousseau, Bruno Clair, Faiveley, Drouhin-Laroze, Prieuré-Roch and Louis Jadot.
fr-chambertin-clos-de-beze.terroir: Slightly stonier and with more limestone than Chambertin, east-facing at 275 to 300 m.
fr-chambertin-clos-de-beze.nerd_note: Rousseau's 1.42 ha and the Damoy family's large holding (about 5.4 ha) make them the biggest names in the Clos.

fr-chambolle-musigny.name: Chambolle-Musigny
fr-chambolle-musigny.summary:
Chambolle-Musigny makes the most perfumed and silky reds of the Côte de Nuits, wines often described as the iron fist in a velvet glove. The village sits at the mouth of the Combe d'Ambin, and its vineyards hold two grand crus at either end: Bonnes-Mares to the north and Musigny to the south.

Between them, the premier crus are among the most sought-after in Burgundy, led by Les Amoureuses, which touches Musigny and costs as much as many grand crus. Les Charmes, Les Cras, Les Sentiers, Les Fuées, Les Baudes, La Combe d'Orveau and Derrière la Grange are also outstanding. The wines are lighter in colour than Gevrey's but extraordinarily aromatic (violet, rose, raspberry) and fine-grained, and age for decades.
fr-chambolle-musigny.terroir: More active limestone and less clay than its neighbours, with thin soils that drain fast; the Combe d'Ambin and Combe d'Orveau bring cool air.
fr-chambolle-musigny.nerd_note: Chambolle added Musigny to its name in 1878. Its premier cru Les Amoureuses, about 5.3 ha, often sells above grand crus such as Clos de Vougeot.

fr-champagne.name: Champagne
fr-champagne.grapes: Pinot Noir, Meunier, Chardonnay (plus tiny amounts of Arbane, Petit Meslier, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, and the trial hybrid Voltis)
fr-champagne.summary:
Champagne is the only French wine region where a single appellation covers everything: 34,200 ha in 319 villages, from the Montagne de Reims to the Aube, all producing wine sold under one name. The legal area was delimited in 1908, extended to the Aube in 1927, and defined as an AOC in 1936. The rules govern every step: hand harvesting of whole bunches (machine harvesting is banned), pressing in fractions (the first 2,050 litres from 4,000 kg are the *cuvée*, the next 500 the *taille*), a maximum yield set each year, second fermentation in the bottle in which the wine is sold, and minimum cellar ageing of 15 months for non-vintage (12 on the lees) and three years for vintage wines.

What you taste comes from that process: the tension between Champagne's cold-climate acidity and the creamy, toasty, brioche notes of yeast autolysis during long lees ageing. Blending across villages, grapes and years (most non-vintage Champagne includes 20 to 50% reserve wine) gives each house its consistent style: Krug's richness, Bollinger's Pinot-driven power, Taittinger's Chardonnay elegance, Pol Roger's balance.

Economics shape everything.
