Grapes sell for some of the highest prices in the wine world, over 7 euros per kilo in recent years, and land in grand cru villages can exceed 1.5 million euros per hectare. Sales dipped to about 266 million bottles in 2025, 152 million of them exported, and stocks are high, so producers cut the 2026 yield to 8,800 kg/ha. Meanwhile the grower movement, led by Anselme Selosse from the 1980s and later by a generation of small producers bottling single villages and parcels, has shifted attention from house blends to terroir.

The appellation area debate, opened in 2003 to adjust the boundary and add about 40 villages, was formally dropped by the growers' union in October 2026, leaving the 319 communes unchanged.
fr-champagne.terroir: Mostly Belemnite and Micraster chalk in the Marne, Kimmeridgian marl in the Aube, with clay, sand and marl in the Marne valley. Cool continental-oceanic climate, average about 11°C, with spring frost and hail risk.
fr-champagne.nerd_note: The pressure inside a Champagne bottle, about 6 atmospheres, is roughly three times that of a car tyre; a cork can leave the bottle at over 40 km/h.

fr-chapelle-chambertin.name: Chapelle-Chambertin
fr-chapelle-chambertin.summary: Chapelle-Chambertin, about 5.5 ha below Clos de Bèze, takes its name from a chapel built in 1155 by the monks of Bèze, destroyed during the Revolution. Its soil is thin and stony over limestone, giving one of the lighter and more delicate Gevrey grand crus, fragrant and red-fruited rather than massive. Rossignol-Trapet, Trapet, Drouhin-Laroze, Pierre Damoy and Louis Jadot are leading names.
fr-chapelle-chambertin.terroir: Shallow soil on hard limestone, just below the Route des Grands Crus.
fr-chapelle-chambertin.nerd_note: Chapelle includes the climats En la Chapelle and Les Gemeaux.

fr-charlemagne.name: Charlemagne
fr-charlemagne.summary: Charlemagne is a grand cru appellation that exists almost entirely on paper. It covers the lieux-dits En Charlemagne in Pernand-Vergelesses and Le Charlemagne in Aloxe-Corton, the historic heart of Corton-Charlemagne, and its wines are virtually always sold under the better-known Corton-Charlemagne name. A handful of growers have occasionally used it to make a point.
fr-charlemagne.terroir: The same marly limestone slopes as Corton-Charlemagne under the Bois de Corton.
fr-charlemagne.nerd_note: Charlemagne is the least-used of Burgundy's 33 grand crus; on most maps it is shown as part of Corton-Charlemagne.

fr-charmes-chambertin.name: Charmes-Chambertin
fr-charmes-chambertin.summary: Charmes-Chambertin, about 12.2 ha below Chambertin and Latricières, is the most accessible Gevrey grand cru, partly because wine from neighbouring Mazoyères-Chambertin (about 18.6 ha) may also be sold as Charmes, giving about 31 ha in all. The name probably comes from chaume, a clearing of scrub, not charm, though the wine is indeed charming: soft, round, fruit-forward Pinot Noir that is approachable young. Dozens of producers make it, from Armand Rousseau, Dugat-Py and Claude Dugat to Taupenot-Merme and Perrot-Minot.
fr-charmes-chambertin.terroir: Deeper soil on the lower part of the grand cru band, at about 260 to 280 m.
fr-charmes-chambertin.nerd_note: INAO's parcel file delimits Charmes-Chambertin and Mazoyères-Chambertin as one 30.9 ha area because Mazoyères may be sold under the Charmes name.

fr-chassagne-montrachet.name: Chassagne-Montrachet
fr-chassagne-montrachet.summary:
Chassagne-Montrachet, at the southern end of the Côte de Beaune's great white zone, makes both reds and whites in quantity. Until the 1980s it was mostly red, but rising demand for Chardonnay has replanted many slopes with white. Its whites are rounder and more floral than Puligny's, with a hazelnut richness; its reds are firm, earthy and good value.

Chassagne shares Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet with Puligny and holds Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet alone. Its premier cru map is complicated, with about 55 named climats: Les Caillerets, La Romanée, Les Ruchottes, Les Chaumées and Les Vergers on the upper slopes north of the village; Morgeot, a large area with an abbey cellar, to the south; and En Remilly and Blanchot Dessus against Saint-Aubin and the Montrachet. Pink Comblanchien-like stone was quarried here for buildings across Burgundy.
fr-chassagne-montrachet.terroir: Limestone, marl and clay; pink and white stone quarries above the village; the reds come mostly from the heavier soils toward Santenay.
fr-chassagne-montrachet.nerd_note: Domaine Ramonet's founder Pierre Ramonet built the estate from 1920s smallholdings and bought his first Montrachet parcel in 1978.

fr-chateau-chalon.name: Château-Chalon
fr-chateau-chalon.summary: Château-Chalon is the grand cru of vin jaune: an appellation of about 50 ha in production (94 ha delimited) on steep marl slopes below a village perched on a rocky spur, where only vin jaune may be made. The Benedictine abbey of Château-Chalon, whose abbesses were drawn from the nobility, developed the wine from the Middle Ages. In poor years growers release no Château-Chalon at all, as happened in 1974, 1980 and 1984. The wines, from Savagnin aged at least six years and three months under the voile, are more intense and long-lived than other vins jaunes: walnut, curry, saffron and salt, lasting a century.
fr-chateau-chalon.terroir: Grey and black Liassic marls on steep, south and southwest-facing slopes below the village, at 250 to 400 m; the cliffs above shelter the vines.
fr-chateau-chalon.nerd_note: The village of Château-Chalon is one of the Plus Beaux Villages de France and its Belvédère Sainte-Anne overlooks the whole appellation.

fr-chateau-grillet.name: Château-Grillet
fr-chateau-grillet.summary: Château-Grillet is one of France's smallest appellations and one of the few that consists of a single estate: about 3.8 ha of Viognier in a sun-trap amphitheatre of terraces above the Rhône at Vérin and Saint-Michel-sur-Rhône, completely enclosed by Condrieu. The Neyret-Gachet family owned it from 1830 until 2011, when François Pinault's Artémis group bought it. Since then the wine, sold in a distinctive brown flute bottle, has been made with more precision, with a second wine from younger vines. Château-Grillet is more restrained and longer-lived than most Condrieu.
fr-chateau-grillet.terroir: A natural amphitheatre of granite terraces facing south and southeast, sheltered from the wind, at about 150 to 250 m.
fr-chateau-grillet.nerd_note: Château-Grillet produces only about 10,000 bottles a year, and the INAO parcel file delimits 3.79 ha.

fr-chateaumeillant.name: Châteaumeillant
fr-chateaumeillant.summary: Châteaumeillant, south of Bourges near the geographical centre of France, is red and rosé only, from Gamay and Pinot Noir on volcanic and schist soils. Its vin gris is a local speciality. It became AOC in 2010.
fr-chateaumeillant.terroir: Mica-schist, sandstone and volcanic rocks, unusual for the Centre-Loire.
fr-chateaumeillant.nerd_note: Châteaumeillant was known as a wine town in Roman times; amphorae from Italy have been found in excavations of the Gallic oppidum here.

fr-chateauneuf-du-pape.name: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
fr-chateauneuf-du-pape.grapes: 13 grape varieties (18 counting colour variants): Grenache Noir, Gris and Blanc, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Counoise, Vaccarèse, Terret Noir, Muscardin, Clairette, Clairette Rose, Bourboulenc, Roussanne, Picpoul Noir, Gris and Blanc, Picardan
fr-chateauneuf-du-pape.summary:
Châteauneuf-du-Pape is the most famous wine of the Southern Rhône and the birthplace of French appellation law. Some 300 growers declared 3,122 ha for the 2025 vintage (3,738 ha are delimited in INAO's parcel file) in Châteauneuf-du-Pape and parts of Orange, Courthézon, Bédarrides and Sorgues, between Orange and Avignon. The 2025 crop was 88,271 hl, an average of only 28 hl/ha.

The village takes its name from the summer castle built by Pope John XXII in the 1320s; only one wall of the keep survived the Wars of Religion and a German demolition in 1944. In 1923 Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié of Château Fortia drew up rules with the growers: a delimited area based on where lavender and thyme grew, a list of grape varieties, a minimum alcohol of 12.5 percent, a ban on rosé, and the triage (sorting out of 5 to 20 percent of the harvest). Recognised by the courts in 1933, they became the model for the 1935 AOC law, and Châteauneuf was among the first AOCs decreed in 1936. In 1954 the village council even banned flying saucers from landing in its vineyards.

The red, about 93 percent of production, is usually a Grenache-led blend with Syrah, Mourvèdre and Cinsault, though some estates use all the permitted varieties (Beaucastel) or pure Grenache (Rayas). It is generous and spicy, with kirsch, garrigue herbs, leather and liquorice, often above 15 percent alcohol, and ages for 20 years or more in good vintages. Whites from Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne and Bourboulenc are rich and honeyed. Most bottles carry the papal coat of arms embossed in the glass.
fr-chateauneuf-du-pape.terroir: The appellation is famous for its galets roulés, rounded quartzite pebbles carried by the ancient Rhône from the Alps and laid on red clay terraces, notably on the plateau of La Crau (Vieux Télégraphe) and around Mont-Redon and Cabrières. They store heat and reflect sun. But the soils are far more varied: sand in the northeast (Rayas, Pignan, Charvin), giving finer, more perfumed Grenache; safres (Miocene sandstone and sand) in the east; and Urgonian limestone in the west near the château. The mistral blows more than 100 days a year. Bush vines (gobelet), some more than 100 years old, are the norm.
fr-chateauneuf-du-pape.nerd_note: Châteauneuf's maximum yield of 35 hl/ha is one of the lowest of any French AOC, and the rules still require growers to discard part of the harvest in the vineyard (le rapé).

fr-chatillon-en-diois.name: Châtillon-en-Diois
fr-chatillon-en-diois.grapes: Gamay, Pinot Noir, Syrah; Aligoté and Chardonnay for white
fr-chatillon-en-diois.summary: Châtillon-en-Diois covers mountain vineyards east of Die at up to 700 m, where Gamay, Pinot Noir and Syrah make light, fresh reds and Aligoté and Chardonnay make crisp whites. About 40 ha (2025) are declared.
fr-chatillon-en-diois.terroir: Limestone scree and marl at altitude in the upper Drôme valley.

fr-chenas.name: Chénas
fr-chenas.summary: Chénas is the smallest cru and the least known, partly because much of its land lies in the Moulin-à-Vent appellation. Its name comes from the oak forests (chênes) that once covered the slopes. The wines are deep and spicy with floral notes and can age; they are some of the best values among the crus.
fr-chenas.terroir: Pink granite on the high western slopes, with alluvial sands lower down.
fr-chenas.nerd_note: Paul-Henri Thillardon, a young Chénas grower, has become a symbol of the cru's revival since 2008.

fr-chevalier-montrachet.name: Chevalier-Montrachet
fr-chevalier-montrachet.summary: Chevalier-Montrachet, about 7.6 ha directly above Le Montrachet in Puligny, is steeper, stonier and higher, and its wines are leaner and more mineral, with less flesh but great finesse and age-worthiness. Domaine Leflaive (about 2 ha), Bouchard Père et Fils (2.5 ha), Louis Jadot (Les Demoiselles), Louis Latour (Les Demoiselles) and Domaine d'Auvenay are among its owners.
fr-chevalier-montrachet.terroir: Thin, stony soil over hard limestone on a steeper slope above Montrachet, at 265 to 290 m.
fr-chevalier-montrachet.nerd_note: Les Demoiselles, a section of Chevalier owned by Jadot and Latour, was added to the grand cru in 1939.

fr-cheverny.name: Cheverny
fr-cheverny.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Orbois, Chenin Blanc; Pinot Noir, Gamay, Côt, Cabernet Franc
fr-cheverny.summary: Cheverny, in the Sologne south of Blois, makes blended wines: whites from Sauvignon with Chardonnay or Orbois, reds from Pinot Noir with Gamay. The blending rules make it unusual in the Loire. The château of Cheverny inspired Hergé's Marlinspike Hall in the Tintin books.
fr-cheverny.terroir: Sand and clay over limestone in the Sologne.
fr-cheverny.nerd_note: Cheverny is one of the few Loire appellations where blending is compulsory: reds combine Pinot Noir with Gamay, and whites combine Sauvignon Blanc with Chardonnay or Orbois.

fr-chinon.name: Chinon
fr-chinon.grapes: Cabernet Franc (Breton), up to 10% Cabernet Sauvignon; Chenin Blanc for white
fr-chinon.summary:
Chinon is the Loire's most famous red-wine appellation, a band of vineyards along the Vienne river around the medieval town where Joan of Arc met the future Charles VII in 1429. Rabelais, born nearby, praised its wines, calling it 'Chinon, little town, great fame'. The grape is Cabernet Franc, locally called Breton, and Chinon shows its full range: light, crunchy reds from the sandy and gravel terraces by the river for drinking cool in their first years, and deep, structured, long-lived wines from the clay-limestone slopes and tuffeau hillsides.

Charles Joguet in Sazilly began bottling single-site Chinons in the 1960s and 1970s, notably Clos de la Dioterie, and Bernard Baudry, Olga Raffault, Philippe Alliet and Couly-Dutheil (Clos de l'Écho, once Rabelais's family vineyard) are references. A little white Chenin and rosé are also made. Good Chinon tastes of raspberry, violet, graphite and pencil lead, with fine tannins, and the best reach 20 years or more.
fr-chinon.terroir: Three terroirs: sand and gravel terraces by the Vienne; clay and flint on the plateau; tuffeau slopes (*coteaux*) with clay-limestone topsoil. The best sites face south above the Vienne in Cravant-les-Coteaux, Sazilly and Chinon itself.
fr-chinon.nerd_note: Couly-Dutheil's Clos de l'Écho was said to have belonged to the family of François Rabelais, who grew up at La Devinière just south of Chinon.

fr-chiroubles.name: Chiroubles
fr-chiroubles.summary: Chiroubles is the highest cru, with vineyards up to 400 to 450 m in a natural amphitheatre of granite. Its wines are the lightest and most delicate of the crus, fragrant and fresh, and in warm years the altitude is now an advantage. The village honours Victor Pulliat, a nineteenth-century ampelographer from Chiroubles who championed grafting to fight phylloxera.
fr-chiroubles.terroir: Steep slopes of pink granite at the highest altitude of any cru, mostly facing east and southeast.
fr-chiroubles.nerd_note: Victor Pulliat (1827 to 1896) planted a collection of more than 2,000 grape varieties in Chiroubles and helped save the region from phylloxera.

fr-chorey-les-beaune.name: Chorey-lès-Beaune
fr-chorey-les-beaune.summary: Chorey-lès-Beaune is the only Côte de Beaune village that sits entirely on the flat land east of the main road, and for that reason it has no premier crus. Its soft, fruity reds are some of the most approachable and affordable in the Côte d'Or, especially from Tollot-Beaut, whose wines are a benchmark for good Pinot Noir from the plain. A village AOC only since 1970, it was previously sold as Côte de Beaune-Villages.
fr-chorey-les-beaune.terroir: Alluvial gravel, sand and clay on the flat, with deeper soil and more frost risk than the slope.
fr-chorey-les-beaune.nerd_note: Château de Chorey, a seventeenth-century moated house, belongs to the Germain family and is now partly a guesthouse.

fr-clairette-de-bellegarde.name: Clairette de Bellegarde
fr-clairette-de-bellegarde.summary: Clairette de Bellegarde is a tiny white-wine appellation for pure Clairette from the commune of Bellegarde, in the Gard between Nîmes and the Camargue, on the edge of the Costières de Nîmes. The wines are soft, floral and low in acidity, best drunk young. It is one of the oldest appellations of the eastern Languedoc and today one of France's smallest by volume, kept alive by a handful of growers.
fr-clairette-de-bellegarde.terroir: Terraces of rounded pebbles (galets roulés) and red clay, left by the ancient Rhône and Durance.
fr-clairette-de-bellegarde.nerd_note: Clairette is one of the oldest grapes of the French Midi; in Bellegarde it has survived as a single-variety appellation while most of the region moved to blends.

fr-clairette-de-die.name: Clairette de Die
fr-clairette-de-die.grapes: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (min 75% for Tradition), Clairette
fr-clairette-de-die.summary: Clairette de Die is the Diois's flagship: a lightly sweet, low-alcohol (about 7 to 8 percent) sparkling wine made mostly from Muscat by the méthode dioise ancestrale, in which fermentation starts in tank, is chilled to pause it, and finishes in bottle without added sugar or yeast. The result is grapey, floral and fresh. Dry traditional-method sparkling wine from the Diois is sold as Crémant de Die. The Cave de Die Jaillance co-operative dominates, but growers such as Achard-Vincent show what organic Muscat can do.
fr-clairette-de-die.terroir: Limestone scree, marl and clay at 200 to 700 m along the Drôme valley; cool nights preserve Muscat's aroma.
fr-clairette-de-die.nerd_note: The méthode dioise is related to the ancestral method of Limoux and Gaillac and predates Champagne's.

fr-clairette-du-languedoc.name: Clairette du Languedoc
fr-clairette-du-languedoc.summary: One of the oldest Languedoc AOCs (1948), pure Clairette from the area around Adissan and Aspiran in the Hérault valley. It is made dry, sweet, or as a 'rancio' aged oxidatively, and as a vin de liqueur. Production is small.
fr-clairette-du-languedoc.terroir: Clay-limestone and red ruffe soils in the Hérault valley.
fr-clairette-du-languedoc.nerd_note: Clairette du Languedoc was France's first white AOC in the Languedoc, granted in 1948.

fr-clos-de-la-roche.name: Clos de la Roche
fr-clos-de-la-roche.summary: Clos de la Roche is the largest and usually the finest grand cru of Morey-Saint-Denis, about 16.9 ha that grew in 1971 when several neighbouring climats were added. Its name refers to a large stone thought to have been used for Celtic rituals. The wines are deep, firm and savoury, with dark fruit and a stony, almost Chambertin-like power. Ponsot, Dujac, Armand Rousseau, Hubert Lignier, Leroy and Arlaud are its leading growers.
fr-clos-de-la-roche.terroir: Thin soil on hard limestone that comes to the surface in places; one of the stoniest grand crus.
fr-clos-de-la-roche.nerd_note: Domaine Ponsot's Clos de la Roche Cuvée Vieilles Vignes comes from vines planted in the 1950s and is famous for being made without new oak.

fr-clos-de-tart.name: Clos de Tart
fr-clos-de-tart.summary:
Clos de Tart is a walled 7.5 ha monopole in Morey-Saint-Denis owned by only three proprietors in almost 900 years: the Bernardine nuns of Notre-Dame de Tart from 1141, the Marey-Monge family from 1791 and the Mommessin family from 1932, until François Pinault's Artémis group bought it in 2017. Unusually, its rows run north to south across the slope, which slows erosion and lets every row see different soils.

The wine is deep, spicy and structured, among the most powerful in Morey, and its old cellars are among the deepest in the Côte. It touches Bonnes-Mares at its southern edge.
fr-clos-de-tart.terroir: Limestone and marl with six distinct soil zones mapped by the estate; the rows cross the contour lines.
fr-clos-de-tart.nerd_note: Clos de Tart was valued at more than 250 million euros when Artémis bought it in 2017, the highest price per hectare ever recorded for a Burgundy vineyard.

fr-clos-de-vougeot.name: Clos de Vougeot
fr-clos-de-vougeot.summary:
Clos de Vougeot is Burgundy's great monument: a single walled vineyard of about 50 ha, created by the Cistercian monks of Cîteaux from 1110 onward and completely enclosed by 1336. The monks used it as a laboratory, separating the wine of different parts of the slope; their cuvée of the upper vineyard was the abbey's gift to popes and kings. Confiscated in 1789, it was sold intact, but it has since been divided among about 80 owners.

Because it runs from the top of the slope (next to Musigny and Grands-Échezeaux) down to the flat land by the road, quality and style vary. The best wines come from the upper and middle parts and from serious growers: dense, spicy, dark-fruited Pinot Noir with firm tannins. The Château du Clos de Vougeot in the middle of the vineyard, with its twelfth-century press house and sixteenth-century Renaissance building, belongs to the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin.
fr-clos-de-vougeot.terroir: Upper part on light limestone soils, middle on limestone with clay, lowest part on deeper alluvial clay; rows run down the slope from about 240 to 270 m.
fr-clos-de-vougeot.nerd_note: Château de la Tour, with about 5.5 ha, is the largest owner and the only one making wine inside the walls.

fr-clos-des-lambrays.name: Clos des Lambrays
fr-clos-des-lambrays.summary: Clos des Lambrays, about 8.8 ha in Morey-Saint-Denis, was promoted to grand cru only in 1981, the first change to the list since the 1930s. Apart from a tiny strip owned by Domaine Taupenot-Merme, it is the monopole of Domaine des Lambrays, which LVMH bought in 2014. Its rows run across a slope that faces east and then northeast, giving wines that are sappy, silky and finely aromatic. Whole-cluster fermentation has long been part of its style.
fr-clos-des-lambrays.terroir: Limestone and marl with a varied exposure that turns slightly northeast at the top; vines planted down the slope.
fr-clos-des-lambrays.nerd_note: The domaine also makes two rare white premier crus in Puligny-Montrachet, Les Folatières and Clos du Cailleret.

fr-clos-saint-denis.name: Clos Saint-Denis
fr-clos-saint-denis.summary: Clos Saint-Denis, about 6.6 ha south of Clos de la Roche, gave its name to the village of Morey in 1927. It is named after the collegiate church of Saint-Denis de Vergy, founded in 1023, whose canons owned it. The wines are fragrant and elegant, with red fruit and spice, lighter than Clos de la Roche. Dujac's version, made with whole clusters, is the benchmark, alongside Ponsot, Bertagna and Arlaud.
fr-clos-saint-denis.terroir: Limestone with a little more clay than Clos de la Roche, gently sloping at about 270 m.
fr-clos-saint-denis.nerd_note: Despite the name, Clos Saint-Denis has had no walls for centuries.

fr-collioure.name: Collioure
fr-collioure.grapes: Grenache, Mourvèdre, Syrah, Carignan; Grenache Blanc, Grenache Gris, Macabeu, Malvoisie, Vermentino
fr-collioure.summary: Collioure covers the same steep terraced schist slopes as Banyuls, between the Pyrenees and the Mediterranean near the Spanish border, but for dry wines. Its reds, built on Grenache with Mourvèdre and Syrah, are dense, spicy and mineral; its whites (AOC since 2002) are rich and saline. The harbour town of Collioure, painted by Matisse and Derain in 1905 when they invented Fauvism, is the centre. Domaine de la Rectorie, Domaine du Mas Blanc, Coume del Mas and Domaine Vial-Magnères are references.
fr-collioure.terroir: Steep terraces of Cambrian schist, held up by dry-stone walls and drained by 'peu de gall' (rooster's foot) channels.
fr-collioure.nerd_note: The Collioure and Banyuls terraces are held up by thousands of kilometres of dry-stone walls; the 'peu de gall' channels, shaped like a rooster's foot, stop storms from washing the soil into the sea.

fr-condrieu.name: Condrieu
fr-condrieu.summary: Condrieu is the birthplace of Viognier and its finest expression: a dry white of apricot, peach blossom, honeysuckle and musk, rich and oily but with a mineral finish, best drunk within a few years. The appellation runs about 20 km south of Côte Rôtie on steep granite terraces across seven communes in three departments. By the late 1960s it was down to roughly a dozen hectares and Viognier was close to extinction; Georges Vernay, the 'pope of Condrieu', led its revival, and today 216 ha (2025) are planted. A few growers make a late-harvest sweet style, and the Vernay family's Coteau de Vernon is the most famous single site.
fr-condrieu.terroir: Granite with a sandy, mica-rich topsoil called arzelle, on steep terraces facing south and southeast at 150 to 300 m.
fr-condrieu.nerd_note: Condrieu's name is said to come from coin du ruisseau (corner of the stream), the confluence of streams at the village.

fr-corbieres.name: Corbières
fr-corbieres.grapes: Carignan, Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Lledoner Pelut, Cinsault; Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc, Macabeu, Marsanne, Roussanne, Vermentino
fr-corbieres.summary: Corbières is the largest appellation of the Languedoc, roughly 10,000 ha in the wild hills of the Aude south of Narbonne and east of Carcassonne. It is a country of Cathar castles (Quéribus, Peyrepertuse), garrigue and scattered villages, and its wines, mostly red and often led by Carignan, range from rustic to impressive. Eleven terroir zones have been identified, from the coastal Fontfroide and Sigean to the high Hautes-Corbières. The best estates include Château de Lastours, Domaine de Villemajou (Gérard Bertrand), Maxime Magnon, Domaine Ledogar and Château La Voulte-Gasparets, whose Cuvée Romain Pauc helped make the area's name.
fr-corbieres.terroir: Very varied: limestone, schist, marl, sandstone and gravel; maritime near the coast, mountain climate inland.
fr-corbieres.nerd_note: The Cathar castles that dominate the Corbières sheltered heretics during the Albigensian Crusade (1209 to 1229); Quéribus, the last to fall, surrendered in 1255.

fr-cornas.name: Cornas
fr-cornas.summary: Cornas, 162 ha (2025) of steep granite in a single commune opposite Valence, makes the most rustic, tannic and wild Syrah of the Northern Rhône. Its name comes from the Celtic for burnt earth: an amphitheatre of terraces facing southeast, sheltered from the north wind, makes it one of the warmest spots in the north. Unlike its neighbours, Cornas must be 100 percent Syrah, with no white grapes. Auguste Clape kept the traditional style alive when others gave up, and today Thierry Allemand, Franck Balthazar, Vincent Paris, Guillaume Gilles, Domaine du Coulet and Alain Voge make cult wines. The best lieux-dits include Reynard, Chaillot, Sabarotte, Les Eygas, La Geynale and Patou.
fr-cornas.terroir: Decomposed granite (gore) on steep terraces with some limestone and clay at the foot; a south-facing bowl that ripens early.
fr-cornas.nerd_note: Thierry Allemand started with almost nothing in 1982, renting terraces nobody else wanted; his Reynard and Chaillot are now among the most sought-after Rhône wines.

fr-correze.name: Corrèze
fr-correze.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Chenin Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc
fr-correze.summary: Corrèze is a small AOC in the Limousin (recognised in 2017) covering three styles: dry whites and reds, wines labelled Coteaux de la Vézère, and the rare vin paillé, a sweet wine made from grapes dried on straw for several weeks. Vineyards that had all but vanished after phylloxera were replanted from the 1980s, around Branceilles in the south and the Vézère valley near Allassac and Voutezac.
fr-correze.terroir: Clay-limestone and sandstone around Branceilles; slate schist in the Vézère valley.
fr-correze.nerd_note: Vin paillé is a Corrèze tradition said to go back centuries, when straw-dried wine was kept for family celebrations.

fr-corton.name: Corton
fr-corton.grapes: Pinot Noir; Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc for white
fr-corton.summary:
Corton is the largest grand cru of Burgundy and the only one of the Côte de Beaune for red wine. The appellation covers about 160 ha around the hill of Corton, across Aloxe-Corton, Ladoix-Serrigny and Pernand-Vergelesses, but the vineyard in production is closer to 100 ha, and its wines vary greatly. Most labels add the climat name, such as Corton Bressandes. The 28 climats include Le Corton at the top of the hill, Les Bressandes, Le Clos du Roi, Les Renardes, Les Pougets, Les Perrières, Les Grèves, Le Rognet and Les Maréchaudes.

Red Corton is firm, earthy and slow to open, often austere young but long-lived; Le Clos du Roi and Les Bressandes are the most refined, Les Renardes the most wild and gamey. A small amount of white Corton, from Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc, also exists. The hill is crowned by the Bois de Corton.
fr-corton.terroir: A hill of Bathonian limestone capped with woods; reds come from the lower and middle slopes on iron-rich, reddish brown marls and limestone, east, southeast and south-facing, from 250 to 330 m.
fr-corton.nerd_note: Domaine de la Romanée-Conti began leasing vines in Bressandes, Clos du Roi and Renardes from the Prince de Mérode in 2009 and has made a Corton ever since.

fr-corton-charlemagne.name: Corton-Charlemagne
fr-corton-charlemagne.summary:
Corton-Charlemagne is one of the world's great white wines and, with about 72 ha, the largest white grand cru of the Côte d'Or. It covers the upper slopes of the hill of Corton facing southwest and west, in Pernand-Vergelesses and Aloxe-Corton, plus a sliver in Ladoix. Legend says the Emperor Charlemagne owned vines here and, when his white beard became stained by red wine, ordered white grapes planted; he did give vineyards here to the abbey of Saulieu in 775.

The wine is powerful and mineral, slower to open than Montrachet and more austere when young, with citrus, flint and spice that need a decade to unwind. Bonneau du Martray (about 9.5 ha), Coche-Dury, Louis Latour, Bouchard Père et Fils, Rapet, Roumier and the Hospices de Beaune (cuvée François de Salins) are among its best sources.
fr-corton-charlemagne.terroir: Marly limestone and Oxfordian marls on the upper hill under the wood, at 280 to 330 m; cool, windy slopes, many facing west.
fr-corton-charlemagne.nerd_note: Wines from Corton-Charlemagne may in theory include Aligoté, a historical tolerance, though nobody uses it today.

fr-costieres-de-nimes.name: Costières de Nîmes
fr-costieres-de-nimes.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Cinsault; whites from Grenache Blanc, Roussanne, Marsanne, Clairette, Vermentino, Viognier
fr-costieres-de-nimes.summary: Costières de Nîmes lies on a plateau between Nîmes and the Camargue, the southernmost outpost of the Rhône Valley vineyards. Its galets roulés, laid down by the ancient Rhône and Durance, are the same type as Châteauneuf's, and its Grenache and Syrah reds are ripe and spicy, with sea breezes keeping them fresh. Promoted to AOC in 1986 as Costières du Gard, renamed in 1989, it moved from Languedoc's interprofession to Inter Rhône in 2004. Its area has fallen sharply, to 2,145 ha in 2025 from 2,844 ha in 2020.
fr-costieres-de-nimes.terroir: A plateau of quartzite pebbles over red clay and sand, at 20 to 140 m; Mediterranean breezes from the Camargue.
fr-costieres-de-nimes.nerd_note: The Mas des Tourelles at Beaucaire makes wine with Roman methods in a reconstructed Gallo-Roman cellar.

fr-cote-de-beaune.name: Côte de Beaune
fr-cote-de-beaune.summary: Côte de Beaune is a confusing name. Beyond being the name of the whole southern half of the Côte d'Or, it is also a small appellation of its own: about 50 ha of vines on the upper slopes and plateau of the Montagne de Beaune, above the Beaune premier crus. The wines, red and white, are fresh and light, with more acidity than Beaune village wine; Joseph Drouhin and Domaine des Croix make good examples.
fr-cote-de-beaune.terroir: Higher, cooler limestone slopes and plateau above Beaune, at 300 to 350 m.
fr-cote-de-beaune.nerd_note: Do not confuse it with Côte de Beaune-Villages, a red-only appellation that covers 16 villages.

fr-cote-de-beaune-villages.name: Côte de Beaune-Villages
fr-cote-de-beaune-villages.summary: Côte de Beaune-Villages is a red-only appellation that can be used by 16 villages of the Côte de Beaune (not Aloxe-Corton, Beaune, Pommard or Volnay). Most is a blend from several communes, sold by négociants; growers in small villages also use it for wine from young vines or less favoured plots. It is soft and early-drinking, a step up from regional Bourgogne rouge.
fr-cote-de-beaune-villages.terroir: Varied; any of the participating villages' red-wine land.
fr-cote-de-beaune-villages.nerd_note: Each participating village may also add its own name, e.g. Chorey-lès-Beaune Côte de Beaune.

fr-cote-de-brouilly.name: Côte de Brouilly
fr-cote-de-brouilly.summary: Côte de Brouilly covers the steep upper slopes of Mont Brouilly, an extinct volcano rising to 484 m, inside the larger Brouilly appellation. Its blue diorite rock, called blue stone (pierre bleue) or cornes vertes, gives deeper, more mineral and more concentrated wines than Brouilly. Château Thivin, the oldest estate on the hill, is the reference. The chapel of Notre-Dame-aux-Raisins on the summit, built in 1857 to ask for protection from oidium, hosts an annual winegrowers' pilgrimage.
fr-cote-de-brouilly.terroir: Blue diorite (an old volcanic rock) and andesite on very steep slopes of all exposures around the hill.
fr-cote-de-brouilly.nerd_note: Château Thivin has been in the Geoffray family since 1877; Claude Geoffray was one of the founders of the appellation.

fr-cote-de-nuits-villages.name: Côte de Nuits-Villages
fr-cote-de-nuits-villages.summary: Côte de Nuits-Villages covers the edges of the Côte de Nuits: Fixin and Brochon in the north, and Premeaux-Prissey (outside the Nuits-Saint-Georges limits), Comblanchien and Corgoloin in the south. The southern villages are famous for the pink Comblanchien limestone quarried for the Paris Opéra floor and Orly airport. The wines are mostly lighter reds with typical Côte de Nuits structure and can be excellent value from good growers.
fr-cote-de-nuits-villages.terroir: Thin soils over Comblanchien limestone at the narrowest point of the Côte, where the slope is barely 200 m wide.
fr-cote-de-nuits-villages.nerd_note: Its official alternative name, Vins fins de la Côte de Nuits, is almost never used on labels.

fr-cote-roannaise.name: Côte Roannaise
fr-cote-roannaise.summary: The Côte Roannaise lies on the east-facing granitic slopes of the Monts de la Madeleine above Roanne. Gamay here gives juicy, mineral reds, closer to the Beaujolais crus than to Touraine. Domaine Sérol and Domaine des Pothiers are leading the revival; the Troisgros family's famous restaurant in Roanne is a big supporter.
fr-cote-roannaise.terroir: Granite and volcanic rocks on east-facing slopes at 400 to 550 m.
fr-cote-roannaise.nerd_note: The local Gamay strain is often called Gamay Saint-Romain, after the village of Saint-Romain-la-Motte.

fr-cote-rotie.name: Côte Rôtie
fr-cote-rotie.summary:
Côte Rôtie, the roasted slope, is the northernmost cru of the Rhône and one of the world's great Syrahs: perfumed with violet, black olive, bacon fat and pepper, silky yet structured, and capable of ageing for 20 years. Its 342 ha (2025) of vines climb terraces so steep, up to 60 percent, that every task is done by hand and each vine is tied to its own stake. Growers may co-ferment up to 20 percent Viognier, which fixes colour and lifts the aroma, though most use far less.

The slope is divided into many lieux-dits, traditionally summed up as Côte Brune north of Ampuis, with darker, iron-rich schist that gives firmer, more tannic wines, and Côte Blonde to the south, with paler granite and gneiss that gives softer, more perfumed wine. Marcel Guigal's three single-site wines, La Mouline (first vintage 1966), La Landonne (1978) and La Turque (1985), known as the La La's, became cult wines from the 1980s and transformed the appellation, which had shrunk to about 70 ha in the 1970s. Today growers such as Jamet, Rostaing, Gilles Barge, Stéphane Ogier, Clusel-Roch, Bernard Levet and Jean-Michel Stephan bottle individual lieux-dits.
fr-cote-rotie.terroir: Mica-schist and gneiss in the north (Côte Brune), granite and leucogranite in the south (Côte Blonde and Condrieu side); southeast-facing terraces along the right bank of the Rhône from Saint-Cyr to Tupin-et-Semons, at 180 to 325 m. The plateau above, added in the 1960s delimitation, is debated.
fr-cote-rotie.nerd_note: Côte Rôtie's 1940 decree allowed some plateau land above the slopes; growers have long debated tightening it, and a 2025 to 2026 discussion in the trade press asked whether a Burgundy-style cru system could work here.

fr-coteaux-bourguignons.name: Coteaux Bourguignons
fr-coteaux-bourguignons.grapes: Gamay, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Aligoté, Melon de Bourgogne, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris
fr-coteaux-bourguignons.summary: Coteaux Bourguignons replaced the old Bourgogne Grand Ordinaire in 2011 as the broadest regional appellation of Burgundy, and it extends into the Beaujolais. It lets producers blend Gamay and Pinot Noir in any proportion and makes a lot of simple, easy-drinking red from Beaujolais Gamay, as well as white from Chardonnay, Aligoté and Melon de Bourgogne. The old name may still be used.
fr-coteaux-bourguignons.terroir: Any land of the Burgundy and Beaujolais regional areas.
fr-coteaux-bourguignons.nerd_note: Bourgogne grand ordinaire remains a legal synonym, though almost no one uses it now.

fr-coteaux-champenois.name: Coteaux Champenois
fr-coteaux-champenois.summary: Coteaux Champenois is the appellation for still wines from the Champagne zone: red, white and rosé. It is rare (often under 0.1% of production) because it uses grapes that could become Champagne, which sells for far more. But it holds history: before bubbles took over, Champagne was known for still red and pale wines, and villages such as Bouzy, Aÿ, Ambonnay and Cumières still make pale, perfumed Pinot Noir. Warmer vintages since 2015 have led growers such as Egly-Ouriet, Bérêche, Bollinger (La Côte aux Enfants in Aÿ) and Paul Bara to make serious, Burgundy-like reds. Village names are often added to the label, such as Bouzy Rouge.
fr-coteaux-champenois.terroir: Same chalk and marl as Champagne; the warmest south-facing slopes are used for red.
fr-coteaux-champenois.nerd_note: Still Champagne was served at Louis XIV's court, and Bouzy Rouge was a fashionable wine in nineteenth-century Paris.

fr-coteaux-d-aix-en-provence.name: Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence
fr-coteaux-d-aix-en-provence.grapes: Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Counoise, Cabernet Sauvignon, Carignan; Vermentino, Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Sauvignon Blanc, Ugni Blanc
fr-coteaux-d-aix-en-provence.summary: Coteaux d'Aix-en-Provence is the western part of Provence, between the Durance and the Mediterranean around Aix. It is cooler and windier than the Var, swept by the mistral. Cabernet Sauvignon has a long history here: Georges Brunet planted it at Château Vignelaure in the 1960s, which inspired Domaine de Trévallon. Rosé dominates, but the reds and whites are serious. Château La Coste, Château Vignelaure and Château Revelette are references.
fr-coteaux-d-aix-en-provence.terroir: Limestone and clay hills with gravel and marl, from the Étang de Berre to the Durance.
fr-coteaux-d-aix-en-provence.nerd_note: Château La Coste mixes wine with contemporary architecture and art, with pavilions by Tadao Ando, Frank Gehry, Renzo Piano and Jean Nouvel among the vines.

fr-coteaux-d-ancenis.name: Coteaux d'Ancenis
fr-coteaux-d-ancenis.grapes: Gamay, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon; Pinot Gris (Malvoisie)
fr-coteaux-d-ancenis.summary: A small appellation around Ancenis on the Loire, between the Pays Nantais and Anjou, specialising in light Gamay reds and rosés, with some Cabernet. Its curiosity is the sweetish Coteaux d'Ancenis Malvoisie, made from Pinot Gris. It was promoted from VDQS to AOC in 2011.
fr-coteaux-d-ancenis.terroir: Schist and granite slopes on both banks.
fr-coteaux-d-ancenis.nerd_note: Malvoisie here means Pinot Gris, a reminder of how many unrelated grapes have borne that name across Europe.

fr-coteaux-de-die.name: Coteaux de Die
fr-coteaux-de-die.summary: Coteaux de Die is a still, dry white from Clairette grown in the Diois. With about 3 ha declared in 2025, it is one of France's rarest appellations.
fr-coteaux-de-die.terroir: Limestone and marl in the Drôme valley.
fr-coteaux-de-die.nerd_note: It shares its delimited area with Clairette de Die and Crémant de Die.

fr-coteaux-de-l-aubance.name: Coteaux de l'Aubance
fr-coteaux-de-l-aubance.summary: The Aubance is the next river north of the Layon, and its slopes make lighter, fresher sweet Chenin. 'Sélection de Grains Nobles' may appear on wines from richer musts. Domaine de Montgilet and Domaine de Bablut are reliable.
fr-coteaux-de-l-aubance.terroir: Schist slopes, cooler and less exposed than the Layon.
fr-coteaux-de-l-aubance.nerd_note: Aubance wines are often more mineral and less overtly sweet than the Layon's, which makes them good food wines.

fr-coteaux-de-saumur.name: Coteaux de Saumur
fr-coteaux-de-saumur.summary: A tiny appellation for sweet Chenin from the Saumur tuffeau, picked overripe or with botrytis. Rare and charming, it shows the lighter, chalkier side of sweet Loire Chenin.
fr-coteaux-de-saumur.nerd_note: In the nineteenth century, sweet Saumur was more famous than the sparkling wine.

fr-coteaux-du-giennois.name: Coteaux du Giennois
fr-coteaux-du-giennois.summary: A small appellation north of Pouilly-Fumé, on both banks of the Loire around Gien and Cosne-sur-Loire. The Sauvignon is light and fresh; reds blend Pinot Noir and Gamay.
fr-coteaux-du-giennois.terroir: Flint and clay, limestone and sand.
fr-coteaux-du-giennois.nerd_note: Its red wines must blend Gamay and Pinot Noir.

fr-coteaux-du-layon.name: Coteaux du Layon
fr-coteaux-du-layon.summary:
The Layon is a small river that runs north-west into the Loire south of Angers, cutting a valley of steep schist slopes, and its sweet Chenin Blanc is one of France's great dessert wines. Morning fogs from the river encourage botrytis; growers pick by successive tries, sometimes into November, to make wines from moelleux to luscious liquoreux, with Chenin's high acidity balancing the sugar. They taste of quince, apricot, honey and acacia, and the best age for decades.

Six villages may add their names (Beaulieu-sur-Layon, Faye-d'Anjou, Rablay-sur-Layon, Rochefort-sur-Loire, Saint-Aubin-de-Luigné, Saint-Lambert-du-Lattay), and Chaume, on the slopes above Rochefort, has the right to 'Premier Cru'. The appellation peaked in fame in the nineteenth century; since the 1990s growers such as Jo Pithon, Patrick Baudouin, Domaine des Forges and Château Pierre-Bise have revived it, with a debate between rich, sugar-laden styles and lighter, fresher wines.
fr-coteaux-du-layon.terroir: Schist, sandstone, carboniferous coal measures (around Saint-Aubin and Chaudefonds) and volcanic rocks, on steep south-facing slopes. The river's mists and the slopes' heat suit botrytis.
fr-coteaux-du-layon.nerd_note: Coal was mined near Saint-Aubin-de-Luigné until the twentieth century, and growers say the coal-bearing schist gives a smoky note to the wines.

fr-coteaux-du-layon-beaulieu-sur-layon.name: Coteaux du Layon Beaulieu-sur-Layon
fr-coteaux-du-layon-beaulieu-sur-layon.summary: Beaulieu-sur-Layon is a Layon village of manor houses and old cellars, giving elegant sweet Chenin; Château Pierre-Bise and Château Soucherie are close by.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-beaulieu-sur-layon.terroir: Schist and volcanic rocks on slopes above the river.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-beaulieu-sur-layon.nerd_note: Six villages may add their name to Coteaux du Layon on sweet Chenin Blanc from botrytised or late-picked grapes.

fr-coteaux-du-layon-faye-d-anjou.name: Coteaux du Layon Faye-d'Anjou
fr-coteaux-du-layon-faye-d-anjou.summary: Faye-d'Anjou is a Layon village on the upper reaches of the river, giving sweet Chenin from schist and clay; Domaine de Juchepie is a leading organic estate here.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-faye-d-anjou.nerd_note: Six villages may add their name to Coteaux du Layon on sweet Chenin Blanc from botrytised or late-picked grapes.

fr-coteaux-du-layon-premier-cru-chaume.name: Coteaux du Layon premier cru Chaume
fr-coteaux-du-layon-premier-cru-chaume.summary: Chaume is the only premier cru of the Loire, a south-facing hillside at Rochefort-sur-Loire overlooking the Layon, giving rich, botrytised Chenin Blanc. It was recognised in 2007 after a long legal battle with neighbouring Quarts de Chaume over names. Château Soucherie, Château Pierre-Bise and Domaine des Forges make reference wines.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-premier-cru-chaume.terroir: Schist, sandstone and carboniferous rocks on a steep, sunny slope where autumn mists from the Layon favour noble rot.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-premier-cru-chaume.nerd_note: The Quarts de Chaume name comes from a quarter of the harvest that medieval tenants owed to the lord, which shows how prized this slope has always been.

fr-coteaux-du-layon-rablay-sur-layon.name: Coteaux du Layon Rablay-sur-Layon
fr-coteaux-du-layon-rablay-sur-layon.summary: Rablay-sur-Layon is a small Layon village on a bend of the river, giving sweet Chenin from schist and sandstone.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-rablay-sur-layon.nerd_note: Six villages may add their name to Coteaux du Layon on sweet Chenin Blanc from botrytised or late-picked grapes.

fr-coteaux-du-layon-rochefort-sur-loire.name: Coteaux du Layon Rochefort-sur-Loire
fr-coteaux-du-layon-rochefort-sur-loire.summary: Rochefort-sur-Loire, where the Layon meets the Loire, is the most famous Coteaux du Layon village, home of the Chaume premier cru and the Quarts de Chaume grand cru. Its sweet Chenins are rich and honeyed with bright acidity. Domaine des Baumard is a long-standing name.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-rochefort-sur-loire.terroir: Schist and sandstone on steep slopes above the river confluence.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-rochefort-sur-loire.nerd_note: Six villages may add their name to Coteaux du Layon on sweet Chenin Blanc from botrytised or late-picked grapes.

fr-coteaux-du-layon-saint-aubin-de-luign.name: Coteaux du Layon Saint-Aubin-de-Luigné
fr-coteaux-du-layon-saint-aubin-de-luign.summary: Saint-Aubin-de-Luigné is a Layon village of steep schist slopes and small domaines, giving concentrated sweet Chenin; Domaine des Forges, Domaine Cady and Philippe Delesvaux are key names.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-saint-aubin-de-luign.terroir: Schist and volcanic rocks (rhyolite, spilite) on steep slopes.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-saint-aubin-de-luign.nerd_note: Six villages may add their name to Coteaux du Layon on sweet Chenin Blanc from botrytised or late-picked grapes. Not to be confused with Saint-Aubin in Burgundy.

fr-coteaux-du-layon-saint-lambert-du-lat.name: Coteaux du Layon Saint-Lambert-du-Lattay
fr-coteaux-du-layon-saint-lambert-du-lat.summary: Saint-Lambert-du-Lattay is a Layon village known for growers such as Domaine Mosse and Domaine Ogereau, giving sweet and dry Chenin. It also hosts a museum of vine and wine of Anjou.
fr-coteaux-du-layon-saint-lambert-du-lat.nerd_note: Six villages may add their name to Coteaux du Layon on sweet Chenin Blanc from botrytised or late-picked grapes.

fr-coteaux-du-loir.name: Coteaux du Loir
fr-coteaux-du-loir.grapes: Pineau d'Aunis, Cabernet Franc, Gamay, Côt; Chenin Blanc
fr-coteaux-du-loir.summary: Coteaux du Loir is the area around Jasnières on the Loir. It is the heartland of Pineau d'Aunis, a pale, peppery red grape that gives light, spicy reds and rosés. Domaine de Bellivière and Le Briseau make good examples.
fr-coteaux-du-loir.terroir: Tuffeau and clay-flint slopes along the Loir.
fr-coteaux-du-loir.nerd_note: Pineau d'Aunis takes its name from the priory of Aunis near Saumur, and tradition says Henry III of England drank its wine; despite the name it is unrelated to Pinot.

fr-coteaux-du-lyonnais.name: Coteaux du Lyonnais
fr-coteaux-du-lyonnais.grapes: Gamay; Chardonnay and Aligoté for white
fr-coteaux-du-lyonnais.summary: Coteaux du Lyonnais is a small AOC on the hills west and southwest of Lyon, continuing the Beaujolais to the south. Its light Gamay reds and fresh Chardonnay whites are the house wines of Lyon's bouchons, and the area has shrunk to a few hundred hectares in production under pressure from the city's suburbs.
fr-coteaux-du-lyonnais.terroir: Granite, gneiss and some limestone and loess on hills from the Monts d'Or to the Monts du Lyonnais.
fr-coteaux-du-lyonnais.nerd_note: Coteaux du Lyonnais was a VDQS from 1952 and became an AOC in 1984.

fr-coteaux-du-quercy.name: Coteaux du Quercy
fr-coteaux-du-quercy.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Merlot, Tannat, Gamay
fr-coteaux-du-quercy.summary: South of Cahors on the Quercy limestone, between the Lot and the Aveyron, this former VDQS became an AOC in 2011. Its reds are based on Cabernet Franc, blended with Malbec, Merlot and Tannat, giving supple, fresh wines that are lighter than Cahors.
fr-coteaux-du-quercy.nerd_note: Cabernet Franc must make up at least 40% of the blend, unusual for the Southwest.

fr-coteaux-du-vendomois.name: Coteaux du Vendômois
fr-coteaux-du-vendomois.grapes: Pineau d'Aunis, Pinot Noir, Gamay, Cabernet Franc; Chenin Blanc
fr-coteaux-du-vendomois.summary: Further up the Loir around Vendôme, this small appellation is known for its vin gris made from Pineau d'Aunis, one of the few appellations where that grape must dominate.
fr-coteaux-du-vendomois.terroir: Tuffeau and clay-flint slopes along the Loir.
fr-coteaux-du-vendomois.nerd_note: The Vendômois vin gris is made essentially from Pineau d'Aunis, pressed quickly to give a pale, peppery rosé.

fr-coteaux-varois-en-provence.name: Coteaux Varois en Provence
fr-coteaux-varois-en-provence.grapes: Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Cabernet Sauvignon; Vermentino, Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Ugni Blanc, Sémillon
fr-coteaux-varois-en-provence.summary: Coteaux Varois en Provence is the cooler heart of the Var, around Brignoles and Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, at 350 to 500 m. Its rosés are fresher and more mineral than those of the coast. Château Miraval in Correns, a village that set out in the 1990s to become France's first fully organic commune, is the most famous estate, although most of Miraval's rosé is sold as Côtes de Provence. Domaine du Deffends and Château La Calisse are good names.
fr-coteaux-varois-en-provence.terroir: Limestone hills and plateaus of the Haut-Var, cooler at altitude.
fr-coteaux-varois-en-provence.nerd_note: Correns, where Miraval is located, is known as the first French village to convert nearly all its farmland to organic agriculture.

fr-cotes-d-auvergne.name: Côtes d'Auvergne
fr-cotes-d-auvergne.summary: Côtes d'Auvergne covers scattered vineyards around Clermont-Ferrand on volcanic soils, with five village names (Boudes, Chanturgue, Châteaugay, Corent, Madargue). Gamay dominates; Corent is famous for rosé. Before phylloxera the Puy-de-Dôme had one of the largest vineyards in France.
fr-cotes-d-auvergne.terroir: Volcanic basalt, marl and limestone on the slopes of the Limagne plain.
fr-cotes-d-auvergne.nerd_note: Before phylloxera the Puy-de-Dôme was one of France's largest wine departments, with tens of thousands of hectares; today only a few hundred remain.

fr-cotes-d-auvergne-boudes.name: Côtes d'Auvergne Boudes
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-boudes.summary: Boudes is the southernmost Côtes d'Auvergne cru, in a warm valley near Issoire, giving reds and rosés from Gamay and Pinot Noir. In the nineteenth century the Auvergne was one of France's largest vineyards, with tens of thousands of hectares, before phylloxera and the rural exodus reduced it to a few hundred.
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-boudes.nerd_note: Côtes d'Auvergne became an AOC in 2011; five crus may add their names.

fr-cotes-d-auvergne-chanturgue.name: Côtes d'Auvergne Chanturgue
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-chanturgue.summary: Chanturgue is a tiny Côtes d'Auvergne cru on a basalt plateau on the northern edge of Clermont-Ferrand, giving Gamay reds. Local legend links it to the origin of coq au vin.
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-chanturgue.nerd_note: Côtes d'Auvergne became an AOC in 2011; five crus may add their names.

fr-cotes-d-auvergne-chateaugay.name: Côtes d'Auvergne Chateaugay
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-chateaugay.summary: Châteaugay is a Côtes d'Auvergne cru below its medieval castle north of Clermont-Ferrand, giving Gamay reds and rosés. In the nineteenth century the Auvergne was one of France's largest vineyards, before phylloxera reduced it to a few hundred hectares.
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-chateaugay.nerd_note: Côtes d'Auvergne became an AOC in 2011; five crus may add their names.

fr-cotes-d-auvergne-corent.name: Côtes d'Auvergne Corent
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-corent.summary: Corent is a Côtes d'Auvergne cru on the volcanic Puy de Corent south of Clermont-Ferrand, traditionally known for rosé from Gamay. The hill was a major Gallic oppidum of the Arverni, and archaeologists have found evidence of feasting with imported Italian wine there.
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-corent.terroir: Basalt and volcanic ash over limestone marl on a volcanic plateau.
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-corent.nerd_note: Côtes d'Auvergne became an AOC in 2011; five crus may add their names.

fr-cotes-d-auvergne-madargues.name: Côtes d'Auvergne Madargues
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-madargues.summary: Madargues is a small Côtes d'Auvergne cru near Riom, giving Gamay reds. Riom and its surroundings were once a busy wine area supplying the Auvergne's towns; Madargues keeps a small part of that tradition alive.
fr-cotes-d-auvergne-madargues.nerd_note: Côtes d'Auvergne became an AOC in 2011; five crus may add their names.

fr-cotes-de-bergerac.name: Côtes de Bergerac
fr-cotes-de-bergerac.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
fr-cotes-de-bergerac.summary: Côtes de Bergerac is the stricter version of Bergerac, with lower yields and higher minimum ripeness. The reds are fuller and often oak-aged, and many of the area's best estates use it for their top cuvées. The whites must be medium-sweet (moelleux).
fr-cotes-de-bergerac.terroir: The same area as Bergerac; the best clay-limestone slopes are used.
fr-cotes-de-bergerac.nerd_note: Côtes de Bergerac Blanc must be moelleux, so a dry white from the same vines is sold as Bergerac Sec.

fr-cotes-de-blaye.name: Côtes de Blaye
fr-cotes-de-blaye.summary: Côtes de Blaye is now a white-only appellation for dry wines from the Blayais, often with Colombard alongside Sauvignon and Sémillon, a legacy of the Cognac-grape plantings on the northern edge of Bordeaux.
fr-cotes-de-blaye.terroir: Clay-limestone and sandy soils north of the citadel.
fr-cotes-de-blaye.nerd_note: Blaye is one of the few places in Bordeaux where Colombard, a Cognac grape, is still a traditional component of white wine.

fr-cotes-de-bordeaux.name: Côtes de Bordeaux
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux.summary: Côtes de Bordeaux is an umbrella created in 2009 (from the 2008 vintage) to bring together several hillside appellations on the right banks of the Garonne, Dordogne and Gironde under one marketable name. Four areas joined first: Blaye (formerly Premières Côtes de Blaye), Cadillac (the reds of the Premières Côtes de Bordeaux), Castillon (formerly Côtes de Castillon) and Francs (formerly Bordeaux-Côtes de Francs); Sainte-Foy joined in 2016. Wines can be sold under the plain Côtes de Bordeaux name, made from any of the areas, or with the area name in front. They are mostly Merlot-based reds, ripe and fresh, often the best value in Bordeaux.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux.terroir: Clay-limestone hills and plateaus on the 'côtes' facing the rivers, generally cooler and later-ripening than the Libournais.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux.nerd_note: Côtes de Bordeaux is one of the few cases where several existing appellations voluntarily merged their identity to gain export clout.

fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-blaye.name: Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-blaye.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Colombard
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-blaye.summary: Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux covers the hilly right bank of the Gironde estuary opposite the Médoc, and is the largest of the Côtes. Its reds are generous Merlot, its whites fresh Sauvignon. Château Bel-Air La Royère, Les Jonqueyres and Haut-Bertinerie are among the best.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-blaye.terroir: Clay-limestone hills with gravel and sand patches near the estuary.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-blaye.nerd_note: Blaye's growers use three names for three tiers: Côtes de Blaye (white only), Blaye Côtes de Bordeaux, and the stricter red Blaye AOC.

fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-cadillac.name: Cadillac Côtes de Bordeaux
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-cadillac.summary: Cadillac Côtes de Bordeaux is the red-wine appellation of the steep slopes along the right bank of the Garonne from Bordeaux to Cadillac, formerly the reds of Premières Côtes de Bordeaux. The views across the river to the Graves are spectacular and the wines, mostly Merlot, are fresh and juicy. Château Reynon (Dubourdieu family), Château Carignan and Clos Chaumont are good examples.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-cadillac.terroir: Steep clay-limestone and gravel slopes along the Garonne.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-cadillac.nerd_note: Not to be confused with the sweet white Cadillac AOC from the same villages.

fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-castillon.name: Castillon Côtes de Bordeaux
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-castillon.summary: Castillon lies immediately east of Saint-Émilion and shares its limestone plateau and slopes, which is why investors from Saint-Émilion moved in from the 1990s. Stephan von Neipperg (Château d'Aiguilhe) and the consultant Stéphane Derenoncourt (Domaine de l'A) showed what the côtes could do, and Clos Puy Arnaud became a biodynamic reference. The wines are Merlot with Cabernet Franc, fresh and mineral. The town is where the English were defeated in 1453, ending the Hundred Years War and three centuries of English Bordeaux.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-castillon.terroir: The eastward continuation of Saint-Émilion's limestone plateau and clay-limestone slopes, with sandy-gravel terraces near the Dordogne.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-castillon.nerd_note: Every summer the town re-enacts the 1453 Battle of Castillon with hundreds of volunteers, horses and cannon.

fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-francs.name: Francs Côtes de Bordeaux
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-francs.summary: Francs is the smallest of the Côtes, north-east of Castillon on the border with the Dordogne department, and one of the highest and coolest parts of the Gironde. The Thienpont family (Château Puygueraud) put it on the map, and Château Le Puy, farmed without chemicals by the Amoreau family for generations, is a cult name among natural-wine drinkers.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-francs.terroir: High clay-limestone plateaus and slopes, cooler than Saint-Émilion.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-francs.nerd_note: When the Japanese manga *Les Gouttes de Dieu* (Kami no Shizuku) featured Château Le Puy's 2003 vintage, the estate's stock sold out almost overnight.

fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-saint-macaire.name: Côtes de Bordeaux-Saint-Macaire
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-saint-macaire.summary: A small appellation for dry, medium-sweet and sweet white wines from ten communes around the medieval town of Saint-Macaire, on the right bank of the Garonne upstream of Sainte-Croix-du-Mont. Production is tiny and mostly local.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-saint-macaire.terroir: Clay-limestone and gravel slopes above the Garonne.
fr-cotes-de-bordeaux-saint-macaire.nerd_note: Saint-Macaire is one of the best-preserved medieval towns of the Gironde, a former river port whose ramparts and arcaded square date from its trading heyday on the Garonne.

fr-cotes-de-bourg.name: Côtes de Bourg
fr-cotes-de-bourg.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec
fr-cotes-de-bourg.summary: Côtes de Bourg covers the steep, hilly country around the old port of Bourg, just upstream of where the Dordogne and Garonne meet. Vines here predate the Médoc, and the Romans planted these slopes. Reds dominate, Merlot with a notable share of Malbec, and they are dark, firm and great value. François Mitjavile of Tertre Rôteboeuf makes Roc de Cambes here, a wine that showed what the appellation can do; Château Falfas is biodynamic, and Fougas, Brulesécaille and Martinat are reliable.
fr-cotes-de-bourg.terroir: Clay-limestone hills and steep slopes facing the Gironde, with gravel patches near the water and limestone caves under Bourg.
fr-cotes-de-bourg.nerd_note: Roc de Cambes, a natural amphitheatre of vines facing the Gironde, was bought in 1988 by François Mitjavile of Tertre Rôteboeuf, and its success showed that Bourg could make wine of classed-growth depth.

fr-cotes-de-duras.name: Côtes de Duras
fr-cotes-de-duras.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle; Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec
fr-cotes-de-duras.summary: Côtes de Duras lies south of Bergerac, around the castle of Duras, with Bordeaux grapes and a particular strength in crisp Sauvignon Blanc. Many growers are organic, and Domaine Mouthes Le Bihan and Domaine de Laulan are good names.
fr-cotes-de-duras.terroir: Clay-limestone and molasse hills between the Dropt and the Garonne.
fr-cotes-de-duras.nerd_note: The novelist Marguerite Duras took her pen name from this village, where her father owned a house.

fr-cotes-de-millau.name: Côtes de Millau
fr-cotes-de-millau.grapes: Gamay, Syrah, Fer Servadou, Cabernet Sauvignon; Chenin Blanc, Mauzac
fr-cotes-de-millau.summary: Vineyards in the Tarn gorges near Millau, close to Norman Foster's famous viaduct, on old limestone and schist terraces that cling to the valley sides. Reds blend Gamay and Syrah with Fer Servadou and Cabernet; whites use Chenin Blanc and Mauzac. The local cooperative makes most of the wine, which is light, peppery and fresh.
fr-cotes-de-millau.terroir: Limestone and schist terraces in the Tarn gorges.
producers: Les Vignerons des Gorges du Tarn
fr-cotes-de-millau.nerd_note: Before phylloxera the Tarn gorges had thousands of hectares of terraced vines; the terraces can still be seen in the scrub.

fr-cotes-de-montravel.name: Côtes de Montravel
fr-cotes-de-montravel.summary: A small appellation for medium-sweet (moelleux) white wines from the Montravel area at the western end of the Bergerac vineyard, made from Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle picked late. The wines are softer and lighter than Monbazillac, with honey and white-peach notes, and are mostly sold locally. Only a handful of growers still declare it.
fr-cotes-de-montravel.nerd_note: It is part of a trio with Montravel (dry) and Haut-Montravel (sweeter).

fr-cotes-de-provence.name: Côtes de Provence
fr-cotes-de-provence.grapes: Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Tibouren, Carignan, Cabernet Sauvignon; Vermentino (Rolle), Clairette, Sémillon, Ugni Blanc
fr-cotes-de-provence.summary:
Côtes de Provence is the largest appellation of Provence, about 20,300 ha across 84 communes of the Var, the Bouches-du-Rhône and a corner of the Alpes-Maritimes, and the engine of the pale-rosé boom. Around 90% of its production is rosé: dry, light salmon-pink, made by direct pressing or short maceration, mostly from Grenache and Cinsault with Syrah and the local Tibouren. The appellation also makes reds and whites, often from the same estates.

It is a huge and diverse area. Five 'dénominations de terroir' highlight distinct zones: Sainte-Victoire (2005, limestone at the foot of Cézanne's mountain, east of Aix), Fréjus (2005, volcanic red rhyolite near the coast, known for Tibouren rosé), La Londe (2008, schist near the sea in the Maures, with whites and rosés), Pierrefeu (2013, between the Maures and the limestone hills) and Notre-Dame des Anges (2019, the inland Maures foothills near Pignans).

The 1955 crus classés are a curiosity: 23 estates were classified while the area was a VDQS, and 18 still use the title, including Château Minuty, Château Sainte-Roseline, Clos Mireille (Domaines Ott), Château de Selle (Ott), Château Roubine and Clos Cibonne, a champion of Tibouren. The classification has never been revised. Rosé's economics are spectacular: a well-branded Provence rosé sells at two to three times the price of a red Côtes du Rhône, and investors including LVMH, Pernod Ricard and the Pitt-Jolie partnership (Miraval) have bought in.
fr-cotes-de-provence.terroir: Two Provences: limestone hills in the north and west (Sainte-Victoire, the Haut-Var) and crystalline schist, gneiss and volcanic rock in the south-east (Maures, Esterel), plus the inland Permian depression of red sandstone and clay. Mistral and sea breezes.
producers: Domaines Ott (Clos Mireille, Château de Selle)
fr-cotes-de-provence.nerd_note: Clos Cibonne, near Toulon, ages its Tibouren rosé under a thin veil of yeast in old casks, a traditional technique that gives it nutty, savoury depth unlike any other Provence rosé.

fr-cotes-de-provence-la-londe.name: Côtes de Provence la Londe
fr-cotes-de-provence-la-londe.summary: Côtes de Provence La Londe (2008) covers coastal vineyards east of Hyères facing the islands of Porquerolles and Port-Cros, giving fine rosés and reds on schist. The schist and the sea winds give La Londe's rosés more tension than those of inland Provence.
fr-cotes-de-provence-la-londe.terroir: Schist and quartz soils with strong maritime influence.

fr-cotes-de-provence-sainte-victoire.name: Côtes de Provence Sainte-Victoire
fr-cotes-de-provence-sainte-victoire.summary: Côtes de Provence Sainte-Victoire (2005) lies at the foot of the limestone Montagne Sainte-Victoire east of Aix, the mountain Cézanne painted more than eighty times. Its rosés and reds are fresher and more structured than coastal Provence thanks to altitude and the mistral.
fr-cotes-de-provence-sainte-victoire.terroir: Limestone, red clay and gravel on the southern flank of the mountain, with cold winters and dry summers.
fr-cotes-de-provence-sainte-victoire.nerd_note: The mountain is visible from almost every vineyard, and some estates name cuvées after Cézanne's paintings.

fr-cotes-de-toul.name: Côtes de Toul
fr-cotes-de-toul.summary: Côtes de Toul, promoted from VDQS (1951) to AOC on 31 March 1998, covers about 110 ha in eight communes west of Toul: Blénod-lès-Toul, Bruley, Bulligny, Charmes-la-Côte, Domgermain, Lucey, Mont-le-Vignoble and Pagney-derrière-Barine. Its speciality is vin gris, a pale, fresh rosé made by pressing red grapes immediately, mostly from Gamay with at least 10 percent Pinot Noir. Pinot Noir makes the red wine and Auxerrois the white.
fr-cotes-de-toul.terroir: Limestone and Jurassic marl on an east-facing escarpment above the Moselle valley, at 200 to 380 m.
fr-cotes-de-toul.nerd_note: Vin gris must blend at least two grape varieties, with no single variety above 85 percent.

fr-cotes-du-forez.name: Côtes du Forez
fr-cotes-du-forez.summary: The Côtes du Forez lie on the eastern slopes of the Monts du Forez, near Boën. The volcanic and granitic soils give fresh Gamay. The cooperative and Domaine Verdier-Logel are the main producers.
fr-cotes-du-forez.terroir: Volcanic basalt and granite on east-facing slopes.
fr-cotes-du-forez.nerd_note: Côtes du Forez is among the furthest-upstream appellations on the Loire itself.

fr-cotes-du-jura.name: Côtes du Jura
fr-cotes-du-jura.grapes: Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard, Trousseau, Pinot Noir
fr-cotes-du-jura.summary: Côtes du Jura is the regional appellation, covering the whole Jura vineyard (about 640 ha in production) from Salins-les-Bains in the north to Saint-Amour in the south. It makes every Jura style. The south of the region, the Sud Revermont around Rotalier and Lons-le-Saunier, has become famous through Jean-François Ganevat, the Labet family and Domaine Pignier, who make single-site Chardonnay of Burgundian finesse.
fr-cotes-du-jura.terroir: Grey, blue and red marls with limestone; the Revermont in the south has warmer slopes and more limestone.
fr-cotes-du-jura.nerd_note: Château d'Arlay claims to be the oldest wine estate in France still in operation by the same lineage of owners, documented since the eleventh century.

fr-cotes-du-marmandais.name: Côtes du Marmandais
fr-cotes-du-marmandais.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Abouriou, Fer Servadou, Malbec, Syrah
fr-cotes-du-marmandais.summary: On both banks of the Garonne around Marmande, upstream of Bordeaux. What sets it apart is Abouriou, a local early-ripening red grape. Elian Da Ros, a former Zind-Humbrecht cellar hand, made the appellation known with his natural, Abouriou-based wines.
fr-cotes-du-marmandais.terroir: Gravel and clay-limestone along the Garonne.
fr-cotes-du-marmandais.nerd_note: Abouriou was grown for years in California under the name 'Early Burgundy' before DNA work identified it.

fr-cotes-du-rhone.name: Côtes du Rhône
fr-cotes-du-rhone.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre (red, together at least 70%) plus many others
fr-cotes-du-rhone.summary:
Côtes du Rhône is the regional appellation of the whole valley, covering 26,777 ha in production in 2025 (down from more than 31,000 ha in 2020) across 167 communes in six departments. It is one of France's largest AOCs; the 2025 harvest was about 920,000 hectolitres of mostly red wine, typically Grenache-based blends from the south. Quality ranges from co-operative bulk wine to excellent bottlings such as Château de Fonsalette (from Rayas), Coudoulet de Beaucastel and Guigal's Côtes du Rhône. The northern Rhône's growers can also use it for declassified Syrah and Viognier.

A few lieux-dits may be added, and Brézème, a small hill of about 30 ha at Livron-sur-Drôme between the north and south, is the only place permitted to put its own name with the Côtes du Rhône name, for mostly pure Syrah.
fr-cotes-du-rhone.terroir: Every soil of the valley, from northern granite to southern pebble terraces, sands and limestone.
fr-cotes-du-rhone.nerd_note: Côtes du Rhône lost about 4,400 ha between 2020 and 2025 as growers pulled out vines under France's grubbing-up scheme.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-brezeme.name: Côtes du Rhône Brézème
fr-cotes-du-rhone-brezeme.grapes: Syrah; Marsanne, Roussanne, Viognier for white
fr-cotes-du-rhone-brezeme.summary: Brézème is a 30 ha hill of terraced limestone and marl at Livron-sur-Drôme, where the Drôme meets the Rhône, halfway between the Northern and Southern Rhône. It is the only lieu-dit allowed to put its own name before Côtes du Rhône on the label. Mostly planted with Syrah, it makes northern-style reds; Jean-Marie Lombard revived it in the 1970s, and the Perrin family now farms Domaine de Bréseyme here.
fr-cotes-du-rhone-brezeme.terroir: Limestone marl terraces held by dry-stone walls on a south-facing hill.
fr-cotes-du-rhone-brezeme.nerd_note: Brézème shows that the line between the Northern and Southern Rhône is not absolute: its Syrah tastes far more northern than its latitude suggests.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages.summary: Côtes du Rhône Villages is the middle tier of the Rhône hierarchy: 8,019 ha in 2025, of which about 2,700 ha are sold under the plain Villages name and about 5,300 ha add one of the named villages. Yields are lower and grape rules stricter than for Côtes du Rhône. The cahier des charges under review by INAO in June 2026 lists 21 named villages: Chusclan, Gadagne, Massif d'Uchaux, Nyons, Plan de Dieu, Puyméras, Roaix, Rochegude, Rousset-les-Vignes, Sablet, Saint-Andéol, Saint-Gervais, Saint-Maurice, Saint-Pantaléon-les-Vignes, Sainte-Cécile, Séguret, Signargues, Suze-la-Rousse, Vaison-la-Romaine, Valréas and Visan. Nyons (2020) is the newest. Many former named villages, from Gigondas (1971) to Cairanne (2015) and Laudun (2024), have graduated to cru.
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages.terroir: Varied: pebble terraces of the Plan de Dieu, limestone hills of Séguret and Sablet, sands of the Massif d'Uchaux and Sainte-Cécile, marl and limestone of the Drôme villages.
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages.nerd_note: Ten of the named villages (Gadagne, Massif d'Uchaux, Nyons, Plan de Dieu, Puyméras, Saint-Andéol, Sainte-Cécile, Signargues, Suze-la-Rousse and Vaison-la-Romaine) cannot use their name on rosé.
contains: Côtes du Rhône Villages Massif d'Uchaux
Côtes du Rhône Villages Plan de Dieu

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-chusclan.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Chusclan
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-chusclan.summary: Gard-bank villages around Chusclan and Bagnols-sur-Cèze north of Laudun, long known for rosé; a named village since 1967. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-gadagne.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Gadagne
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-gadagne.summary: Five communes east of Avignon around Châteauneuf-de-Gadagne, on pebble terraces like Châteauneuf's; a named village since 2012. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-massif-d-ucha.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Massif d'Uchaux
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-massif-d-ucha.summary: A wooded massif of sandstone and sand north of Orange, recognised in 2005; red only, known for fine, perfumed Grenache from estates such as Château Saint-Estève and Domaine de la Guicharde. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-nyons.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Nyons
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-nyons.summary: Olive capital of the Drôme provençale, recognised in 2020, with limestone hills at altitude giving fresh reds. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-plan-de-dieu.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Plan de Dieu
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-plan-de-dieu.summary: A flat plateau of pebble-strewn garrigue between Orange and Vaison, once Templar land, making ripe, powerful Grenache-based reds. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-puymeras.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Puyméras
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-puymeras.summary: Hill vineyards in Puyméras, Faucon and Mérindol-les-Oliviers near Vaison-la-Romaine at up to 400 m, giving fresh, spicy reds. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-roaix.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Roaix
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-roaix.summary: A small village between Rasteau and Séguret with limestone and marl slopes; a named village since 1967. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-rochegude.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Rochegude
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-rochegude.summary: A village with a medieval château north of Orange, on pebble and sand terraces. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-rousset-les-v.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Rousset-les-Vignes
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-rousset-les-v.summary: A high village in the Drôme provençale on limestone, recognised in 1969, making fresh reds. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-sablet.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Sablet
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-sablet.summary: A village below the Dentelles near Gigondas on sandy soils (its name means sand), known for fine reds and some of the best whites of the Villages. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-saint-andeol.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Saint-Andéol
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-saint-andeol.summary: Four Ardèche communes around Saint-Marcel-d'Ardèche and Bourg-Saint-Andéol on the right bank, the only named village in the Ardèche. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-saint-gervais.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Saint-Gervais
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-saint-gervais.summary: A Gard village on a terrace above the Cèze, recognised in 1974; Domaine Sainte-Anne put it on the map. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-saint-maurice.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Saint-Maurice
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-saint-maurice.summary: Saint-Maurice-sur-Eygues in the Drôme, recognised in 1967, with pebble terraces along the Eygues. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-saint-pantale.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Saint-Pantaléon-les-Vignes
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-saint-pantale.summary: A Drôme village near Valréas, recognised in 1969, with sandy and limestone soils. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-sainte-cecile.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Sainte-Cécile
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-sainte-cecile.summary: Sainte-Cécile-les-Vignes and neighbours north of Orange, recognised in 2016, on pebble and sand terraces. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-seguret.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Séguret
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-seguret.summary: A perched medieval village below the Dentelles, with limestone slopes giving structured reds and fine whites. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-signargues.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Signargues
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-signargues.summary: Four Gard communes west of Avignon on pebble terraces, recognised in 2005; red only. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-suze-la-rouss.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Suze-la-Rousse
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-suze-la-rouss.summary: Villages around the castle of Suze-la-Rousse, home of the Université du Vin, recognised in 2016. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-vaison-la-rom.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Vaison-la-Romaine
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-vaison-la-rom.summary: Vineyards in Buisson and Villedieu near the Roman town of Vaison, recognised in 2016. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-valreas.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Valréas
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-valreas.summary: The largest named village, in the papal enclave (Enclave des Papes) of the Vaucluse surrounded by the Drôme, recognised in 1967. It is a named village (dénomination géographique complémentaire) of the Côtes du Rhône Villages AOC.

fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-visan.name: Côtes du Rhône Villages Visan
fr-cotes-du-rhone-villages-visan.summary: Visan, in the Vaucluse next to the Enclave des Papes, has been a named village of the Côtes du Rhône Villages since the 1960s, with pebbly terraces and limestone hills giving generous reds and some whites. It is listed in the cahier des charges but not drawn as a separate area in INAO's October 2026 parcel file, so its boundary may be missing from the map.

fr-cotes-du-roussillon.name: Côtes du Roussillon
fr-cotes-du-roussillon.grapes: Grenache, Carignan, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Lledoner Pelut; Grenache Blanc, Grenache Gris, Macabeu, Malvoisie, Marsanne, Roussanne, Vermentino
fr-cotes-du-roussillon.summary: The regional dry-wine appellation of Roussillon, covering most of the Pyrénées-Orientales. Reds blend Grenache, Carignan, Syrah and Mourvèdre; the whites, from Grenache Blanc and Gris and Macabeu, have improved greatly. The best dry wines of the region are often sold under it or as IGP Côtes Catalanes.
