fr-cotes-du-roussillon.terroir: Alluvial terraces, schist, granite, limestone; dry, windy, sunny.
fr-cotes-du-roussillon.nerd_note: The Côtes Catalanes IGP is used by many top Roussillon growers for wines that do not fit AOC rules, such as single-variety Carignan or Grenache Gris.

fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages.name: Côtes du Roussillon Villages
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages.grapes: Grenache, Carignan, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Lledoner Pelut
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages.summary: Côtes du Roussillon Villages is red only, from the northern half of the department, mainly the Agly valley. Five villages may add their names: Caramany (granite and gneiss), Latour-de-France (schist), Lesquerde (granite), Tautavel (limestone, near the famous prehistoric cave) and Les Aspres (clay-limestone terraces south of the Têt, the only one outside the Agly). The wines are dense, spicy and powerful, from old Grenache and Carignan, often on very low yields.
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages.terroir: Agly valley schist, granite and limestone; Les Aspres clay-silt terraces.
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages.nerd_note: Tautavel is famous for 'Tautavel Man', fossils about 450,000 years old found in the Caune de l'Arago cave, some of the oldest human remains in Europe.

fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-caramany.name: Côtes du Roussillon Villages Caramany
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-caramany.summary: Caramany is a village of the Agly valley on gneiss and granite, giving firm, fragrant reds, often with a high share of old Carignan.
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-caramany.nerd_note: Côtes du Roussillon Villages allows a handful of villages to add their names.

fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-les-aspr.name: Côtes du Roussillon Villages Les Aspres
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-les-aspr.summary: Les Aspres, between the Têt and Tech valleys south of Perpignan, is the newest Côtes du Roussillon Villages name (2017), for reds with a significant share of Syrah and Mourvèdre.
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-les-aspr.terroir: Gravel terraces, clay and schist at the foot of the Pyrenees.
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-les-aspr.nerd_note: Côtes du Roussillon Villages allows a handful of villages to add their names.

fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-lesquerd.name: Côtes du Roussillon Villages Lesquerde
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-lesquerd.summary: Lesquerde is a granite village of the upper Agly valley, giving bright, mineral reds. Lesquerde lies in the Fenouillèdes, the granite hills that belonged to Languedoc rather than Catalan Roussillon until the Revolution.
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-lesquerd.nerd_note: Côtes du Roussillon Villages allows a handful of villages to add their names.

fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-tautavel.name: Côtes du Roussillon Villages Tautavel
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-tautavel.summary: Tautavel, in the Agly valley, is famous for the 'Tautavel Man', human remains about 450,000 years old found in the Arago cave. Its reds from Grenache, Syrah, Carignan and Mourvèdre are dense and spicy.
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-tautavel.terroir: Limestone and black schist below cliffs.
fr-cotes-du-roussillon-villages-tautavel.nerd_note: Côtes du Roussillon Villages allows a handful of villages to add their names.

fr-cotes-du-vivarais.name: Côtes du Vivarais
fr-cotes-du-vivarais.summary: Côtes du Vivarais lies in the southern Ardèche around the Gorges de l'Ardèche and Vallon-Pont-d'Arc, near the Chauvet Cave. Its light, fruity Grenache and Syrah reds and rosés come from limestone plateaux; the area has fallen to only 120 ha (2025).
fr-cotes-du-vivarais.terroir: Limestone plateaux and garrigue around the Ardèche gorges.
fr-cotes-du-vivarais.nerd_note: Domaine Gallety makes the appellation's best-known age-worthy reds.

fr-coulee-de-serrant.name: Savennières Coulée de Serrant
fr-coulee-de-serrant.summary: One of the few French appellations owned by a single estate: 7 ha of steep slope over a small valley running down to the Loire, planted by Cistercian monks in 1130. Nicolas Joly's family bought it in 1962; he converted to biodynamics in 1981 and became the most famous evangelist of biodynamic winemaking in the world. The wine, harvested in several tries with some botrytis, is rich and powerful, notoriously variable, and capable of decades of ageing.
fr-coulee-de-serrant.terroir: Schist and volcanic rhyolite with very thin soils on a steep, south-facing ravine.
producers: Nicolas Joly (Clos de la Coulée de Serrant)
fr-coulee-de-serrant.nerd_note: Joly writes that the vines are cultivated by horse and that the estate's purpose is to let the vineyard express itself; he founded the group La Renaissance des Appellations in 2001.

fr-cour-cheverny.name: Cour-Cheverny
fr-cour-cheverny.summary: Cour-Cheverny is one of France's rarest appellations and the only one for Romorantin, a white grape that King François I is said to have brought from Burgundy to the town of Romorantin in 1519. The wines are dry or off-dry, with high acidity, notes of honey, beeswax and citrus, and can age decades. Philippe Tessier, François Cazin and Hervé Villemade make it.
fr-cour-cheverny.terroir: Sand and clay with flint in the Sologne.
fr-cour-cheverny.nerd_note: DNA work shows Romorantin is one of the offspring of Pinot and Gouais Blanc, which makes it a full sibling of Chardonnay.

fr-cremant-d-alsace.name: Crémant d'Alsace
fr-cremant-d-alsace.grapes: Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Chardonnay
fr-cremant-d-alsace.summary: Crémant d'Alsace, recognised by decree on 24 August 1976, is traditional-method sparkling wine made with a second fermentation in bottle, at least 9 months on the lees and no release until 12 months after bottling. Mostly based on Pinot Blanc and Auxerrois, with Chardonnay, Riesling and Pinot Gris, it is fresh, creamy and apple-scented; rosé is made only from Pinot Noir. Grapes for crémant are earmarked in the vineyard before harvest and picked earlier. It has been Alsace's growth category in the 2020s while still-wine sales declined, and producers such as Pierre Sparr, Wolfberger, Dopff au Moulin (which pioneered it in the early twentieth century), Lucien Albrecht and Cave de Turckheim make large volumes.
fr-cremant-d-alsace.terroir: Grown across the whole Alsace AOC area; cooler sites and earlier picking give the necessary acidity.
fr-cremant-d-alsace.nerd_note: Julien Dopff learned the Champagne method in Épernay and began making sparkling wine in Riquewihr in 1900, 76 years before the crémant appellation existed.

fr-cremant-de-bordeaux.name: Crémant de Bordeaux
fr-cremant-de-bordeaux.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle, Ugni Blanc, Colombard, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
fr-cremant-de-bordeaux.summary: Crémant de Bordeaux is traditional-method sparkling wine, made white or rosé with at least nine months on the lees. It grew from a nineteenth-century tradition of Bordeaux sparkling wine centred on Bourg and the Entre-Deux-Mers, and has become one of the few growth categories in the region as growers look for alternatives to red. The rosés, often Merlot and Cabernet Franc, are especially popular.
fr-cremant-de-bordeaux.terroir: Grapes come from across the Gironde, mostly cool clay-limestone sites in the Entre-Deux-Mers and Blaye that keep acidity.
fr-cremant-de-bordeaux.nerd_note: Bordeaux had its own sparkling wine houses before the First World War, and Crémant production has grown sharply since 2020 as growers redirect vineyards away from unsold red.

fr-cremant-de-bourgogne.name: Crémant de Bourgogne
fr-cremant-de-bourgogne.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Aligoté, Gamay (max 20%), Melon de Bourgogne, Sacy
fr-cremant-de-bourgogne.summary: Crémant de Bourgogne is Burgundy's traditional-method sparkling wine, created in 1975 to replace Bourgogne mousseux. It is made mostly from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, with second fermentation in bottle and at least 9 months on the lees (24 months for Éminent and 36 for Grand Éminent, two quality tiers introduced in 2016). It now accounts for more than 10 percent of Burgundy's production, and much of it comes from the Châtillonnais in the north, the Auxerrois, Rully and the Mâconnais. Houses such as Bailly-Lapierre, Louis Bouillot, Veuve Ambal and Simonnet-Febvre are the big names.
fr-cremant-de-bourgogne.terroir: Grown across Burgundy, especially the cooler Châtillonnais (on limestone like that of Champagne's Côte des Bar) and the Auxerrois.
fr-cremant-de-bourgogne.nerd_note: The cellars of Bailly-Lapierre are dug into an old underground quarry on the Yonne that once supplied stone for Paris monuments.

fr-cremant-de-die.name: Crémant de Die
fr-cremant-de-die.summary: Crémant de Die, created in 1993, is the dry, traditional-method sparkling wine of the Diois, made mostly from Clairette with Aligoté and a little Muscat. It is crisp and lightly floral, and with only 64 ha (2025) it is one of the smaller crémant appellations.
fr-cremant-de-die.terroir: Limestone and marl slopes in the Drôme valley.

fr-cremant-de-limoux.name: Crémant de Limoux
fr-cremant-de-limoux.grapes: Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc, Mauzac, Pinot Noir
fr-cremant-de-limoux.summary: Crémant de Limoux, created in 1990, is the traditional-method sparkling wine of Limoux, with Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc dominant, Mauzac in a minor role, and Pinot Noir for rosé. It has more finesse and less of Mauzac's green-apple tang than Blanquette, and is a well-priced alternative to Champagne.
fr-cremant-de-limoux.terroir: Clay-limestone at altitude, cooler than the Mediterranean plain.
fr-cremant-de-limoux.nerd_note: The Sieur d'Arques cooperative is by far the largest producer, alongside family houses such as Antech, whose ancestors made Blanquette in the nineteenth century.

fr-cremant-de-loire.name: Crémant de Loire
fr-cremant-de-loire.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, Grolleau, Orbois
fr-cremant-de-loire.summary: Crémant de Loire is the Loire's regional traditional-method sparkling wine, covering Anjou, Saumur, Touraine and Cheverny, with at least 12 months on the lees. Chenin and Chardonnay dominate the whites; the rosés use Cabernet Franc and Pinot Noir. It is one of France's three largest crémants, with Alsace and Burgundy, and a growing alternative to Champagne.
fr-cremant-de-loire.terroir: Mostly the tuffeau of Saumur and Touraine; houses age it in tuffeau caves.
fr-cremant-de-loire.nerd_note: Saumur's houses can sell the same wine as Saumur Brut or Crémant de Loire; the difference lies in production rules such as whole-cluster pressing and minimum lees ageing.

fr-cremant-du-jura.name: Crémant du Jura
fr-cremant-du-jura.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Poulsard, Trousseau, Savagnin
fr-cremant-du-jura.summary: Crémant du Jura, created in the mid-1990s, is the traditional-method sparkling wine of the Jura, mostly from Chardonnay, and now accounts for about a quarter of the region's production. It is crisp and fine, and the Jura has made sparkling wine since the nineteenth century.
fr-cremant-du-jura.terroir: Grown across the Jura AOC area.

fr-criots-batard-montrachet.name: Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet
fr-criots-batard-montrachet.summary: Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet, about 1.6 ha south of Bâtard entirely in Chassagne, is the smallest and rarest of the Montrachet family. Its stony soil (criots probably means a place full of stones) gives a fine, mineral wine. Only a handful of producers bottle it: Blain-Gagnard, Fontaine-Gagnard, Roger Belland, Joseph Drouhin and Hubert Lamy.
fr-criots-batard-montrachet.terroir: Stony, thin soil on a small slope south of Bâtard at about 240 m.
fr-criots-batard-montrachet.nerd_note: Total annual production is typically under 10,000 bottles, the smallest output of the five Montrachet grand crus.

fr-crozes-hermitage.name: Crozes-Hermitage
fr-crozes-hermitage.grapes: Syrah (up to 15% Marsanne and Roussanne); Marsanne and Roussanne for white
fr-crozes-hermitage.summary: Crozes-Hermitage is the largest appellation of the Northern Rhône (2,139 ha in 2025, still growing) and surrounds the hill of Hermitage on the east bank across 11 communes. Most is on flatter terraces and gentle hills, and the wines are fresh, fruity, peppery Syrah to drink young; the best, from the granite hills of the north around Gervans and Larnage or the pebbly terraces of Les Chassis to the south, approach Hermitage. The Cave de Tain co-operative makes a large share. Growers such as Alain Graillot (whose domaine his sons continue), Yann Chave, Combier, Domaine des Entrefaux and Dard et Ribo built its modern reputation.
fr-crozes-hermitage.terroir: Granite hills in the north (Gervans, Erôme, Serves), loess and clay around Mercurol and Larnage, and glacial pebble terraces of Les Chassis and Les Sept Chemins in the south.
fr-crozes-hermitage.nerd_note: Jaboulet's Domaine de Thalabert, first bottled separately in the 1960s, was the first Crozes-Hermitage to be taken seriously by critics.

fr-duche-d-uzes.name: Duché d'Uzès
fr-duche-d-uzes.grapes: Syrah (min 40%) and Grenache (min 20%) for red; Viognier (min 40%) and Grenache Blanc for white
fr-duche-d-uzes.summary: Duché d'Uzès became an AOC in July 2013 after a campaign that began in 1989, covering garrigue hills around the old ducal town of Uzès, between Nîmes and Alès. All its wines are blends: reds based on Syrah and Grenache, rosés, and whites led by Viognier. Its 285 ha (2025) produced 9,089 hl at only 32 hl/ha. The appellation celebrates the 'royal vines' of Arpaillargues-et-Aureilhac.
fr-duche-d-uzes.terroir: Limestone garrigue, marls and sandstones on low hills at the foot of the Cévennes.
fr-duche-d-uzes.nerd_note: Uzès is not in INAO's parcel delimitation file of October 2026, so its boundary on the map may be drawn from communes.

fr-echezeaux.name: Echezeaux
fr-echezeaux.summary:
Échezeaux, in the commune of Flagey-Échezeaux, is the second-largest grand cru of the Côte de Nuits at about 37.7 ha, made up of 11 lieux-dits stretched from the Clos de Vougeot wall up toward the woods. The size and the mix of soils mean that Échezeaux is the most variable of the Vosne grand crus. The upper parts, such as Les Échezeaux du Dessus, Les Poulaillères and En Orveaux, give the most refined wine.

At its best Échezeaux is fragrant, spicy and supple, more approachable than Grands-Échezeaux. Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, Emmanuel Rouget (from Henri Jayer's vines), Mongeard-Mugneret, Arnoux-Lachaux, Dujac, Anne Gros, Grivot and Georges Noëllat are among about 80 owners.
fr-echezeaux.terroir: Brown limestone and marl, deeper at the bottom near the Clos de Vougeot wall, thinner and stonier at the top under the woods.
fr-echezeaux.nerd_note: The name comes from chesaux, an old word for a group of houses; the official register spells it without an accent.

fr-entraygues-le-fel.name: Entraygues - Le Fel
fr-entraygues-le-fel.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Mauzac; Fer Servadou, Cabernet Franc, Gamay
fr-entraygues-le-fel.summary: Tiny terraced vineyards on granite and schist at the confluence of the Lot and Truyère, in the north of the Aveyron. The whites, mostly Chenin Blanc, are crisp and mineral, and the reds blend Fer Servadou and Cabernet Franc. Laurent Mousset is the reference producer.
fr-entraygues-le-fel.nerd_note: Entraygues means 'between waters' in Occitan, referring to the two rivers.

fr-entre-deux-mers.name: Entre-deux-Mers
fr-entre-deux-mers.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle; Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc for red
fr-entre-deux-mers.summary: Entre-deux-Mers is the large district between the Garonne and the Dordogne, and the appellation of the same name has long been Bordeaux's crisp, dry white: Sauvignon Blanc-led, often with Sémillon and Muscadelle, unoaked and meant for oysters from Arcachon. From the 2023 vintage the INAO also allowed red Entre-deux-Mers with stricter rules than Bordeaux rouge, such as a planting density of at least 4,500 vines per hectare, a ban on thermovinification, and 21 months of ageing before release, so the first reds reached shelves in 2025. It is an attempt to lift a district hit hard by the collapse of bulk red prices. The sub-denomination Entre-deux-Mers-Haut-Benauge covers nine communes in the south.
fr-entre-deux-mers.terroir: Clay-limestone plateaus and slopes, with gravel patches and silty boulbènes; cooler and later than the Médoc.
fr-entre-deux-mers.nerd_note: The red Entre-deux-Mers rules ban thermovinification, the heat-extraction technique widely used for cheap, fruity reds, a deliberate signal that the new wines are meant to sit above basic Bordeaux rouge.

fr-entre-deux-mers-haut-benauge.name: Entre-deux-Mers Haut-Benauge
fr-entre-deux-mers-haut-benauge.summary: Entre-deux-Mers Haut-Benauge covers nine communes of the old county of Benauge around Targon and the castle of Benauge, giving dry Sauvignon-Sémillon whites under the Entre-deux-Mers name and sweet whites as Bordeaux Haut-Benauge.
fr-entre-deux-mers-haut-benauge.terroir: Clay-limestone plateau and slopes in the heart of the Entre-Deux-Mers.

fr-estaing.name: Estaing
fr-estaing.grapes: Fer Servadou, Gamay; Chenin Blanc, Mauzac
fr-estaing.summary: A tiny appellation on the Lot below the medieval village and castle of Estaing, a stop on the pilgrimage road to Santiago, with vines on steep schist and limestone terraces. Reds blend Fer Servadou and Gamay; whites use Chenin Blanc and Mauzac. Production is very small and almost all drunk in the Aveyron.
fr-estaing.terroir: Terraced slopes of schist and limestone.
fr-estaing.nerd_note: With only about twenty hectares, Estaing is one of France's smallest AOCs.

fr-faugeres.name: Faugères
fr-faugeres.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Lledoner Pelut, Cinsault; Grenache Blanc, Marsanne, Roussanne, Vermentino
fr-faugeres.summary: Faugères, north of Béziers in the foothills of the Cévennes, is entirely on schist, the same rock as Banyuls and Priorat. Its reds are smooth and fragrant, with dark fruit, garrigue and a mineral, slightly smoky edge. It was among the first Languedoc AOCs (1982 for reds and rosés). Domaine Léon Barral, Domaine Alquier, Château des Estanilles and Mas d'Alezon are leading estates. The village's old windmills overlook the vineyards.
fr-faugeres.terroir: Devonian and Carboniferous schist, hard and fractured, on hills at 200 to 400 m.
fr-faugeres.nerd_note: Faugères whites became AOC only in 2005; before that the area was red and rosé only.

fr-fiefs-vendeens.name: Fiefs Vendéens
fr-fiefs-vendeens.grapes: Pinot Noir, Gamay, Cabernet Franc, Négrette; Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Grolleau Gris
fr-fiefs-vendeens.summary: Fiefs Vendéens covers five scattered zones in the Vendée department south of Nantes (Brem, Mareuil, Pissotte, Vix and Chantonnay). Its fresh rosés, light reds and whites are mostly drunk by the summer crowds on the Atlantic beaches. Domaine Saint-Nicolas at Brem, biodynamic, is the reference producer.
fr-fiefs-vendeens.terroir: Schist and clay near the coast; limestone further inland.
fr-fiefs-vendeens.nerd_note: Cardinal Richelieu began his career as bishop of Luçon in the Vendée, and local tradition says he favoured the wines of Mareuil.

fr-fiefs-vendeens-brem.name: Fiefs Vendéens Brem
fr-fiefs-vendeens-brem.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Gamay
fr-fiefs-vendeens-brem.summary: Brem lies near the Atlantic coast at Brem-sur-Mer, giving Chenin-based whites and fresh reds; Thierry Michon's biodynamic Domaine Saint-Nicolas made the area known.
fr-fiefs-vendeens-brem.terroir: Schist and sandy soils swept by sea winds.
fr-fiefs-vendeens-brem.nerd_note: Fiefs Vendéens became an AOC in 2011; its five named areas each have their own grape mix.

fr-fiefs-vendeens-chantonnay.name: Fiefs Vendéens Chantonnay
fr-fiefs-vendeens-chantonnay.summary: Chantonnay is the inland, eastern area of Fiefs Vendéens, giving reds and rosés from Pinot Noir and Gamay. The Vendée's wines are said to have been favoured by Cardinal Richelieu, who was bishop of nearby Luçon before he became Louis XIII's chief minister.
fr-fiefs-vendeens-chantonnay.nerd_note: Fiefs Vendéens became an AOC in 2011; its five named areas each have their own grape mix.

fr-fiefs-vendeens-mareuil.name: Fiefs Vendéens Mareuil
fr-fiefs-vendeens-mareuil.grapes: Pinot Noir, Gamay, Cabernet Franc, Chenin Blanc
fr-fiefs-vendeens-mareuil.summary: Mareuil, on the Lay river, is the largest area of Fiefs Vendéens, best known for red and rosé from Pinot Noir, Gamay and Cabernet Franc (with some Négrette), and Chenin whites. Jérémie Mourat's estate is a leading producer.
fr-fiefs-vendeens-mareuil.nerd_note: Fiefs Vendéens became an AOC in 2011; its five named areas each have their own grape mix.

fr-fiefs-vendeens-pissotte.name: Fiefs Vendéens Pissotte
fr-fiefs-vendeens-pissotte.summary: Pissotte, near Fontenay-le-Comte, is a small area of Fiefs Vendéens giving whites from Chenin and Chardonnay and light reds. The Vendée's wines are said to have been favoured by Cardinal Richelieu, who was bishop of nearby Luçon.
fr-fiefs-vendeens-pissotte.nerd_note: Fiefs Vendéens became an AOC in 2011; its five named areas each have their own grape mix.

fr-fiefs-vendeens-vix.name: Fiefs Vendéens Vix
fr-fiefs-vendeens-vix.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Franc
fr-fiefs-vendeens-vix.summary: Vix lies on the edge of the Marais Poitevin in southern Vendée, giving whites from Chenin, Chardonnay and Sauvignon and fresh reds.
fr-fiefs-vendeens-vix.terroir: Limestone and clay on the edge of the marshes.
fr-fiefs-vendeens-vix.nerd_note: Fiefs Vendéens became an AOC in 2011; its five named areas each have their own grape mix.

fr-fitou.name: Fitou
fr-fitou.grapes: Carignan, Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Lledoner Pelut
fr-fitou.summary: Fitou was the first Languedoc red AOC, in 1948, ahead of the region's revival. It has two separate parts: a coastal zone around Fitou, Leucate and Treilles on limestone near the Étang de Leucate, and an inland mountain zone around Tuchan, Paziols and Villeneuve-les-Corbières on schist. Reds are dark, spicy and sturdy. The Mont Tauch cooperative in Tuchan is the largest producer.
fr-fitou.terroir: Clay-limestone near the coast; schist and limestone in the mountain zone.
fr-fitou.nerd_note: Fitou's two zones are separated by part of the Corbières appellation, so the appellation is cut in two.

fr-fixin.name: Fixin
fr-fixin.summary: Fixin is a small village just north of Gevrey-Chambertin whose reds are firm, dark and earthy, like a slightly rustic Gevrey. Most wine is red, from premier crus such as Clos de la Perrière, Clos Napoléon, Les Hervelets, Les Arvelets and Clos du Chapitre. Wines from neighbouring Brochon may be sold as Fixin or Côte de Nuits-Villages. Fixin also has a link to Napoleon: Claude Noisot, an officer of his Imperial Guard, built a park and commissioned a statue of the emperor awakening to immortality by François Rude in 1847.
fr-fixin.terroir: Steep slopes of limestone and marl; Clos de la Perrière sits on an old quarry at the top of the village.
fr-fixin.nerd_note: Clos de la Perrière, a monopole of the Joliet family, was ranked as a tête de cuvée, alongside Chambertin, in Dr Jules Lavalle's 1855 classification of Burgundy.

fr-fleurie.name: Fleurie
fr-fleurie.summary: Fleurie is the most popular cru and, as its name suggests, the most floral: violet, iris and red berries over a silky, elegant texture. Its slopes of pure pink granite surround a village crowned by the chapel of La Madone, built in the 1870s on the hilltop above the vines. In 2023 more than 85 percent of Fleurie's growers voted to apply for premier cru status for seven lieux-dits (Les Moriers, Poncié, Les Garants, La Madone, La Roilette, Grille Midi and La Chapelle des Bois), about 27 percent of the appellation; INAO's decision is expected to take years.
fr-fleurie.terroir: A single granite massif with sandy gore; La Roilette next to Moulin-à-Vent has more clay and gives fuller wine.
fr-fleurie.nerd_note: The Cave de Fleurie co-operative, long led by Marguerite Chabert, popularised the cru in Lyon and Paris after the Second World War.

fr-floc-de-gascogne.name: Floc de Gascogne
fr-floc-de-gascogne.grapes: Colombard, Gros Manseng, Ugni Blanc, Folle Blanche; Merlot, Cabernet, Tannat for rosé
fr-floc-de-gascogne.summary: Floc de Gascogne is a liqueur wine (vin de liqueur), made by adding young Armagnac to unfermented grape juice, in the Armagnac area, then resting it for several months before release. Its name means 'bouquet of flowers' in Gascon. Served chilled as an aperitif, it comes in white and rosé versions.
fr-floc-de-gascogne.terroir: The Armagnac area's sandy (Bas-Armagnac) and clay-limestone soils.
fr-floc-de-gascogne.nerd_note: The Armagnac must be from the same estate as the grape juice, a rule that keeps Floc a farm product.

fr-fronsac.name: Fronsac
fr-fronsac.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec
fr-fronsac.summary: Fronsac is a set of hills on the right bank of the Dordogne just west of Libourne, overlooking the confluence with the Isle. In the eighteenth century its wines were fashionable at Versailles, partly thanks to the Maréchal de Richelieu, Duc de Fronsac, and priced above Saint-Émilion. Today it is one of the best-value right-bank appellations: firm, dark, slightly rustic Merlot with Cabernet Franc, mineral and long-lived. Château de la Dauphine, Villars, Dalem, Fontenil and Les Trois Croix are references.
fr-fronsac.terroir: Limestone hills capped by clay and the *molasse du Fronsadais* (sandstone and clay), steeper and higher than most of the right bank. The Tertre de Fronsac rises 75 m above the river.
fr-fronsac.nerd_note: Legend says Charlemagne built a fort on the Tertre de Fronsac in 769 to watch the river; whatever stood there, the hill controlled traffic on the Dordogne for centuries.

fr-fronton.name: Fronton
fr-fronton.grapes: Négrette (at least 50%), Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Gamay, Malbec, Fer Servadou
fr-fronton.summary: Fronton is Toulouse's local wine, from terraces between the Tarn and the Garonne. It is the home of Négrette, a red grape with violet and liquorice notes, which must make up at least half of the blend. Local legend says the Knights Hospitaller brought it from Cyprus in the Middle Ages; the story is colourful but unproven, and the grape appears to be a local variety. Reds are supple and aromatic; rosés are popular. Château Bellevue la Forêt and Château Plaisance lead.
fr-fronton.terroir: Three terraces of the Tarn: gravel and boulbènes (silty clay) on the lower terraces, and red, iron-rich 'rouget' soils higher up.
fr-fronton.nerd_note: Négrette is prone to rot in humid weather, so it thrives only in Fronton's well-drained terraces and dry autan wind.

fr-gaillac.name: Gaillac
fr-gaillac.grapes: Duras, Braucol (Fer Servadou), Prunelard, Syrah, Gamay; Mauzac, Len de l'El (Loin de l'Œil), Ondenc, Muscadelle, Sauvignon Blanc
fr-gaillac.summary:
Gaillac, on the Tarn east of Toulouse, is one of the oldest vineyards in France and probably the most varied. Roman potters at Montans made amphorae for the local wine, and the Benedictines of Saint-Michel (972) built its medieval trade. It makes every style: red, white, rosé, dry, sweet and sparkling.

Its secret weapon is its grapes. Reds blend Duras and Braucol (the local name for Fer Servadou), often with Syrah; whites use Mauzac (green-apple and pear), Len de l'El (an Occitan name meaning 'far from the eye', for its long stalks), Ondenc and Muscadelle. The *méthode gaillacoise*, or ancestral method, makes a sparkling wine in a single fermentation, finished in the bottle without added sugar or yeast, a technique much older than Champagne's second fermentation. Robert Plageoles and his son Bernard revived forgotten grapes (Ondenc, Prunelard, Verdanel, Mauzac Noir) and a sherry-like *vin de voile*. Today, natural-wine producers such as Domaine de Brin, Causse Marines and Nicolas Carmarans keep up the experimentation.
fr-gaillac.terroir: Three zones: gravel terraces of the Tarn's left bank, limestone plateau on the right bank (the premières côtes and Cordes area), and the sand and granite of the Cunac plateau near Albi. The south-easterly 'vent d'autan' dries the grapes.
fr-gaillac.nerd_note: Gaillac's 'vin de voile', aged under a veil of yeast in old barrels like Jura's vin jaune, was revived by Robert Plageoles from local tradition.

fr-gaillac-premieres-cotes.name: Gaillac premières côtes
fr-gaillac-premieres-cotes.grapes: Mauzac, Len de l'El, Ondenc, Muscadelle, Sauvignon Blanc
fr-gaillac-premieres-cotes.summary: A sub-appellation for dry and sweet whites from the limestone hills on the right bank of the Tarn, with stricter ripeness rules than plain Gaillac. It is rarely seen on labels, since most growers sell under the better-known Gaillac name or with mentions such as doux or perlé.
fr-gaillac-premieres-cotes.terroir: Limestone hillsides on the right bank of the Tarn.
fr-gaillac-premieres-cotes.nerd_note: Despite its age, the name appears on only a handful of bottles.

fr-gevrey-chambertin.name: Gevrey-Chambertin
fr-gevrey-chambertin.summary:
Gevrey-Chambertin is the largest red village of the Côte d'Or and the home of nine grand crus, more than any other commune. In 1847 the village of Gevrey added the name of its most famous vineyard, Chambertin, starting a fashion that spread down the Côte. Its reds are the most powerful and structured of the Côte de Nuits: dark fruit, spice, earth and firm tannin, built to age.

The appellation spreads unusually far onto flatter land east of the main road, and village-level quality varies widely. The best premier crus lie on two slopes. North of the Combe de Lavaux, the southeast-facing Côte Saint-Jacques holds Clos Saint-Jacques, Lavaut Saint-Jacques, Les Cazetiers and Combe au Moine, often as fine as the grand crus. South of the village, a continuous band of grand crus runs from Mazis-Chambertin and Ruchottes past Chambertin and Clos de Bèze to Latricières and Mazoyères at the Morey border. Gevrey's growers range from historic names such as Armand Rousseau to modern stars such as Denis Mortet, Fourrier, Claude Dugat and Duroché.
fr-gevrey-chambertin.terroir: Bajocian and Bathonian limestones with marls; the Combe de Lavaux spreads a cone of scree and gravel that gives the village land unusual depth. Slopes face east and southeast at 250 to 380 m.
fr-gevrey-chambertin.nerd_note: Some Gevrey-Chambertin village wine legally comes from Brochon, which shares a strip of the appellation.

fr-gigondas.name: Gigondas
fr-gigondas.grapes: Grenache (max 80%) with at least 15% Syrah and/or Mourvèdre; whites from Clairette from 2022
fr-gigondas.summary: Gigondas sits under the jagged limestone spires of the Dentelles de Montmirail, and its vineyards climb from 100 to more than 500 m, among the highest in the Southern Rhône. It was the first village to break away from the Côtes du Rhône Villages and become a cru in 1971. The reds are powerful, spicy and structured, with dark fruit, garrigue and a fresh edge from altitude, often compared to a more rustic Châteauneuf. A small amount of rosé is made, and since September 2022 white Gigondas, based on Clairette, has also been allowed. The appellation had 1,184 ha in 2025.
fr-gigondas.terroir: Triassic and Jurassic limestone and marl under the Dentelles, with sandy and clay terraces lower down; the higher sites (Les Hautes Garrigues, Le Colombier) give the freshest wines.
fr-gigondas.nerd_note: Château de Saint-Cosme's cellars include Gallo-Roman fermentation vats cut into the rock.

fr-givry.name: Givry
fr-givry.summary: Givry, south of Mercurey, is a red-wine village whose fame dates to King Henri IV, who is said to have favoured it (and a mistress who lived here). Its 37 premier crus include Clos Salomon, Clos du Cellier aux Moines and Clos Jus. The reds are fragrant, light-bodied and fresh; the whites are crisp and stony.
fr-givry.terroir: Limestone slopes and combes, with stony white soils on the upper slopes.
fr-givry.nerd_note: Clos du Cellier aux Moines was a Cistercian vineyard of the abbey of La Ferté from 1130; its cellar still stands.

fr-grand-roussillon.name: Grand Roussillon
fr-grand-roussillon.summary: An old regional VDN appellation covering the whole of Roussillon, with the same grapes and mutage rules as Rivesaltes. It is almost never used today, since producers prefer Rivesaltes, Maury or Banyuls. Wines labelled 'rancio' can be found under the name in old stocks.
fr-grand-roussillon.nerd_note: Grand Roussillon is one of France's most obscure AOCs, with production in some years close to zero.

fr-grands-echezeaux.name: Grands-Echezeaux
fr-grands-echezeaux.summary: Grands-Échezeaux, about 9.1 ha on flatter land next to the top wall of Clos de Vougeot and just below Musigny, is considered the finer and more consistent of the two Échezeaux grand crus. Its wines are dense, structured and deeply aromatic, with the power of Vosne and some of Musigny's perfume. Domaine de la Romanée-Conti owns about 3.5 ha, and Mongeard-Mugneret, Joseph Drouhin, Gros Frère et Sœur and Lamarche share most of the rest.
fr-grands-echezeaux.terroir: Deeper, flatter brown limestone soils with clay, at about 260 m.
fr-grands-echezeaux.nerd_note: The Cistercian monks of Cîteaux owned and worked Grands-Échezeaux alongside the Clos de Vougeot.

fr-graves.name: Graves
fr-graves.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc; Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle
fr-graves.summary: Graves takes its name from its gravel, the only major French appellation named after a soil. Since 1987 it has meant the southern part of the old district, from Cadaujac and Saint-Médard-d'Eyrans south past Podensac, Portets and Langon, wrapping around Cérons, Barsac and Sauternes. The reds are softer and earlier-drinking than Pessac-Léognan, with the same smoky earthiness; the dry whites, often Sémillon-rich and barrel-fermented, are some of the best value white wines in France. Clos Floridène, created by Denis and Florence Dubourdieu, Château de Chantegrive, Vieux Château Gaubert and Château Rahoul are reliable.
fr-graves.terroir: Sand and gravel terraces on the left bank of the Garonne, with more sand and clay in the south. The pine forest at the back gives cool nights.
fr-graves.nerd_note: Graves is one of the few places in Bordeaux where Sémillon still dominates dry whites, and old-vine Sémillon from here is the closest thing to the region's historic white style.

fr-graves-de-vayres.name: Graves de Vayres
fr-graves-de-vayres.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon
fr-graves-de-vayres.summary: Graves de Vayres is a small island of gravel on the left bank of the Dordogne opposite Libourne, around the communes of Vayres and Arveyres. It makes supple, Merlot-based reds and some dry whites, and owes its separate appellation to its gravelly soils, unusual in the Entre-Deux-Mers. The Renaissance Château de Vayres overlooks the river.
fr-graves-de-vayres.terroir: Gravel terraces left by the Dordogne, distinct from the surrounding clay-limestone.
fr-graves-de-vayres.nerd_note: The name refers to a gravel terrace of the Dordogne and has nothing to do with the Graves district on the Garonne, which makes it the only 'Graves' on the right bank.

fr-graves-superieures.name: Graves Supérieures
fr-graves-superieures.summary: Graves Supérieures is a sweet or medium-sweet white wine appellation covering the Graves area. It is a survivor from the days when much of the southern Graves made semi-sweet wine for the Dutch and Belgian markets. Production is small today, mostly late-harvested Sémillon from estates near Cérons and Barsac, and the wines are softer and lighter than Sauternes. It is useful for nerds hunting rare aged bottles, which can be surprisingly cheap.
fr-graves-superieures.terroir: The same gravel and sand as Graves, with sweet-wine sites near the Ciron and the Garonne where morning mists encourage botrytis in good years.
fr-graves-superieures.nerd_note: Graves Supérieures does not require botrytis, so wines range from late-harvest moelleux to genuinely nobly rotten liquoreux depending on vintage and estate.

fr-gres-de-montpellier.name: Grés de Montpellier
fr-gres-de-montpellier.summary: Grés de Montpellier is a red-only appellation for the hills and terraces around Montpellier, between the Hérault and Vidourle valleys. Recognised in 2003 as a named terroir of Coteaux du Languedoc, it now has its own AOC specification (amended in 2025), covering 45 communes. Blends must include at least two of Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre, with Carignan, Cinsault and Morrastel as supporting grapes, and wines rest until at least 15 September after the harvest.
fr-gres-de-montpellier.terroir: Poor, stony hillsides ('grés' in Occitan) of limestone, sandstone, marl and rounded quartz pebbles left by an ancient Rhône delta; Mediterranean climate with sea breezes.
fr-gres-de-montpellier.nerd_note: The Cistercian abbey of Valmagne, founded in 1138, still makes wine within the appellation and keeps its huge oak casks in the nave of its church.

fr-grignan-les-adhemar.name: Grignan-les-Adhémar
fr-grignan-les-adhemar.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Cinsault, Mourvèdre, Carignan; whites from Viognier, Marsanne, Roussanne, Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Bourboulenc
fr-grignan-les-adhemar.summary: Grignan-les-Adhémar was called Coteaux du Tricastin until 2010, when growers changed its name to escape association with the Tricastin nuclear plant after a uranium leak in 2008. It covers hills and plateaux of the Drôme provençale around the château of Grignan, where Madame de Sévigné's daughter lived. Its 971 ha (2025, down from 1,270 in 2020) make light, fruity reds and some fresh whites.
fr-grignan-les-adhemar.terroir: Limestone, sandy and pebbly soils on plateaux and hills, with mistral exposure.
fr-grignan-les-adhemar.nerd_note: The name honours the Adhémar family, lords of Grignan whose Renaissance château dominates the town.

fr-griotte-chambertin.name: Griotte-Chambertin
fr-griotte-chambertin.summary: Griotte-Chambertin, about 2.7 ha in a slight hollow below Chambertin, is the smallest of Gevrey's grand crus. Its name is often linked to griotte (sour cherry), which suits the wine's bright red-cherry fruit, though it may come from criot, a stony place. The wines are aromatic and fleshy, with a lovely freshness. Ponsot, Fourrier, Claude Dugat, Joseph Drouhin and Chézeaux are among a small group of owners.
fr-griotte-chambertin.terroir: A shallow bowl of stony soil over limestone that traps heat; just below Chambertin.
fr-griotte-chambertin.nerd_note: With so little land, a whole year's Griotte-Chambertin is often barely a thousand cases for the whole world.

fr-gros-plant-du-pays-nantais.name: Gros Plant du Pays nantais
fr-gros-plant-du-pays-nantais.summary: Gros Plant is the local name for Folle Blanche, a Cognac grape, and its wine is famously lean and tart. It was a VDQS until it became AOC in 2011. With sur lie ageing, the best examples are bracing, saline and perfect with oysters.
fr-gros-plant-du-pays-nantais.terroir: Same soils as Muscadet; the grape is prone to rot, so it is planted on the driest sites.
fr-gros-plant-du-pays-nantais.nerd_note: Folle Blanche was the main Cognac grape before phylloxera; in Nantes it survives as a wine grape.

fr-haut-medoc.name: Haut-Médoc
fr-haut-medoc.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
fr-haut-medoc.summary:
The Haut-Médoc appellation covers the 29 communes of the southern Médoc that are not entitled to, or choose not to use, one of the six communal names. It is a patchwork that runs from the suburbs of Bordeaux at Blanquefort and Le Taillan to Saint-Seurin-de-Cadourne north of Saint-Estèphe, and from the river to the forest edge. Five 1855 classed growths use it: La Lagune (third) and Cantemerle (fifth) on the southern sands and gravel near Ludon and Macau; La Tour Carnet, Belgrave and Camensac (fourth and fifth) inland at Saint-Laurent.

Quality varies with distance from the estuary. The best non-classified estates, such as Sociando-Mallet at Saint-Seurin and Lanessan at Cussac, make long-lived, Cabernet-driven reds that compete with classed growths. The appellation is also home to many Crus Bourgeois, including five 2025 Exceptionnels (Malescasse, de Malleret, Paloumey, Reysson, du Taillan).
fr-haut-medoc.terroir: Mixed Garonne gravels near the river, with sand, clay and limestone further inland. Southern estates on sandy gravel (La Lagune, Cantemerle) give softer, more perfumed wine; northern ones on gravel over clay give firmer, Saint-Estèphe-like structure.
fr-haut-medoc.nerd_note: Château Cantemerle was added to the 1855 list in September 1855, months after the original April document, because its owner protested that it had been forgotten; its name was squeezed in at the bottom of the fifth growths.

fr-haut-montravel.name: Haut-Montravel
fr-haut-montravel.summary: The sweetest of the Montravel trio, from a few villages in the east of the area, made from overripe or botrytised Sémillon, Sauvignon and Muscadelle picked in successive passes. In good years it rivals Monbazillac, but production is tiny because most growers now prefer to make dry Montravel.
fr-haut-montravel.nerd_note: Very small production; most growers prefer to make dry Montravel.

fr-haut-poitou.name: Haut-Poitou
fr-haut-poitou.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay; Cabernet Franc, Gamay, Pinot Noir
fr-haut-poitou.summary: A small appellation north of Poitiers, best known for crisp Sauvignon Blanc from the cooperative of Neuville-de-Poitou, which made the name in the 1980s. It became AOC in 2011.
fr-haut-poitou.nerd_note: Haut-Poitou lies on the plateau north of Poitiers, about 70 km south of the Loire itself, on the road toward Cognac country.

fr-hermitage.name: Hermitage
fr-hermitage.grapes: Syrah (up to 15% Marsanne and Roussanne); Marsanne and Roussanne for white
fr-hermitage.summary:
Hermitage is a single south-facing hill of 137 ha (2025) rising above Tain-l'Hermitage on the east bank of the Rhône, and it has been one of France's most famous wines for three centuries. Legend says a knight, Gaspard de Stérimberg, returned wounded from the crusade against the Albigensians in 1224 and was granted the hill by Queen Blanche of Castile to live as a hermit; the chapel of Saint-Christophe at the top recalls him. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries Hermitage sold for prices close to Lafite, and some Bordeaux was 'hermitagé', strengthened with Hermitage.

Red Hermitage is a powerful, dense, long-lived Syrah: black fruit, smoke, leather and spice that need 10 to 30 years. About a third of the hill makes white Hermitage, mostly Marsanne, which can age for decades into honeyed, nutty depths, and a little vin de paille. Traditionally the wines are blended from several of the hill's lieux-dits (Les Bessards, L'Hermite, Le Méal, Les Greffieux, Péléat, Les Rocoules, Les Diognières, Les Murets, Beaume), each adding a different element; Jean-Louis Chave's Hermitage is the model of this approach, while Chapoutier bottles single sites.
fr-hermitage.terroir: A granite block in the west (Les Bessards, Varogne) that the Rhône detached from the Massif Central; further east, loess, clay, alpine pebbles and limestone deposits (Le Méal, Les Greffieux, Les Murets). Terraces at 120 to 340 m, facing due south.
fr-hermitage.nerd_note: Hermitage may legally be spelled Ermitage, and Chapoutier uses that spelling for its single-site 'Ermitage' wines such as Le Pavillon and L'Ermite.

fr-irancy.name: Irancy
fr-irancy.grapes: Pinot Noir with up to 10% César
fr-irancy.summary: Irancy is the red-wine village of the Auxerrois, a natural amphitheatre of slopes 15 km southwest of Chablis that became a village AOC in 1999. Pinot Noir dominates, but growers may add up to 10 percent César, an old, dark and tannic local grape. The wines are fresh, red-fruited and peppery, with more grip than most regional Burgundy, and from good growers they age for a decade. Cherry orchards share the slopes, and the village celebrates them as much as its wine.
fr-irancy.terroir: Kimmeridgian marls and limestone on south and southeast-facing slopes; the Côte de Palotte and Les Mazelots are its best-known climats.
fr-irancy.nerd_note: César, thought to be a cross of Pinot Noir and Argant, survives almost only here; Domaine Colinot is known for rare pure César bottlings sold as Bourgogne.

fr-irouleguy.name: Irouléguy
fr-irouleguy.grapes: Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon; Gros Manseng, Petit Manseng, Petit Courbu
fr-irouleguy.summary: Irouléguy is France's only Basque wine appellation, a small vineyard in the Pyrenean foothills near Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port on the pilgrimage route to Santiago. Monks of the Roncesvalles abbey planted the first vines. Steep slopes are terraced on red sandstone at up to 400 m. Tannat dominates the reds, which are fresher and more mineral than Madiran's. Domaine Arretxea, Domaine Ilarria, Domaine Brana and the cooperative are the main producers.
fr-irouleguy.terroir: Red sandstone (grès rouge), schist, ophite and limestone on steep, terraced mountain slopes.
fr-irouleguy.nerd_note: Labels often say 'Irulegi', the Basque spelling, and the cooperative's top wines bear Basque names.

fr-jasnieres.name: Jasnières
fr-jasnieres.summary: Jasnières is a single south-facing slope of tuffeau about 4 km long above the Loir river (the Loire's tributary, without the 'e'), north of Tours. Its dry and occasionally sweet Chenin is lean, piercing and mineral. Domaine de Bellivière (Éric and Christine Nicolas) and Pascal Janvier put it back on the map in the 1990s.
fr-jasnieres.terroir: South-facing tuffeau slope with clay-flint on top; a cool, northern site.
fr-jasnieres.nerd_note: The Loir valley's growers dig cellars and homes into the tuffeau cliffs, and some still live in troglodyte houses.

fr-julienas.name: Juliénas
fr-julienas.summary: Juliénas, named after Julius Caesar, is one of the most rustic and firmly structured crus. Its wines are dense and spicy with dark red fruit and need a year or two in bottle. The village's Cellier de la Vieille Église, a deconsecrated church turned tasting room, is decorated with Bacchic scenes.
fr-julienas.terroir: Granite in the west, older schist and alluvium in the east; slopes facing east and southeast at 250 to 400 m.
fr-julienas.nerd_note: The Château de Juliénas has one of the longest cellars in the Beaujolais.

fr-jurancon.name: Jurançon
fr-jurancon.grapes: Petit Manseng, Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu, Camaralet, Lauzet
fr-jurancon.summary:
Jurançon, in the foothills of the Pyrenees south and west of Pau, makes one of France's great sweet wines without relying on botrytis. Petit Manseng's tiny, thick-skinned berries are left on the vine into November or December, shrivelling (passerillage) in the dry foehn wind from Spain while keeping vibrant acidity. The result tastes of pineapple, mango, quince, ginger and honey, with a tangy freshness that sets it apart from Sauternes.

The legend says that when the future Henri IV was born in Pau in 1553, his grandfather rubbed his lips with garlic and a drop of Jurançon. In 1975 the appellation added Jurançon Sec, now about half the production, mostly from Gros Manseng. Vineyards on steep slopes are often trained high to avoid frost and rot, and the best are terraced. Henri Ramonteu of Domaine Cauhapé, Charles Hours of Clos Uroulat, Domaine de Souch and Clos Lapeyre are the reference producers.
fr-jurancon.terroir: Steep hills of clay, limestone and *poudingue* (a conglomerate of Pyrenean pebbles) at 300 to 400 m, with the warm, dry foehn wind in autumn.
fr-jurancon.nerd_note: Late-harvest Petit Manseng can hang into December, and in some years pickers bring in shrivelled bunches after the first snow on the Pyrenees.

fr-l-etoile.name: L'Etoile
fr-l-etoile.grapes: Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard (for vin de paille)
fr-l-etoile.summary: L'Étoile is a small white-wine appellation around the village of L'Étoile near Lons-le-Saunier. Its name, the star, may refer to the five hills around the village or to the star-shaped fossils of crinoids (pentacrines) in its limestone. It makes Chardonnay and Savagnin, vin jaune and vin de paille, and its crisp, mineral whites are some of the finest in the Jura.
fr-l-etoile.terroir: Marl and limestone with star-shaped crinoid fossils; five small hills around the village.
fr-l-etoile.nerd_note: L'Étoile and Château-Chalon (vin jaune only) are the two Jura appellations with no red wine.

fr-la-clape.name: La Clape
fr-la-clape.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan; Bourboulenc, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne, Marsanne, Vermentino
fr-la-clape.summary: La Clape is a limestone massif between Narbonne and the sea that was an island in Roman times, before silt from the Aude joined it to the mainland. Its vineyards sit in hollows among garrigue and pines, with the sea on two sides. The cru is famous for whites based on Bourboulenc (here called Malvoisie), which keep a saline freshness despite the heat. Reds are Syrah and Mourvèdre-rich. AOC since 2015. Château Pech Redon, Château de la Négly, Château Rouquette-sur-Mer and Gérard Bertrand's Château l'Hospitalet are references.
fr-la-clape.terroir: Limestone massif with marl and clay; sea influence, wind and very little rain.
fr-la-clape.nerd_note: La Clape is one of the few Languedoc crus where white wine has equal standing with red.

fr-la-grande-rue.name: La Grande Rue
fr-la-grande-rue.summary: La Grande Rue, a 1.65 ha strip between Romanée-Conti and La Tâche, is the monopole of Domaine François Lamarche. It was left as a premier cru in the 1930s, reportedly because the family did not apply for grand cru status, and was only promoted in 1992. The wine is fine and elegant with red fruit and spice; quality has improved markedly under Nicole Lamarche since the 2000s.
fr-la-grande-rue.terroir: Same brown limestone as its neighbours, on a narrow strip running up the slope.
fr-la-grande-rue.nerd_note: Its narrowness means the rows run the full height of the slope, so each row sees the whole range of soils.

fr-la-liviniere.name: Minervois-la-Livinière
fr-la-liviniere.summary: Minervois-La Livinière was the Languedoc's first communal cru, recognised in 1999, covering six communes around La Livinière on the limestone Petit Causse. Its reds are deep, structured and age well. Clos Centeilles, Château Sainte Eulalie, Château Maris and Domaine Combe Blanche are leading producers.
fr-la-liviniere.terroir: Limestone and marl on the south-facing slopes of the Petit Causse, at 150 to 300 m.
fr-la-liviniere.nerd_note: Patricia Boyer-Domergue of Clos Centeilles planted and saved old varieties such as Piquepoul Noir, Riveyrenc and Œillade.

fr-la-romanee.name: La Romanée
fr-la-romanee.summary: La Romanée, about 0.85 ha just above Romanée-Conti, is France's smallest appellation. It is a monopole of the Comte Liger-Belair family, who bought it in 1815. For decades the wine was made and sold by négociants such as Bouchard Père et Fils; since the 2002 vintage Louis-Michel Liger-Belair has made all of it himself. The wine is concentrated and finely structured, with dark fruit and a firm, mineral line, and needs long ageing.
fr-la-romanee.terroir: Steeper than Romanée-Conti, with thin soil over limestone; rows run across the slope in the upper part.
fr-la-romanee.nerd_note: La Romanée is the smallest AOC in France at 0.84 ha in INAO's parcel file.

fr-la-tache.name: La Tâche
fr-la-tache.summary: La Tâche, about 6.06 ha south of Romanée-Conti, is the other great monopole of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti. The domaine bought the original La Tâche in 1933 and merged it with the adjoining Les Gaudichots, expanding the grand cru to its current size. The wine is darker, more exuberant and spicier than Romanée-Conti, often more impressive young, and ages for decades.
fr-la-tache.terroir: Varied exposure from east to southeast, with steeper upper slopes; brown limestone with clay over limestone and marl.
fr-la-tache.nerd_note: Tâche means a task or piece of work, perhaps a plot worked by a sharecropper.

fr-ladoix.name: Ladoix
fr-ladoix.summary: Ladoix (officially the commune of Ladoix-Serrigny) is the northern gateway to the Côte de Beaune and the least known of the villages around the hill of Corton, even though part of its land is classified as Corton and Corton-Charlemagne grand cru. Its village and premier cru wines, such as Les Joyeuses, La Micaude, Le Bois Roussot and Les Grêchons, are supple, fruity reds and bright whites that offer some of the best prices in the Côte d'Or. Many growers here also sell wine as Côte de Beaune-Villages or under the Aloxe-Corton name, which shares some of Ladoix's slopes.
fr-ladoix.terroir: Limestone and marl at the eastern foot of the Corton hill, with some Côte de Nuits-style rocks at Buisson where the two côtes meet.
fr-ladoix.nerd_note: Ladoix sits at the boundary between the Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune: the hamlet of Buisson marks where Comblanchien limestone gives way to Beaune's marls.

fr-lalande-de-pomerol.name: Lalande-de-Pomerol
fr-lalande-de-pomerol.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec
fr-lalande-de-pomerol.summary: Lalande-de-Pomerol is Pomerol's northern neighbour, across the Barbanne stream, covering Lalande and Néac. It makes Merlot-dominated reds in a plush, Pomerol-like style at a third of the price, and several Pomerol and Saint-Émilion owners make wine here (La Fleur de Boüard of the Angélus family, Château Siaurac, Château de Chambrun). The twelfth-century church at Lalande was built by the Knights Hospitaller.
fr-lalande-de-pomerol.terroir: Gravel and sand in the south near Pomerol, more clay and limestone at Néac.
fr-lalande-de-pomerol.nerd_note: Néac was once a separate appellation; it merged into Lalande-de-Pomerol in 1954, one of the few cases of a Bordeaux appellation disappearing.

fr-languedoc.name: Languedoc
fr-languedoc.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Cinsault, Lledoner Pelut; Grenache Blanc, Roussanne, Marsanne, Vermentino, Bourboulenc, Clairette, Picpoul, Viognier
fr-languedoc.summary:
AOC Languedoc is the regional appellation that replaced the old Coteaux du Languedoc. Approved by the INAO in 2006 and applied from 2007, it covers the whole Languedoc and Roussillon, from Nîmes to the Spanish border, so any AOC wine in the region can be declassified into it. Reds must blend at least two of the main grapes (Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre), and many are excellent value.

Beneath it sit 'dénominations géographiques complémentaires' that can follow the Languedoc name. Some are well known: Grès de Montpellier (the terraces around Montpellier), older village names such as Saint-Georges-d'Orques, Saint-Christol, Saint-Drézéry and La Méjanelle, Pézenas (volcanic and schist hills around the town of Molière), Sommières (near the Gard), Cabrières (schist and limestone near Clermont-l'Hérault, on its way to its own AOC), Saint-Saturnin (Larzac foothills), and Quatourze (gravel near Narbonne). Montpeyroux, long one of them, became an AOC in its own right in 2026.

The appellation can feel like a catch-all, but it gives estates a recognisable name and lets the best terroirs climb toward cru status.
fr-languedoc.terroir: Every soil of the Mediterranean arc: limestone garrigue, schist, galets roulés, villafranchian terraces, basalt and marl; altitude from sea level to 400 m.
producers: Domaine de la Grange des Pères
fr-languedoc.nerd_note: Molière toured the Languedoc with his troupe from the 1640s and staged plays at Pézenas, whose growers now use his name on their wines.

fr-languedoc-cabrieres.name: Languedoc Cabrières
fr-languedoc-cabrieres.summary: Cabrières is a Languedoc terroir on schist north of Pézenas, long known for rosé and for Clairette; its reds are spicy and fresh.
fr-languedoc-cabrieres.terroir: Schist with volcanic and limestone outcrops.
fr-languedoc-cabrieres.nerd_note: Languedoc lets several historic terroirs add their name to the regional appellation for wines grown under stricter rules.

fr-languedoc-la-mejanelle.name: Languedoc La Méjanelle
fr-languedoc-la-mejanelle.summary: La Méjanelle lies on the eastern edge of Montpellier towards the airport, a terrace of large round pebbles (galets) like those of Châteauneuf-du-Pape, giving warm, generous reds. Château de Flaugergues, one of Montpellier's eighteenth-century 'folies', is the classic estate.
fr-languedoc-la-mejanelle.terroir: Thick beds of rounded quartz pebbles over red clay.
fr-languedoc-la-mejanelle.nerd_note: Languedoc lets several historic terroirs add their name to the regional appellation for wines grown under stricter rules.

fr-languedoc-quatourze.name: Languedoc Quatourze
fr-languedoc-quatourze.summary: Quatourze is a small Languedoc terroir near Narbonne on a pebble terrace beside the Aude, giving full-bodied, sun-baked reds; Château Notre-Dame du Quatourze is the main estate.
fr-languedoc-quatourze.nerd_note: Languedoc lets several historic terroirs add their name to the regional appellation for wines grown under stricter rules.

fr-languedoc-saint-christol.name: Languedoc Saint-Christol
fr-languedoc-saint-christol.summary: Saint-Christol, east of Montpellier, is a Languedoc terroir of pebbly terraces giving sunny, spicy reds; the village cooperative is central.
fr-languedoc-saint-christol.terroir: Rounded pebbles and red clay on Villafranchian terraces.
fr-languedoc-saint-christol.nerd_note: Languedoc lets several historic terroirs add their name to the regional appellation for wines grown under stricter rules.

fr-languedoc-saint-drezery.name: Languedoc Saint-Drézéry
fr-languedoc-saint-drezery.summary: Saint-Drézéry is the smallest named terroir of Languedoc, north-east of Montpellier, giving ripe, structured reds; Château Puech-Haut is its best-known estate.
fr-languedoc-saint-drezery.nerd_note: Languedoc lets several historic terroirs add their name to the regional appellation for wines grown under stricter rules.

fr-languedoc-saint-georges-d-orques.name: Languedoc Saint-Georges-d'Orques
fr-languedoc-saint-georges-d-orques.summary: Saint-Georges-d'Orques, west of Montpellier, is one of Languedoc's historic red terroirs: in the eighteenth century its wines were exported widely, and Thomas Jefferson ordered them for his cellar. Today they are supple Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre blends.
fr-languedoc-saint-georges-d-orques.nerd_note: Languedoc lets several historic terroirs add their name to the regional appellation for wines grown under stricter rules.

fr-languedoc-saint-saturnin.name: Languedoc Saint-Saturnin
fr-languedoc-saint-saturnin.summary: Saint-Saturnin lies at the foot of the Larzac plateau, a cool, high Languedoc terroir known for its 'vin d'une nuit', a rosé of one night's skin contact, and for firm, aromatic reds.
fr-languedoc-saint-saturnin.terroir: Limestone scree and clay at the foot of the plateau.
fr-languedoc-saint-saturnin.nerd_note: Languedoc lets several historic terroirs add their name to the regional appellation for wines grown under stricter rules.

fr-latricieres-chambertin.name: Latricières-Chambertin
fr-latricieres-chambertin.summary: Latricières-Chambertin, about 7.4 ha directly south of Chambertin, is cooled by air flowing from the Combe Grisard at the Morey border, which gives it a fresh, sometimes austere style with fine minerality and spice. Its soil is thin and its rock hard. Leroy, Trapet, Rossignol-Trapet, Faiveley, Drouhin-Laroze and Arnoux-Lachaux make it.
fr-latricieres-chambertin.terroir: Shallow, stony soil over hard limestone; cool air from the Combe Grisard.
fr-latricieres-chambertin.nerd_note: The name probably derives from tricière, a poor soil fit only for scrub.

fr-laudun.name: Laudun
fr-laudun.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre; whites from Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne, Viognier
fr-laudun.summary: Laudun became the 18th cru of the Rhône Valley when INAO's national committee approved its promotion on 11 September 2024, with effect from the 2024 vintage. A Côtes du Rhône Villages with its own name since 1967, it covers about 512 ha (2025) in Laudun-l'Ardoise, Saint-Victor-la-Coste and Tresques on the Gard bank. Laudun is unusual for its whites, about 30 percent of production, which are fresh and floral from limestone and sand; rosé is no longer allowed under the cru name. Its reds are spicy and medium-bodied.
fr-laudun.terroir: Three soils: sandy sandstone (safres), pebble terraces on the plateau of the Camp de César, and limestone slopes; Roman remains on the plateau show ancient settlement.
fr-laudun.nerd_note: Laudun's promotion came 57 years after it gained a village name, and the cru excluded rosé even though the village was once known for it.

fr-les-baux-de-provence.name: Les Baux de Provence
fr-les-baux-de-provence.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault, Counoise, Cabernet Sauvignon, Carignan; Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Vermentino, Marsanne, Roussanne
fr-les-baux-de-provence.summary: Les Baux-de-Provence is a small appellation around the limestone Alpilles hills and the medieval village of Les Baux. It is often called France's most organic appellation: most of its estates are organic or biodynamic, partly because the dry, mistral-swept climate makes it easy. The reds are spicy and herbal. Domaine de Trévallon, founded by Eloi Dürrbach in 1973, is the most famous estate, but it sells as IGP Alpilles because its blend of roughly equal Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah exceeds the Cabernet limit set when the AOC was created in 1995. Domaine Hauvette, Château Romanin and Mas de la Dame are references.
fr-les-baux-de-provence.terroir: Limestone scree and clay on the slopes of the Alpilles; windy, dry.
fr-les-baux-de-provence.nerd_note: Domaine de Trévallon, Provence's most famous red, is not allowed to use the appellation because it has too much Cabernet Sauvignon.

fr-limoux.name: Limoux
fr-limoux.grapes: Mauzac, Chardonnay, Chenin Blanc, Pinot Noir; Merlot, Malbec, Cabernet, Syrah, Grenache for red
fr-limoux.summary:
Limoux, in the upper Aude valley south of Carcassonne, is cool for the south of France: influenced by both the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, at 200 to 500 m. It makes three sparkling wines. Blanquette de Limoux, mostly Mauzac, is made by the traditional method; Blanquette Méthode Ancestrale is pure Mauzac, fermented once in the bottle without added sugar or yeast, and low in alcohol; and Crémant de Limoux, more Chardonnay and Chenin. Limoux also makes barrel-fermented still Chardonnay (Limoux blanc, with a famous charity auction, Toques et Clochers) and reds.

Limoux claims to have made the world's first sparkling wine. A document from 1531 records the monks of the abbey of Saint-Hilaire buying flasks of 'blanquette', and local legend says they discovered that wine bottled before fermentation finished would sparkle. The claim predates Dom Pérignon by over a century, but the 1531 document does not prove the wine was sparkling; it is a beloved local story rather than established fact.
fr-limoux.terroir: Clay-limestone, sandstone and gravel in four zones: Autan, Méditerranéen, Océanique and Haute Vallée, with altitudes up to 500 m.
fr-limoux.nerd_note: Blanquette means 'little white one', from the white down on the underside of Mauzac leaves.

fr-lirac.name: Lirac
fr-lirac.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault; whites from Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc
fr-lirac.summary: Lirac lies on the Gard bank of the Rhône opposite Châteauneuf-du-Pape, across Lirac, Roquemaure, Saint-Laurent-des-Arbres and Saint-Geniès-de-Comolas. It makes red, white and rosé from 848 ha (2025). Its reds have become far more serious since the 2000s, when Châteauneuf estates such as Mordorée and Pegau, and growers like Domaine de la Rocalière, raised the bar. Roquemaure's port shipped wine branded CdR under a 1737 royal edict, one of the earliest regulated origins in France.
fr-lirac.terroir: Galets roulés on the eastern terraces facing Châteauneuf, sands and limestone garrigues to the west.
fr-lirac.nerd_note: Saint Valentine's relics are said to have been brought to Roquemaure in 1868, and the town holds a Valentine's festival.

fr-listrac-medoc.name: Listrac-Médoc
fr-listrac-medoc.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
fr-listrac-medoc.summary: Listrac sits inland, on the edge of the pine forest west of Moulis, and it is the 'roof of the Médoc', reaching 43 m above sea level. Its wines are firmer and fresher than the riverside communes, traditionally a bit austere in youth, with dark fruit and a mineral, limestone-driven finish. More Merlot is planted here than anywhere else in the Haut-Médoc because the clay-limestone soils suit it. Château Clarke (Edmond de Rothschild Heritage), Fourcas Hosten, Fourcas Dupré and Fonréaud are the reference estates, and Château Reverdi was named a Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel in 2025.
fr-listrac-medoc.terroir: Three gravel ridges of Pyrenean origin run through a plateau of clay and limestone, the only real limestone of the Médoc.
fr-listrac-medoc.nerd_note: Listrac also makes a significant amount of dry white wine (Château Clarke's Le Merle Blanc, Fonréaud's Le Cygne), sold as Bordeaux because the appellation is red-only.

fr-loupiac.name: Loupiac
fr-loupiac.summary: Loupiac faces Barsac across the Garonne on the right bank, and makes sweet wines from botrytised Sémillon on south and west-facing clay-limestone slopes. The wines are generally a little lighter and fresher than Sauternes, closer to a rich moelleux in lesser years, and they are excellent value. Château Loupiac-Gaudiet, Clos Jean and Château du Cros are references.
fr-loupiac.terroir: Clay-limestone and gravel slopes above the river, with morning fogs rising from the Garonne.
fr-loupiac.nerd_note: Loupiac has a Gallo-Roman villa with mosaics beside its church, and local tradition claims it as the estate of the poet Ausonius, a claim Saint-Émilion makes too.

fr-luberon.name: Luberon
fr-luberon.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Cinsault; whites from Vermentino, Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne, Ugni Blanc
fr-luberon.summary: Luberon (Côtes du Luberon until 2009) covers the slopes on both sides of the Luberon mountains between Cavaillon and Manosque, in the regional nature park. Its 2,781 ha (2025) make mostly rosé and fresh whites, with Provençal character, and some reds. Château La Canorgue (setting of the film A Good Year), Château Val Joanis and the Marrenon co-operative are known producers.
fr-luberon.terroir: Limestone, marl and sandy soils at 200 to 450 m; cooler and drier than the Rhône plain.
fr-luberon.nerd_note: Luberon is an Inter Rhône appellation even though it is geographically in Provence.

fr-lussac-saint-emilion.name: Lussac-Saint-Émilion
fr-lussac-saint-emilion.summary: Lussac is the northernmost satellite, cooler and later-ripening, with a mix of clay-limestone in the south and sand and gravel to the north. The wines are fresh, fruit-forward Merlot. The cooperative and family estates such as Château de Barbe Blanche, Château Lyonnat and Château de Lussac are the references.
fr-lussac-saint-emilion.terroir: Clay, limestone, sand and gravel; the cooler northern position shows in fresher acidity.
fr-lussac-saint-emilion.nerd_note: The four satellites lie north of the Barbanne stream, which also marks Pomerol's northern edge; before the appellation laws of 1936 their wines were often sold simply as Saint-Émilion.

fr-macon.name: Mâcon
fr-macon.grapes: Chardonnay; Gamay and Pinot Noir for reds
fr-macon.summary: Mâcon is the umbrella appellation of the Mâconnais and its three tiers: plain Mâcon (red, white and rosé), Mâcon-Villages (white only, from a list of villages) and Mâcon followed by one of 27 village names, such as Mâcon-Lugny, Mâcon-Azé, Mâcon-Milly-Lamartine, Mâcon-Chardonnay, Mâcon-Uchizy, Mâcon-Fuissé or Mâcon-Pierreclos. Some village names may also be used for reds. The whites are fresh, ripe and unoaked, with apple, pear and white flowers; at their best, from growers such as Héritiers du Comte Lafon (Milly-Lamartine) or Guillot-Broux (Cruzille), they are serious and long-lived. The reds, mostly Gamay, are light and fruity.
fr-macon.terroir: Limestone and marl ridges running north to south across the Mâconnais, with clay valleys and some granite in the south and west.
fr-macon.nerd_note: The village of Chardonnay near Tournus gives its name to the Mâcon-Chardonnay appellation; whether the grape takes its name from the village or vice versa is still debated.

fr-macon-villages.name: Mâcon Villages
fr-macon-villages.summary: Mâcon-Villages is the white-only Mâcon appellation for Chardonnay from a long list of villages in the Mâconnais, a step above plain Mâcon. It gives bright, juicy, unoaked whites and is the everyday white of Burgundy; cooperatives such as Lugny and Prissé-Sologny-Verzé, and growers such as Héritiers du Comte Lafon and Domaine de la Bongran, show how good it can be.
fr-macon-villages.terroir: Limestone and marl hills between the Saône and the Grosne valley.

fr-macvin-du-jura.name: Macvin du Jura
fr-macvin-du-jura.grapes: Grape must from Jura varieties fortified with Marc du Jura
fr-macvin-du-jura.summary: Macvin du Jura, an AOC since 1991, is a vin de liqueur: unfermented grape must blended with Marc du Jura aged at least 14 months, then aged in oak for a year. It may be white, red or rosé and is served chilled as an aperitif or with dessert. The Jura claims it dates from the fourteenth century, when it was made by the abbesses of Château-Chalon.
fr-macvin-du-jura.terroir: Grown across the Jura AOC area.
fr-macvin-du-jura.nerd_note: The name may derive from vin maqué (crushed) or from 'mac', the local word for marc.

fr-madiran.name: Madiran
fr-madiran.grapes: Tannat (60 to 80%), Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Fer Servadou (Pinenc)
fr-madiran.summary:
Madiran is the kingdom of Tannat, a grape with more tannin and colour than almost any other, and its wines are among the most structured reds in France: black fruit, liquorice and spice, with tannins that need years to soften. In the 1980s Alain Brumont of Château Montus and Château Bouscassé showed that 100% Tannat aged in new oak could rival great Bordeaux, and his Montus Prestige made the appellation's name.

Madiran is also where micro-oxygenation was invented: in the early 1990s Patrick Ducournau of Domaine Mouréou developed a technique to bubble tiny, controlled amounts of oxygen into wine to soften Tannat's tannins, and it spread worldwide. A 2006 study in *Nature* by Roger Corder linked the high procyanidin content of Tannat wines to the longevity of people in the Gers, which briefly made Madiran famous as a 'healthy wine'. Today, growers like Château d'Aydie and Domaine Labranche-Laffont make fresher, less oaky styles.
fr-madiran.terroir: Clay-limestone, siliceous clay and pebbly boulbènes on hills rising from the Adour, with Pyrenean influence and dry, warm autumns.
fr-madiran.nerd_note: Tannat is also Uruguay's national grape, taken there by Basque immigrants in the nineteenth century.

fr-malepere.name: Malepère
fr-malepere.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache, Lledoner Pelut, Syrah
fr-malepere.summary: Malepère, south-west of Carcassonne, is the most Atlantic-influenced Languedoc appellation, and Merlot leads its blends, with Cabernet Franc and Malbec alongside Grenache and Syrah. Its wines are close to Bordeaux in style, with soft tannins and fresh fruit. It was promoted from VDQS to AOC in 2007.
fr-malepere.terroir: Clay-limestone and sandstone hills around the Malepère massif.
fr-malepere.nerd_note: Malepère has the highest proportion of Bordeaux grapes of any Languedoc AOC.

fr-maranges.name: Maranges
fr-maranges.summary: Maranges is the southernmost appellation of the Côte de Beaune, a 1989 merger of three villages in Saône-et-Loire (Cheilly-, Dezize- and Sampigny-lès-Maranges) whose wines were previously sold as Côte de Beaune-Villages. It makes sturdy, rustic, red-fruited reds that are among the best values in the Côte d'Or. Its premier crus, such as La Fussière and Le Clos des Loyères, lie on south-facing slopes.
fr-maranges.terroir: Marl and limestone on a south-facing hill; slightly warmer than the rest of the Côte.
fr-maranges.nerd_note: Maranges was the first appellation of the Côte de Beaune created by merging villages rather than recognising one.

fr-marc-du-jura.name: Marc du Jura
fr-marc-du-jura.summary: Marc du Jura is the Jura's grape-pomace brandy, aged at least two years in oak, which became an AOC in 2015. It is also the spirit used to fortify Macvin. It is listed here for completeness; it is a spirit appellation rather than a wine.

fr-marcillac.name: Marcillac
fr-marcillac.summary: Marcillac is a tiny appellation in the Aveyron near Rodez, in a natural amphitheatre of red soils, and its wine is made almost entirely from Fer Servadou, called Mansois here. The wines are bright, peppery and redcurrant-scented, with a mineral iron note from the soil. Domaine du Cros and the Valon cooperative are the main producers. Monks of the abbey of Conques, a major stop on the pilgrimage to Santiago, planted the vineyards.
fr-marcillac.terroir: The 'rougier', red, iron-rich clay and sandstone of the Permian, on steep slopes.
fr-marcillac.nerd_note: The miners and steelworkers of nearby Decazeville kept the wine alive in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; it was their daily wine.

fr-margaux.name: Margaux
fr-margaux.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
fr-margaux.summary:
Margaux is the largest and the most southerly of the Médoc's great communal appellations, and the one with the most classed growths: 21, from first growth Château Margaux to fifth growths Dauzac and du Tertre. It spreads across five communes: Margaux and Cantenac (merged as Margaux-Cantenac in 2017), Soussans, Labarde and Arsac. The appellation was finalised in 1954 after long arguments about which villages belonged.

Margaux's reputation is for perfume: violets, roses and red fruit layered over Cabernet's cassis, with silkier tannins than Pauillac. The best wines (Margaux, Palmer, Rauzan-Ségla, Brane-Cantenac, Giscours, Malescot Saint-Exupéry, Durfort-Vivens) combine that fragrance with real depth. The size and number of estates also mean variable quality; the 1970s and 1980s saw several underperformers, and the turnaround since then is one of the Médoc's success stories.

Palmer is the cult name here, regularly priced above several seconds, and its biodynamic farming and *Historical XIXth Century Wine* (a blend with northern Rhône Syrah, recalling the old practice of 'hermitaging' claret) show a progressive streak.
fr-margaux.terroir: The thinnest, finest gravel of the Médoc, often over limestone, with less clay than further north. Poor, well-drained soils restrict vigour and give delicacy rather than power. The Cantenac plateau and the gravel around Margaux village are the classic sites; Arsac and Soussans sit on sandier, later-ripening soils.
fr-margaux.nerd_note: A bottle of 1787 Margaux engraved 'Th.J.', supposedly from Thomas Jefferson's order, was valued at 500,000 dollars until a New York merchant knocked it over at a dinner in 1989. All the 'Jefferson bottles' came from the collector Hardy Rodenstock and are now widely regarded as forgeries.

fr-marsannay.name: Marsannay
fr-marsannay.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay (rosé from Pinot Noir)
fr-marsannay.summary:
Marsannay, at the northern gate of the Côte de Nuits on the outskirts of Dijon, is the only village appellation in the Côte d'Or that can be red, white and rosé. Covering Couchey, Marsannay-la-Côte and Chenôve, it was long Dijon's source of everyday wine and became famous after 1919 for rosé (Clair de Marsannay), which earned the appellation status before the reds. Since 1987 it has been a full village AOC.

Today the reds are the story: perfumed, crunchy Pinot Noir from climats such as Clos du Roy, Les Longeroies and Au Champ Salomon, which growers have been pushing for premier cru status. They are lighter than Gevrey's but often among the best-value reds in Burgundy.
fr-marsannay.terroir: Limestone and marl slopes facing east and southeast, cooled by air from the Combe de Fixin and the Ouche valley; some vines on alluvial fans.
fr-marsannay.nerd_note: Marsannay's growers have applied for premier cru status for about 14 climats, including Clos du Roy and Les Longeroies; INAO's parcel register of October 2026 still lists no Marsannay premier cru.

fr-maury.name: Maury
fr-maury.grapes: Grenache Noir, Grenache Gris, Grenache Blanc, Macabeu, Muscat; Carignan, Syrah, Mourvèdre for Maury Sec
fr-maury.summary: Maury, in the upper Agly valley in the north of Roussillon, sits on a band of black schist between the limestone ridges of the Corbières and the Fenouillèdes, beneath the Cathar castle of Quéribus. It makes Grenache-based vins doux naturels in both oxidative and reductive (grenat, vintage) styles. Its old *hors d'âge* wines, aged in barrels and bonbonnes left in the sun, are among the great oxidative wines of the world. Since 2011, Maury Sec has been a separate category for dry reds, recognising the area's success with old-vine Grenache, Carignan and Syrah. Mas Amiel, founded in 1816, with its famous field of glass bonbonnes, and the Vignerons de Maury are the main producers.
fr-maury.terroir: Black schist (Albian marl) in a valley sheltered by limestone ridges; very dry and windy.
fr-maury.nerd_note: According to the estate's story, Raymond Amiel won Mas Amiel from the Bishop of Perpignan in a game of cards in 1816.

fr-mazis-chambertin.name: Mazis-Chambertin
fr-mazis-chambertin.summary: Mazis-Chambertin, about 9.1 ha at the northern end of Gevrey's grand cru belt below Ruchottes, combines Mazis-Haut, close to Clos de Bèze in quality, and Mazis-Bas, on deeper soil. The wines are dense and deeply coloured with dark fruit and a wild, gamey edge. Armand Rousseau, Faiveley, Bernard Dugat-Py, Harmand-Geoffroy and the Hospices de Beaune (cuvée Madeleine Collignon) are notable sources.
fr-mazis-chambertin.terroir: Brown limestone soils with more clay and depth on the lower part.
fr-mazis-chambertin.nerd_note: The Hospices de Beaune's Mazis-Chambertin cuvée Madeleine Collignon is one of the auction's most expensive red lots.

fr-mazoyeres-chambertin.name: Mazoyères-Chambertin
fr-mazoyeres-chambertin.summary: Mazoyères-Chambertin, about 18.6 ha south of Charmes at the Morey border, is a grand cru that hardly anyone puts on a label because its wine may legally be sold as Charmes-Chambertin, a better-known name. A handful of growers, such as Camus, Perrot-Minot and Taupenot-Merme, insist on the original name. The wines are often a little firmer and more structured than Charmes, from slightly cooler soils.
fr-mazoyeres-chambertin.terroir: Limestone with more clay at the southern end of Gevrey's grand cru belt, next to Clos de la Roche in Morey.
fr-mazoyeres-chambertin.nerd_note: The spelling varies: Mazoyères and Mazoyères-Chambertin are both seen; the name is thought to come from mas, a farmhouse.

fr-medoc.name: Médoc
fr-medoc.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
fr-medoc.summary:
The Médoc AOC covers the northern third of the peninsula, the old Bas-Médoc, around Bégadan, Saint-Yzans, Blaignan, Valeyrac and Lesparre. It has no classed growths but it is the heartland of the Crus Bourgeois, and three of the fourteen 2025 Exceptionnels (La Cardonne, Castéra and Laujac) are here.
