The wines are firm, fresh and often more Merlot-driven than further south, with dark fruit, graphite and a savoury, slightly rustic edge in youth. They are the Médoc's best value: well-made bottles from Château Potensac, La Tour de By or Goulée age a decade or more at a fraction of Pauillac prices.

The appellation also legally covers the Haut-Médoc area, so any Médoc red can use the name, but in practice it is used by estates north of Saint-Estèphe.
fr-medoc.terroir: Flatter land with more clay and limestone and less gravel than the Haut-Médoc. The best sites are the gravel islands near the estuary at Bégadan, Valeyrac and Saint-Christoly. Clay holds water in drought years and ripens later in cool ones, which is why Merlot is often half the blend.
fr-medoc.nerd_note: The northern Médoc's best sites are gravel 'islands' rising out of former marsh at Bégadan, Valeyrac and Saint-Christoly; between them lie reclaimed *palus* meadows, still drained by channels first dug under the Dutch engineers of the seventeenth century.

fr-menetou-salon.name: Menetou-Salon
fr-menetou-salon.summary: Menetou-Salon is Sancerre's neighbour to the south-west, near Bourges, on the same Kimmeridgian marl. The Sauvignon whites and Pinot Noir reds are similar to Sancerre, often fresher and better value. Domaine Henry Pellé and Philippe Gilbert are the leading producers.
fr-menetou-salon.nerd_note: Jacques Cœur, the great merchant and treasurer of Charles VII, owned a château at Menetou-Salon in the fifteenth century.

fr-mercurey.name: Mercurey
fr-mercurey.summary: Mercurey is the largest and best-known village of the Côte Chalonnaise, making mostly red wine with more structure and depth than its neighbours: dark cherry, earth and firm tannin. It has about 32 premier crus, among them Clos des Myglands, Clos du Roy, Clos l'Évêque and Clos des Barraults, and some of Burgundy's best value reds come from producers such as Faiveley, which built a large estate here, the Château de Chamirey and Domaine François Raquillet.
fr-mercurey.terroir: Limestone with clay and marl; the premier crus lie on the slopes north and west of the village.
fr-mercurey.nerd_note: Mercurey is believed to take its name from a Roman temple to Mercury on the old road between Chalon and Autun.

fr-meursault.name: Meursault
fr-meursault.summary:
Meursault is the largest white-wine village of the Côte d'Or and the one that defines rich, round, nutty Chardonnay: butter, hazelnut, toast and ripe orchard fruit over a backbone of acidity. It has no grand crus, but its premier crus rival them. Les Perrières, on stony soil high in the south, is the most mineral and is often called a grand cru in waiting; Les Genevrières is floral and fine; Les Charmes is the broadest and most generous; and Les Gouttes d'Or, Le Porusot, Les Bouchères and Blagny add more nuances.

Meursault also excels in single-lieu-dit village wines. Climats such as Les Tessons, Les Narvaux, Les Luchets, Le Clos de la Barre, Les Rougeots and Les Tillets are bottled separately by growers such as Coche-Dury, Roulot and Lafon and command premier cru prices. Meursault's cellars, cut deep into the limestone, allow long, slow ageing on the lees. The Paulée de Meursault, a harvest feast revived by Count Jules Lafon in 1923, is the last of the Trois Glorieuses.
fr-meursault.terroir: Marl and limestone with more stone on the upper slopes; the premier crus lie south toward Puligny, facing east and southeast at 230 to 300 m.
fr-meursault.nerd_note: A small amount of red Meursault is made, but the Santenots climats sell their red as Volnay; Blagny's red is sold as Blagny.

fr-minervois.name: Minervois
fr-minervois.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Lledoner Pelut, Cinsault; Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc, Macabeu, Marsanne, Roussanne, Vermentino
fr-minervois.summary: Minervois lies on the southern slopes of the Montagne Noire, between Narbonne and Carcassonne, in an amphitheatre facing south toward the Canal du Midi and the Aude. It takes its name from Minerve, a cliff-top village where 140 Cathars were burned in 1210. The reds, Syrah and Grenache-led, are smoother and more fragrant than Corbières. The area is divided into several zones, from the cool, high Petit Causse to the warm, lower Canal du Midi area. In June 2025 the INAO opened consultation on Cazelles, a proposed new named area (DGC).
fr-minervois.terroir: Limestone, schist, sandstone and marl, on terraces descending from the Montagne Noire (up to 400 m) to the Aude valley.
fr-minervois.nerd_note: The village of Minerve, on a rocky spur between two gorges, was besieged by Simon de Montfort in 1210; 140 Cathars who refused to recant were burned.

fr-monbazillac.name: Monbazillac
fr-monbazillac.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris, Muscadelle
fr-monbazillac.summary: Monbazillac is the Southwest's answer to Sauternes: sweet white wine from botrytised grapes on the south bank of the Dordogne, facing Bergerac. The same autumn mists that rise from the river encourage noble rot, and the rules require hand harvesting in successive tries. The wines are rich, honeyed and often lighter and cheaper than Sauternes, with Muscadelle adding a floral note. Château Tirecul la Gravière, whose Cuvée Madame shows what great Monbazillac can be, and the cooperative that owns the sixteenth-century Château de Monbazillac are reference points. The appellation went through a crisis in the 1990s when some producers made wine from machine-harvested, chaptalised grapes; it has since banned machine harvesting.
fr-monbazillac.terroir: North-facing clay-limestone slopes above the Dordogne, cool enough for slow ripening and humid enough for botrytis.
fr-monbazillac.nerd_note: Monbazillac's vineyards face north, unlike most sweet-wine sites; the cooler exposure keeps acidity and helps mists linger.

fr-montagne-saint-emilion.name: Montagne-Saint-Émilion
fr-montagne-saint-emilion.summary: Montagne is the largest of the four Saint-Émilion satellites north of the Barbanne stream, and its hilly limestone terrain is the most varied. It absorbed the old Parsac appellation in the 1970s. Wines are Merlot-based, plump and often excellent value; the best (Vieux Château Saint-André, Château Montaiguillon, Château Faizeau) age a decade.
fr-montagne-saint-emilion.terroir: Clay-limestone hills and plateau similar to Saint-Émilion's, with some sand and gravel.
fr-montagne-saint-emilion.nerd_note: Montagne's Écomusée du Libournais and its windmill at Calon recall a time when the hills grew grain as well as vines.

fr-montagny.name: Montagny
fr-montagny.summary: Montagny is the white-only appellation at the southern end of the Côte Chalonnaise, covering Montagny-lès-Buxy, Buxy, Jully-lès-Buxy and Saint-Vallerin. It has about 49 premier crus, and more than half the appellation is classified premier cru, a legacy of an old rule based on alcohol rather than site that was reformed in 1989. The Cave des Vignerons de Buxy dominates production; the wines are crisp, nutty and dry.
fr-montagny.terroir: Limestone and marl hills at 250 to 400 m, cooler than the northern Chalonnaise.
fr-montagny.nerd_note: For decades any Montagny reaching 11.5 percent alcohol could be called premier cru; a reform in 1989 tied the title to named climats instead.

fr-monthelie.name: Monthélie
fr-monthelie.summary: Monthélie lies just above Meursault next to Volnay, and its best slopes are a continuation of Volnay's: premier crus such as Sur la Velle, Les Champs Fulliots and Les Duresses give light, fragrant reds that resemble a rustic Volnay at a lower price. A few growers also make fresh whites. The village is one of the smallest and least known in the Côte de Beaune, which makes it a happy hunting ground for value.
fr-monthelie.terroir: Limestone and marl on south and southeast slopes, some facing Volnay; higher sites on the hill toward Auxey.
fr-monthelie.nerd_note: The name is often written without an accent, Monthelie; the official register uses Monthélie.

fr-montlouis-sur-loire.name: Montlouis-sur-Loire
fr-montlouis-sur-loire.summary: Montlouis faces Vouvray across the Loire on the south bank, between the Loire and the Cher. It makes the same Chenin styles (dry, sweet and sparkling), and was long considered Vouvray's little brother. Since the 2000s a group of growers led by Jacky Blot (Domaine de la Taille aux Loups) and François Chidaine has made it a source of some of the Loire's finest dry Chenin, often more precise and mineral than Vouvray. Montlouis growers also launched 'Pétillant Originel', a méthode ancestrale sparkling wine bottled before fermentation ends.
fr-montlouis-sur-loire.terroir: Clay-flint and sand over tuffeau on a plateau between the two rivers; slightly sandier and earlier-ripening than Vouvray.
producers: Domaine de la Taille aux Loups
fr-montlouis-sur-loire.nerd_note: Montlouis was historically sold as Vouvray until a 1938 ruling gave it its own appellation.

fr-montpeyroux.name: Montpeyroux
fr-montpeyroux.summary: Montpeyroux, in the foothills of the Larzac, became the Languedoc's newest communal AOC in 2026 after nearly 30 years of campaigning. The INAO's national committee approved its specification in June 2025, and the appellation replaces the former 'Languedoc Montpeyroux' name. It covers Montpeyroux and three neighbouring communes (Arboras, Lagamas and Saint-Jean-de-Fos), about 500 ha, and is red only. The campaign was led by 35 producers, 16 of them independent estates, and began with a first INAO visit in 1996. Domaine d'Aupilhac (Sylvain Fadat), Domaine Alain Chabanon and the Castelbarry cooperative are references. The village's name comes from 'Mont Pierreux', stony mountain.
fr-montpeyroux.terroir: Limestone scree, marl and the blue marl of the Larzac foothills; altitudes of 150 to 400 m with cool nights.
fr-montpeyroux.nerd_note: Sylvain Fadat of Aupilhac plants old Carignan and Cinsault on north-facing terraces at Les Cocalières, a high, cool amphitheatre of volcanic and limestone soils.

fr-montrachet.name: Montrachet
fr-montrachet.summary:
Le Montrachet is the most famous white wine vineyard in the world: about 8 ha split almost equally between Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet. Its name, from mont rachet (bald hill), describes the scrubby slope above it, and its fame was already established in the eighteenth century. Montrachet combines richness and mineral tension like no other site: a dense, layered texture, aromas of citrus, honey, nuts and smoke, and a finish that lasts for minutes. It can age for decades.

About 18 owners share it. The Marquis de Laguiche family (about 2 ha, made by Joseph Drouhin), Bouchard Père et Fils, Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (0.68 ha), Domaine des Comtes Lafon, Domaine Leflaive, Ramonet, Jacques Prieur and Baron Thénard are among them.
fr-montrachet.terroir: A gentle 3 percent slope facing east-southeast at 250 to 270 m, on thin brown limestone soil over hard Bathonian limestone; it catches sun from dawn to dusk and drains perfectly.
fr-montrachet.nerd_note: Alexandre Dumas is said to have written that Montrachet should be drunk kneeling with head bared.

fr-montravel.name: Montravel
fr-montravel.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle; Merlot for red
fr-montravel.summary: Montravel lies at the western end of the Bergerac area, next to Saint-Émilion's eastern neighbours. It makes dry whites (Sauvignon and Sémillon), and since 2001, Merlot-dominated reds. The philosopher Michel de Montaigne lived at his castle in Saint-Michel-de-Montaigne in the heart of the appellation, where his library tower survives.
fr-montravel.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes continuing those of Castillon.
fr-montravel.nerd_note: Montaigne wrote his *Essais* in the tower of his château in Montravel.

fr-morey-saint-denis.name: Morey-Saint-Denis
fr-morey-saint-denis.grapes: Pinot Noir (some Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc)
fr-morey-saint-denis.summary:
Morey-Saint-Denis is the small village between Gevrey-Chambertin and Chambolle-Musigny, and its wines sit between them in style: the structure of Gevrey with some of Chambolle's perfume. It holds four complete grand crus (Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos des Lambrays and Clos de Tart) and a slice of Bonnes-Mares. For decades its growers sold the village wine under the names of its more famous neighbours, which kept Morey relatively obscure and good value.

Premier crus such as Les Ruchots, Clos de la Bussière, Les Monts Luisants, Clos Sorbè and Les Millandes give sappy, earthy reds. Les Monts Luisants is also the source of one of Burgundy's rarest whites: Domaine Ponsot's Clos des Monts Luisants was planted with Aligoté in 1911.
fr-morey-saint-denis.terroir: Limestone over marl; the gravelly scree of the Combe Grisard and Combe de la Roche feeds the lower slopes.
fr-morey-saint-denis.nerd_note: The village added Saint-Denis to its name in 1927, after its grand cru Clos Saint-Denis.

fr-morgon.name: Morgon
fr-morgon.summary:
Morgon is the second-largest cru and, with Moulin-à-Vent, the most powerful and age-worthy. Its wines are so distinctive that the locals have a verb for them: a Morgon that has aged into notes of kirsch, cherry and earth is said to morgonner. The appellation surrounds the village of Villié-Morgon, and its six climats (Côte du Py, Corcelette, Les Charmes, Grand Cras, Douby and Les Micouds) are often bottled separately.

Morgon is also the birthplace of natural wine: Marcel Lapierre and Jean Foillard, inspired by Jules Chauvet, began making unsulphured, wild-yeast Gamay here in the early 1980s. Their wines, along with Guy Breton's and those of a younger wave (Jean-Claude Lapalu, Mathieu Lapierre, Jean-Louis Dutraive, Julie Balagny), made Morgon a byword for vibrant, honest wine.
fr-morgon.terroir: Granite in the west, but the famous Côte du Py, an extinct volcanic hill, has blue schist and pyrite-rich rock called roche pourrie (rotten rock) that gives Morgon its distinctive mineral character. Gravel and clay in Grand Cras and Les Charmes.
fr-morgon.nerd_note: INAO's parcel file delimits Morgon at about 1,340 ha in the single commune of Villié-Morgon.

fr-moselle.name: Moselle
fr-moselle.grapes: Auxerrois, Müller-Thurgau, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Riesling, Gewurztraminer; Pinot Noir, Gamay
fr-moselle.summary: The French Moselle AOC, a VDQS from 1995 to 2010, covers scattered vineyards in three zones of the Moselle department: south of Metz along the Moselle (Ancy-Dornot, Scy-Chazelles), around Sierck-les-Bains and Contz-les-Bains near the Luxembourg border, and the Seille valley around Vic-sur-Seille. Production is tiny, about 1,500 hl a year, mostly crisp whites from Auxerrois and Müller-Thurgau, with some Pinot Noir. It is the upstream French end of the same river that becomes the Mosel in Germany and the Moselle in Luxembourg.
fr-moselle.terroir: Limestone and marl in the Metz area, Keuper marl and limestone near Sierck, marl around Vic-sur-Seille.
fr-moselle.nerd_note: Château de Vaux, a restored estate on the slopes west of Metz run by the Molozay family, led the revival of Moselle wine in the 1990s.

fr-moulin-a-vent.name: Moulin-à-Vent
fr-moulin-a-vent.summary:
Moulin-à-Vent is the king of Beaujolais: the most structured and age-worthy of the crus, often compared to Burgundy and aged in oak. The appellation covers Romanèche-Thorins and Chénas and takes its name from a sixteenth-century windmill that still stands among the vines, a listed historic monument. Its pink granite is shot through with veins of manganese, credited with the wines' depth and their ability to age for 10 to 20 years.

The best climats, such as Les Thorins, Champ de Cour, La Rochelle, Les Carquelins and Rochegrès, are bottled separately by producers such as Château des Jacques (Louis Jadot), Richard Rottiers, Yvon Métras and Paul Janin. Old Moulin-à-Vent takes on truffle, spice and cherry notes that can confuse blind tasters into guessing Pinot Noir.
fr-moulin-a-vent.terroir: Pink granite with manganese veins, decomposed into sandy gore; gentle slopes at 250 to 300 m around the windmill.
fr-moulin-a-vent.nerd_note: The wine was once called Romanèche-Thorins; the windmill's name was adopted when the appellation was created in 1936.

fr-moulis.name: Moulis-en-Médoc
fr-moulis.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
fr-moulis.summary: Moulis is the smallest communal appellation of the Médoc and one of its most rewarding for drinkers. Its heart is the Grand Poujeaux gravel ridge on the border with Listrac and Arcins, where Château Chasse-Spleen, Poujeaux, Maucaillou and Branas Grand Poujeaux make dense, long-lived reds that often taste like classed growths at half the price. No estate was classified in 1855, partly because the area was less fashionable with brokers at the time.
fr-moulis.terroir: Western Moulis shares Listrac's clay-limestone; the eastern Grand Poujeaux area has deep Garonne gravel similar to Margaux and Saint-Julien.
fr-moulis.nerd_note: Chasse-Spleen ('chase away melancholy') is often said to have been named after a remark by Lord Byron or a poem by Baudelaire; the story is unproven, but the estate has leaned into it with a contemporary art centre.

fr-muscadet.name: Muscadet
fr-muscadet.summary: Regional Muscadet covers the whole Nantais area and is the lightest, simplest version of the wine: dry, crisp, saline white for the seafood platters of the Atlantic coast. Most volume is sold under the more precise sub-regional names, especially Sèvre et Maine.
fr-muscadet.terroir: Mixed Armorican rocks; flatter, more fertile land than the sub-regions.
fr-muscadet.nerd_note: The grape's name, Melon de Bourgogne, recalls its Burgundian origin; it is a natural cross of Pinot and Gouais Blanc, sibling of Chardonnay and Aligoté.

fr-muscadet-coteaux-de-la-loire.name: Muscadet Coteaux de la Loire
fr-muscadet-coteaux-de-la-loire.summary: The smallest and least known of the Muscadet appellations, on schist and granite slopes along both banks of the Loire upstream of Nantes, around Ancenis and Champtoceaux. The wines are firmer and more mineral than Sèvre et Maine, with a hint of the Anjou schist.
fr-muscadet-coteaux-de-la-loire.terroir: Steep schist and granite slopes overlooking the river, with good drainage.
fr-muscadet-coteaux-de-la-loire.nerd_note: Champtoceaux, proposed as a cru communal in 2025, would be the first cru outside Sèvre et Maine.

fr-muscadet-cotes-de-grandlieu.name: Muscadet Côtes de Grandlieu
fr-muscadet-cotes-de-grandlieu.summary: Created in 1994, this appellation surrounds the Lac de Grand-Lieu south-west of Nantes, one of France's largest natural lakes in winter. Sandy and granitic soils give soft, aromatic Muscadet, best drunk young.
fr-muscadet-cotes-de-grandlieu.terroir: Granite, schist and sandy soils; the lake moderates temperatures.
fr-muscadet-cotes-de-grandlieu.nerd_note: The Lac de Grand-Lieu's water level varies hugely between seasons, and the lake is a major bird reserve.

fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine.name: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine.summary:
Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, named after the two rivers that cross it south-east of Nantes, produces the large majority of Muscadet and almost all the best. The traditional *sur lie* style means the wine stays on its fine lees through the winter in underground glass-lined tanks and is bottled directly off them, often with a light prickle of carbon dioxide; the lees add texture, a breadlike note and freshness.

The story of the last fifteen years is the crus communaux, sub-zones defined by bedrock with minimum lees ageing of 18 months or more (24 months or more for some) and lower yields. Clisson (granite), Gorges (gabbro and quartzite) and Le Pallet (gneiss and gabbro) were recognised in 2011; Château-Thébaud, Goulaine, Monnières-Saint-Fiacre and Mouzillon-Tillières followed in 2019. In August 2025 the INAO opened public consultation on three more (Champtoceaux, La Haye-Fouassière and Vallet), which were still awaiting final approval in 2026. The cru wines show a depth, smoky minerality and ageing potential (10 to 20 years) that few people expect from Muscadet. Producers such as Domaine de l'Écu, Jo Landron, Domaine de la Pépière, Luneau-Papin, Jérémie Huchet and Michel Brégeon proved the point.
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine.terroir: Rolling plateau cut by the Sèvre and Maine rivers. Each cru maps to a rock: granite at Clisson and Château-Thébaud, gabbro at Gorges and Mouzillon-Tillières, gneiss at Le Pallet and Monnières-Saint-Fiacre, and schist and gneiss at Goulaine.
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine.nerd_note: Muscadet sur lie must spend the winter on its lees and cannot be bottled before 1 March after the harvest; the cru wines spend far longer on lees, which is why they are usually released two or more years after the vintage.

fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-clisson.name: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine Clisson
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-clisson.summary: Clisson is a Muscadet cru communal (2011) on the granite around the Italianate town of Clisson, where wines must spend at least two years on their lees. The result is a richer, more textured Melon de Bourgogne with salty, nutty depth that ages for a decade or more. Domaine de la Pépière is a reference.
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-clisson.terroir: Granite and its weathered sandy soils (arène).
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-clisson.nerd_note: Muscadet's crus communaux, created from 2011, require long ageing on the lees and lower yields than basic Muscadet Sèvre et Maine.

fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-gorges.name: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine Gorges
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-gorges.summary: Gorges is a Muscadet cru communal (2011) on gabbro, a dark, hard magmatic rock, giving firm, smoky, slow-maturing Melon de Bourgogne after long lees ageing.
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-gorges.terroir: Gabbro and quartz, poor and stony.
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-gorges.nerd_note: Muscadet's crus communaux, created from 2011, require long ageing on the lees and lower yields than basic Muscadet Sèvre et Maine.

fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-le-pallet.name: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine Le Pallet
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-le-pallet.summary: Le Pallet is a Muscadet cru communal (2011) on gneiss and gabbro east of Nantes, giving mineral, structured Melon de Bourgogne after extended lees ageing.
fr-muscadet-sevre-et-maine-le-pallet.nerd_note: Muscadet's crus communaux, created from 2011, require long ageing on the lees and lower yields than basic Muscadet Sèvre et Maine. Le Pallet is the birthplace of the medieval philosopher Peter Abelard.

fr-muscat-de-beaumes-de-venise.name: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise
fr-muscat-de-beaumes-de-venise.grapes: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (and Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge)
fr-muscat-de-beaumes-de-venise.summary: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is a vin doux naturel: Muscat grapes partly fermented and then fortified with grape spirit to keep their sweetness, at about 15 percent alcohol and at least 110 g/l of sugar. The wine is golden, floral and grapey, with orange blossom, apricot and lychee, best drunk young and chilled. Pliny mentioned the Muscat of the area, and the AOC dates from 1945. Planted area has fallen to 227 ha (2025) as demand for sweet wine declined.
fr-muscat-de-beaumes-de-venise.terroir: Limestone and sandy marl slopes around Beaumes-de-Venise and Aubignan.
fr-muscat-de-beaumes-de-venise.nerd_note: Some growers make pink or red-tinged versions from the red-berried Muscat à Petits Grains Rouge.

fr-muscat-de-frontignan.name: Muscat de Frontignan
fr-muscat-de-frontignan.grapes: Muscat à Petits Grains (Blanc and Rouge)
fr-muscat-de-frontignan.summary: Muscat de Frontignan, from the coast between Sète and Montpellier, is one of France's oldest and most famous sweet wines; Voltaire and Thomas Jefferson ordered it, and it was one of the first AOCs (1936). It is a vin doux naturel: fermentation of Muscat à Petits Grains is stopped by adding grape spirit, keeping at least 110 g/l of sugar. The result is golden and aromatic, with apricot, orange blossom and honey. The cooperative makes most of it, and its twisted bottle is famous. There is also a vin de liqueur version.
fr-muscat-de-frontignan.terroir: Limestone and clay with pebbles, between the Étang de Thau and the sea, near the Gardiole massif.
fr-muscat-de-frontignan.nerd_note: Muscat à Petits Grains is often called Muscat de Frontignan in other countries, including Australia, after this town.

fr-muscat-de-lunel.name: Muscat de Lunel
fr-muscat-de-lunel.summary: A small VDN appellation around Lunel, east of Montpellier, on terraces of galets roulés. Its Muscats are rich and aromatic. In 2025 the INAO launched a revised specification adding controlled irrigation and environmental rules.
fr-muscat-de-lunel.terroir: Villafranchian terraces of pebbles and red clay.
fr-muscat-de-lunel.nerd_note: Lunel's Jewish community was famous in the Middle Ages for its rabbinical school; the town's wine trade goes back to the same era.

fr-muscat-de-mireval.name: Muscat de Mireval
fr-muscat-de-mireval.summary: A small VDN appellation next to Frontignan, on the slopes of the Gardiole massif facing the Étang de Vic. Its Muscat à Petits Grains gives aromatic, honeyed wines with at least 110 g/l of sugar. Rabelais, who studied medicine in Montpellier, is said to have enjoyed its wine.
fr-muscat-de-mireval.nerd_note: Mireval and Frontignan share the slopes of the Gardiole massif, but Mireval's vines face the Étang de Vic on red clay and limestone scree.

fr-muscat-de-rivesaltes.name: Muscat de Rivesaltes
fr-muscat-de-rivesaltes.grapes: Muscat à Petits Grains, Muscat of Alexandria
fr-muscat-de-rivesaltes.summary: Muscat de Rivesaltes is a VDN made from Muscat à Petits Grains and Muscat of Alexandria across most of Roussillon. It is bottled young to keep its aromas of citrus, mint, peach and flowers, and drunk chilled. 'Muscat de Noël' is released before Christmas.
fr-muscat-de-rivesaltes.terroir: Schist, granite, limestone and alluvial terraces.
fr-muscat-de-rivesaltes.nerd_note: Muscat de Rivesaltes covers more ground than any other French Muscat appellation, overlapping with most of Roussillon's other zones.

fr-muscat-de-saint-jean-de-minervois.name: Muscat de Saint-Jean-de-Minervois
fr-muscat-de-saint-jean-de-minervois.summary: The highest and freshest of the Languedoc Muscats, from a limestone plateau at about 250 m in the north of the Minervois. Late harvest gives lighter, more delicate VDN with good acidity. Domaine de Barroubio is the reference.
fr-muscat-de-saint-jean-de-minervois.terroir: Limestone causse, cool for the region.
fr-muscat-de-saint-jean-de-minervois.nerd_note: It is harvested later than other Languedoc Muscats, sometimes in October.

fr-muscat-du-cap-corse.name: Muscat du Cap Corse
fr-muscat-du-cap-corse.summary: Muscat du Cap Corse is a vin doux naturel from the narrow, mountainous northern peninsula of Corsica, made from Muscat à Petits Grains, often slightly raisined on the vine. The mutage keeps it sweet and aromatic, with notes of apricot, orange and honey, and the island's schist gives freshness. It is one of the finest Muscats in France. Clos Nicrosi, Domaine Antoine Arena and Domaine Leccia make it.
fr-muscat-du-cap-corse.terroir: Schist slopes on the Cap Corse peninsula and around Patrimonio.
fr-muscat-du-cap-corse.nerd_note: It is the only Corsican vin doux naturel and one of the youngest VDN appellations in France.

fr-musigny.name: Musigny
fr-musigny.summary:
Musigny is the grand cru for those who believe the greatest red Burgundy should be about grace rather than power. About 10.9 ha at the southern end of Chambolle-Musigny, just above Clos de Vougeot, it combines Les Musigny and Les Petits Musigny with part of La Combe d'Orveau. The wine is famous for its silky texture and haunting perfume of violets, roses and red fruit, yet it lasts for decades.

Comte Georges de Vogüé owns about 7.1 ha, two thirds of the vineyard, and is the only producer of Musigny blanc, a rare Chardonnay replanted in the 1990s and sold as Bourgogne blanc until 2015 while the vines matured. Jacques-Frédéric Mugnier, Georges Roumier (a tiny parcel), Leroy, Joseph Drouhin, Jacques Prieur, Faiveley and Louis Jadot also make it.
fr-musigny.terroir: Steeper than its neighbours, with little topsoil over hard limestone and some red clay; facing east at 260 to 300 m.
fr-musigny.nerd_note: Musigny is the only grand cru in the Côte de Nuits allowed to produce both red and white wine.

fr-nuits-saint-georges.name: Nuits-Saint-Georges
fr-nuits-saint-georges.grapes: Pinot Noir (some Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc)
fr-nuits-saint-georges.summary:
Nuits-Saint-Georges is the commercial town that gave the Côte de Nuits its name, and, after Gevrey-Chambertin, the largest appellation of the Côte de Nuits, extending south into Premeaux-Prissey. It has no grand crus but 41 premier crus, more than any other Côte de Nuits village. The reds are the firmest and most earthy of the côte: dark fruit, spice, iron and tannin that need time.

The appellation falls into three parts. North of the town, next to Vosne-Romanée, Aux Boudots, Aux Cras, Aux Murgers, Les Damodes and Aux Chaignots give finer, more Vosne-like wines. South of the town, Les Saints-Georges, Les Vaucrains, Les Cailles, Les Pruliers and Les Porrets give deeper, more structured wine. Further south in Premeaux, walled monopoles such as Clos de la Maréchale, Clos des Forêts Saint-Georges, Clos de l'Arlot and Clos des Corvées round it off. Les Saints-Georges, whose name the town added in 1892, has long been proposed for grand cru status; the growers' application was still under study at INAO in 2026.
fr-nuits-saint-georges.terroir: Varied: limestone, marl and alluvial fans from the Meuzin valley; the southern slope is steeper and stonier.
fr-nuits-saint-georges.nerd_note: The white Nuits-Saint-Georges premier cru Les Perrières from Domaine Henri Gouges comes from a mutant Pinot Noir that turned white, propagated by Henri Gouges in the 1930s and sometimes called Pinot Gouges.

fr-orleans.name: Orléans
fr-orleans.summary: A small appellation around Orléans, with pale rosé and reds from Pinot Meunier (here called Gris Meunier) and Pinot Noir, and whites from Chardonnay (Auvernat). It was among the great vineyards of France in the Middle Ages.
fr-orleans.terroir: Sand and gravel terraces on the Loire.
fr-orleans.nerd_note: Orléans vinegar, a famous slow-fermented wine vinegar, comes from the city's wine trade.

fr-orleans-clery.name: Orléans-Cléry
fr-orleans-clery.summary: A tiny red-only appellation of Cabernet Franc from five communes around Cléry-Saint-André, south-west of Orléans. The gravel terraces give light, crunchy reds. It survives thanks to a handful of growers on the edge of the Orléans suburbs.
fr-orleans-clery.nerd_note: Louis XI, who loved Cléry, was buried in the basilica there in 1483.

fr-pacherenc-du-vic-bilh.name: Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh
fr-pacherenc-du-vic-bilh.grapes: Petit Manseng, Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu, Arrufiac, Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon
fr-pacherenc-du-vic-bilh.summary: Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh is the white-wine twin of Madiran, from the same area. Its name in Gascon means 'posts in a row' (*piquets en rang*), from the old way of training vines on stakes. It is made dry or sweet; the sweet versions, from Petit and Gros Manseng shrivelled on the vine (passerillé), can be picked as late as December. The local Arrufiac grape, nearly extinct, was revived by the Plaimont cooperative and Alain Brumont.
fr-pacherenc-du-vic-bilh.terroir: The same clay-limestone and boulbènes as Madiran.
fr-pacherenc-du-vic-bilh.nerd_note: Some producers pick a last batch of shrivelled Manseng for sweet Pacherenc as late as the end of December.

fr-palette.name: Palette
fr-palette.grapes: Mourvèdre, Grenache, Cinsault and many others; Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Ugni Blanc, Muscat and others
fr-palette.summary: Palette is one of the smallest AOCs in France, a few dozen hectares on north-facing limestone slopes on the outskirts of Aix-en-Provence, and it is largely the creation of a single estate, Château Simone. The Rougier family has owned Simone since 1830, and its old vines, a mix of dozens of varieties including some pre-phylloxera survivors, give red, white and rosé wines of unusual depth and longevity. Château Simone's white, mostly Clairette, ages in old barrels and develops honey, herbs and resin over decades. Château Crémade and Château Henri Bonnaud are the other producers.
fr-palette.terroir: North-facing slopes of limestone scree (calcaire de Langesse) and clay, cooler than the surroundings, near the Arc river.
fr-palette.nerd_note: Château Simone's cellars were dug by Carmelite monks in the sixteenth century, and some of its vines are among the oldest in Provence.

fr-patrimonio.name: Patrimonio
fr-patrimonio.grapes: Nielluccio (dominant in reds); Vermentinu (Vermentino) for white
fr-patrimonio.summary: Patrimonio, at the base of Cap Corse near Saint-Florent, was Corsica's first AOC (1968) and is its most famous. It sits in an amphitheatre of limestone and schist facing the Gulf of Saint-Florent, and Nielluccio, Corsica's name for Sangiovese, gives firm, dark, spicy reds that age well. The Vermentinu whites are rich and saline. Antoine Arena (and his sons), Domaine Leccia, Yves Leccia, Domaine Gentile and Clos de Bernardi are leading producers.
fr-patrimonio.terroir: Limestone (unusual in Corsica), clay and schist in an amphitheatre facing the sea.
fr-patrimonio.nerd_note: Patrimonio is the only part of Corsica with large limestone outcrops, which is why Nielluccio does particularly well there.

fr-pauillac.name: Pauillac
fr-pauillac.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
fr-pauillac.summary:
If one appellation defines Cabernet Sauvignon, it is Pauillac. Three of the five first growths (Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild) and 18 classed growths in all share about 1,200 ha around a small river port, and the style they make is the template copied around the world: blackcurrant and cedar, pencil shavings and tobacco, firm but fine tannins, and the ability to age for half a century. Cabernet Sauvignon often makes up 70 to 90% of the grand vin.

The commune has three main gravel plateaus. In the north, by the hamlet of Le Pouyalet, Lafite and Mouton face each other across a lane, with Pontet-Canet, d'Armailhac, Clerc Milon and Duhart-Milon around them. In the centre, the Bages plateau carries Lynch-Bages, Haut-Bages Libéral and Croizet-Bages; inland are Grand-Puy-Lacoste, Batailley and Haut-Batailley. In the south, at Saint-Lambert, Latour and the two Pichons sit against the Saint-Julien border, separated from Léoville Las Cases by the Juillac stream. Lafite's wines tend to perfume and finesse, Latour's to power and density, Mouton's to exotic richness.

Below the classed growths, Pauillac is almost entirely accounted for: few appellations have so little room for unknowns. The cooperative La Rose Pauillac and second wines (Carruades de Lafite, Les Forts de Latour, Le Petit Mouton, Réserve de la Comtesse) are the entry points.
fr-pauillac.terroir: Deep Garonne gravel croupes, up to 30 m high and several metres deep, over a subsoil of marl, clay and the iron-cemented *alios*. The gravel forces roots down several metres, gives excellent drainage after rain, and stores heat. Latour's 47-ha Enclos runs down to the estuary meadows, which reduces frost and cools hot nights.
producers: Château Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande
fr-pauillac.nerd_note: The tower on Latour's label is not the medieval fort of Saint-Maubert that gave the estate its name; that tower vanished long ago, and the round tower in the vines is a seventeenth-century dovecote.

fr-pecharmant.name: Pécharmant
fr-pecharmant.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec
fr-pecharmant.summary: Pécharmant is the best red appellation of the Bergerac area, on the hills north-east of the town. Its name is said to come from 'pech charmant', the charming hill. A subsoil of iron-rich clay called *tran* gives firm, deep, long-lived reds. Château de Tiregand and Domaine du Haut-Pécharmant lead.
fr-pecharmant.terroir: Sand and gravel over an iron-rich clay hardpan ('tran').
fr-pecharmant.nerd_note: The 'tran' hardpan is so hard that it blocks roots, keeping yields low.

fr-pernand-vergelesses.name: Pernand-Vergelesses
fr-pernand-vergelesses.summary: Pernand-Vergelesses is tucked into a side valley behind the hill of Corton, and its steep west-facing slopes include a large part of Corton-Charlemagne, the En Charlemagne climat. The village wines are now best known for their whites: lively, citrusy Chardonnay grown higher and cooler than in Meursault, which benefits in hot years. The reds come mostly from premier crus such as Île des Vergelesses (opposite Savigny's Les Vergelesses), Les Fichots and Creux de la Net, and are fresh, spicy and fine.
fr-pernand-vergelesses.terroir: Limestone and marl on cool, steep slopes at up to 350 m, some facing west; the village lies in a combe sheltered from the main slope.
fr-pernand-vergelesses.nerd_note: Bonneau du Martray, Pernand's most famous estate and one of Corton-Charlemagne's largest owners, was bought by Stan Kroenke (owner of Screaming Eagle) in 2017.

fr-pessac-leognan.name: Pessac-Léognan
fr-pessac-leognan.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc for red; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Sauvignon Gris for white
fr-pessac-leognan.summary:
Pessac-Léognan is the northern Graves, carved out in 1987 so that the historic estates closest to Bordeaux could stand apart from the cheaper southern Graves. Its ten communes run from Mérignac and Pessac (now suburbs, with vineyards between houses and tram lines) south to Léognan and Martillac, where the vines sit in clearings in the pine forest. All the estates of the Graves classification are here.

It is the one Bordeaux appellation that is great for both red and dry white. The reds blend Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot in near-equal proportions and have a signature smoky, mineral, tobacco-leaf character, sometimes described as hot gravel. The whites, barrel-fermented Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, are among France's finest: Haut-Brion Blanc, La Mission Haut-Brion Blanc, Domaine de Chevalier and Smith Haut Lafitte age 20 years or more. The late Denis Dubourdieu's research at the University of Bordeaux on skin contact, lees ageing and thiols shaped modern white Bordeaux, much of it here.

Haut-Brion, a 1855 first growth, and La Mission Haut-Brion face each other across the Avenue Jean Jaurès in Pessac, surrounded by the city.
fr-pessac-leognan.terroir: Deep gravel terraces mixed with sand and clay, warmer than the Médoc because of the urban heat island and distance from the estuary. In the south, gravel croupes in forest clearings give cooler nights that keep the whites fresh.
fr-pessac-leognan.nerd_note: Haut-Brion is the only wine estate mentioned in Samuel Pepys's diary: on 10 April 1663 he drank 'a sort of French wine called Ho Bryan' at the Royal Oak tavern in London.

fr-petit-chablis.name: Petit Chablis
fr-petit-chablis.summary: Petit Chablis is the entry level of Chablis: Chardonnay grown mostly on the higher plateaus and Portlandian limestone that surround the Kimmeridgian slopes. It now covers roughly 1,000 ha and has grown fast since the 1990s as frost protection improved. The wines are light, crisp and citrusy, made to be drunk within two or three years, and are some of the best-value white Burgundies. The name says small, but in warm vintages good growers make Petit Chablis that tastes like village Chablis.
fr-petit-chablis.terroir: Portlandian limestone, slightly younger and harder than Kimmeridgian, on exposed plateau tops; more wind and frost.
fr-petit-chablis.nerd_note: The Kimmeridgian versus Portlandian argument split Chablis in the 1970s: traditionalists such as William Fèvre fought expansion onto Portlandian soils, while others argued exposure mattered more than rock.

fr-pic-saint-loup.name: Pic Saint-Loup
fr-pic-saint-loup.summary: Pic Saint-Loup takes its name from the 658-m limestone peak that rises north of Montpellier like a shark's fin. Its vineyards, in 17 communes around Saint-Martin-de-Londres, Valflaunès and Lauret, are the coolest and wettest in the Languedoc, with cold nights from the Cévennes. That made it the first area of the region to specialise in Syrah, which gives fresh, peppery, violet-scented reds with Grenache and Mourvèdre. It was recognised as an AOC in its own right in 2017, starting with the 2016 vintage, and registered as an EU PDO in July 2023, after decades as a named area of Coteaux du Languedoc. Domaine de l'Hortus (Jean Orliac), Château de Cazeneuve, Clos Marie, Mas Bruguière and Ermitage du Pic Saint-Loup are references.
fr-pic-saint-loup.terroir: Jurassic and Cretaceous limestone, marl and scree in a combe between the Pic Saint-Loup and the Montagne de l'Hortus; altitude 150 to 300 m; one of the wettest parts of the Languedoc.
fr-pic-saint-loup.nerd_note: Legend says three brothers, Loup, Guiral and Clair, fell in love with the same woman; when she died, each retreated to a peak to live as a hermit, and the highest peak took Loup's name.

fr-picpoul-de-pinet.name: Picpoul de Pinet
fr-picpoul-de-pinet.summary: Picpoul de Pinet is the Languedoc's oyster wine: a crisp, lemony, saline white made only from Piquepoul Blanc, grown around Pinet on the shores of the Étang de Thau, where Bouzigues oysters are farmed. The grape's name means 'lip stinger' for its acidity. It became a separate AOC in 2013 (registered in the EU from 2017) after decades as a named area of Coteaux du Languedoc. It is one of the region's great commercial success stories, with distinctive embossed 'Neptune' bottles. Cooperatives at Pomérols and Pinet make most of it, alongside estates like Château de Pinet and Domaine Félines Jourdan.
fr-picpoul-de-pinet.terroir: Limestone, clay and sand near the Étang de Thau, with sea breezes.
fr-picpoul-de-pinet.nerd_note: The Thau lagoon produces about 10% of France's oysters, and Picpoul growers and oyster farmers jointly market 'the perfect pairing'.

fr-pierrevert.name: Pierrevert
fr-pierrevert.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Cinsault, Mourvèdre, Carignan; Grenache Blanc, Vermentino, Clairette, Roussanne, Marsanne
fr-pierrevert.summary: Pierrevert is a small appellation in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, along the Durance near Manosque, at the cool northern edge of Provence, with vineyards up to 600 m. It is the only appellation in the department. Its wines, mostly rosé, are fresh and mineral.
fr-pierrevert.terroir: Clay-limestone and gravel terraces along the Durance, at altitude.
fr-pierrevert.nerd_note: Pierrevert's altitude makes it one of the coolest Mediterranean appellations in France, close to the lavender fields of Valensole.

fr-pineau-des-charentes.name: Pineau des Charentes
fr-pineau-des-charentes.grapes: Ugni Blanc, Colombard, Montils, Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc; Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon
fr-pineau-des-charentes.summary: Pineau des Charentes is the liqueur wine of the Cognac region, made by blending fresh grape must with Cognac at least a year old, then ageing it, partly in oak, for at least 18 months before release. A legend says a sixteenth-century grower accidentally poured must into a barrel containing Cognac and found the result delicious years later. It is made white or rosé and served chilled.
fr-pineau-des-charentes.terroir: The chalky soils of Cognac (Grande and Petite Champagne, Borderies, Fins Bois).
fr-pineau-des-charentes.nerd_note: Pineau is made by mutage, like the vins doux naturels, but with Cognac instead of neutral spirit, and before fermentation starts.

fr-pomerol.name: Pomerol
fr-pomerol.summary:
Pomerol is a small, flat, unassuming plateau north-east of Libourne, with no village to speak of, no grand châteaux and no classification, and yet it makes the most expensive red wines of Bordeaux. About 800 ha are shared by around 130 producers, many farming fewer than 10 ha. Petrus, Le Pin and Lafleur sell for more than the Médoc first growths.

The style is opulent and velvety: Merlot dominates, typically 70 to 100%, with Cabernet Franc adding perfume. Great Pomerol tastes of plum, black cherry, truffle, violets and iron, with dense but silky tannins and a texture that seems to fill the mouth. It is approachable earlier than Pauillac but can age 30 years or more.

Fame came late. In the nineteenth century Pomerol was considered part of Saint-Émilion's lesser hinterland. Madame Edmond Loubat, owner of Petrus from 1925 to 1961, and the Libourne négociant Jean-Pierre Moueix, who took over distribution and then ownership, turned Petrus into a luxury brand served at the 1953 coronation of Elizabeth II and then in New York. The Thienponts of Belgium (Vieux Château Certan from 1924, Le Pin from 1979), the Guinaudeaus at Lafleur and the Durantous at L'Église-Clinet built the rest of the legend.

No classification has ever been proposed seriously; producers argue that the market, and the soil map, already rank them.
fr-pomerol.terroir: Pomerol is a plateau of gravel and clay sloping gently from about 40 m in the east to the sands near Libourne in the west. Its highest point holds a lens of dense, swelling blue-grey smectite clay, the 'buttonhole', on which Petrus sits; around it are gravel and clay (Lafleur, Vieux Château Certan, L'Évangile, La Conseillante), with sand further west. A subsoil of *crasse de fer*, iron-rich hardpan, is said to give Pomerol its iron and truffle notes. Clay keeps Merlot supplied with water in drought, which explains its consistency in hot vintages.
fr-pomerol.nerd_note: Petrus traditionally picks only in the afternoon, once the dew has dried, with a crew large enough to bring in its roughly 11.5 ha in two or three afternoons; in a rainy vintage of the 1980s it famously hired a helicopter to hover over the vines and blow-dry the grapes.

fr-pommard.name: Pommard
fr-pommard.summary:
Pommard is the most famous red-only village of the Côte de Beaune and the source of its most powerful wine: deep in colour, firm, earthy and long-lived, often compared to the Côte de Nuits. Its name was one of the most widely known in the world in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, which encouraged imitation and fraud before the AOC era.

Pommard has no grand crus, but two premier crus are often proposed for promotion. Les Rugiens, next to Volnay, is split into Rugiens Bas, the finer lower part with red, iron-rich soil, and Rugiens Hauts. Les Grands Épenots and Les Petits Épenots, toward Beaune, give more elegant and aromatic wine; within them the Comte Armand domaine's Clos des Épeneaux monopole is a classic. Other notable climats include Les Pézerolles, Les Jarolières and Les Charmots.
fr-pommard.terroir: Heavier brown clay over limestone, more clay than Volnay, with red iron-rich soils in Les Rugiens; the village sits at the mouth of a broad combe.
fr-pommard.nerd_note: The Pièce des Présidents of the 2025 Hospices de Beaune auction, a barrel of Pommard premier cru Les Rugiens, sold for around $460,000.

fr-pouilly-fuisse.name: Pouilly-Fuissé
fr-pouilly-fuisse.summary:
Pouilly-Fuissé is the leading white appellation of the Mâconnais, about 800 ha delimited across four communes (Fuissé, Solutré-Pouilly, Vergisson and Chaintré) beneath the limestone cliffs of Solutré and Vergisson. The wines are richer and riper than Mâcon, often barrel-fermented, with citrus, peach, hazelnut and a firm mineral finish, and the best age for a decade or more.

After a 13-year campaign led by growers' union president Frédéric-Marc Burrier, 22 climats were promoted to premier cru from the 2020 vintage, covering about 194 ha, roughly a quarter of the appellation. They include Sur la Roche and Les Crays under Vergisson, Le Clos de Solutré and En Servy at Solutré, Les Ménétrières, Le Clos and Les Brûlés at Fuissé, and Aux Quarts, Le Clos Reyssier and Les Chevrières at Chaintré. They were the Mâconnais's first premier crus.
fr-pouilly-fuisse.terroir: Jurassic limestone and marl on steep slopes and scree fans below the cliffs of Solutré and Vergisson, at 200 to 400 m; facing east and south. Chaintré, further south, has warmer, clay-rich soils.
fr-pouilly-fuisse.nerd_note: The 22 premier crus were approved in late 2020 for that vintage; they were the first premier crus anywhere in the Mâconnais.

fr-pouilly-fume.name: Pouilly-Fumé
fr-pouilly-fume.summary:
Pouilly-Fumé sits on the east bank of the Loire facing Sancerre, around the town of Pouilly-sur-Loire. The name 'Fumé', smoky, refers to the grey bloom on ripe Sauvignon berries or to the smoky, gunflint note of wines from the flint soils, depending on whom you ask. The wines are white only, Sauvignon Blanc, often a little rounder and spicier than Sancerre.

Didier Dagueneau (1956 to 2008), a former motorcycle racer known for his wild hair and uncompromising standards, changed Pouilly-Fumé by showing it could rival the world's great whites: he cut yields, used barrels and made single-terroir wines such as Silex and Pur Sang. His son Louis-Benjamin continues the work. Château du Nozet (Ladoucette), Château de Tracy and Jonathan Pabiot are other leaders.
fr-pouilly-fume.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl, Portlandian limestone and flint (silex) on clay, on gentle slopes above the Loire; Saint-Andelain's flint hill is the most famous site.
fr-pouilly-fume.nerd_note: Alexandre Bain, a natural-wine producer whose Pouilly-Fumé was refused the appellation in the mid-2010s as atypical, now sells it as Vin de France; his case is often cited in debates about how appellations judge typicity.

fr-pouilly-loche.name: Pouilly-Loché
fr-pouilly-loche.summary: Pouilly-Loché is the smallest of the Pouilly appellations, about 35 ha in the commune of Loché just south of Pouilly-Fuissé. Its whites are lighter and fresher than Pouilly-Fuissé, and may also be sold as Pouilly-Vinzelles. Since the 2024 vintage one climat, Les Mûres (about 7 ha), has been classified premier cru, approved on 18 November 2024. The Cave des Grands Crus Blancs co-operative makes much of the wine.
fr-pouilly-loche.terroir: Limestone and clay on gentle east-facing slopes near the Saône plain.
fr-pouilly-loche.nerd_note: Wines from Pouilly-Loché may legally be sold as Pouilly-Vinzelles, but the reverse is not allowed.

fr-pouilly-sur-loire.name: Pouilly-sur-Loire
fr-pouilly-sur-loire.summary: A survivor of the pre-phylloxera Loire: white wine from Chasselas, once the grape of the area, which supplied table grapes to Paris. Only a few hectares remain, with Domaine Serge Dagueneau et Filles among the last producers.
fr-pouilly-sur-loire.nerd_note: Pouilly-sur-Loire is one of the last French appellations built on Chasselas, a grape that once covered the Pouilly hills.

fr-pouilly-vinzelles.name: Pouilly-Vinzelles
fr-pouilly-vinzelles.summary: Pouilly-Vinzelles covers about 70 ha around Vinzelles and Loché, between Pouilly-Fuissé and the Saône. Its whites are similar to Pouilly-Fuissé but a little lighter. Three premier crus were recognised from the 2024 vintage: Les Quarts (about 12.5 ha, on the same slope as Pouilly-Fuissé's Aux Quarts), Les Longeays and Les Pétaux.
fr-pouilly-vinzelles.terroir: Limestone and marl with some granite-derived sands, on east-facing slopes.
fr-pouilly-vinzelles.nerd_note: The Bret brothers of La Soufrandière were key advocates of the 2024 premier cru promotion.

fr-premieres-cotes-de-bordeaux.name: Premières Côtes de Bordeaux
fr-premieres-cotes-de-bordeaux.summary: Premières Côtes de Bordeaux once covered red and white wines from a 60 km strip of slopes on the right bank of the Garonne, from Bordeaux to Cadillac. Since the 2008 vintage its reds have moved to Cadillac Côtes de Bordeaux, and the name now applies only to sweet and semi-sweet white wines. It is a small, mostly local category of moelleux.
fr-premieres-cotes-de-bordeaux.terroir: Steep clay-limestone and gravel slopes overlooking the Garonne.
fr-premieres-cotes-de-bordeaux.nerd_note: The 'Premières' in the name meant the first slopes upstream from the city, not a quality ranking.

fr-puisseguin-saint-emilion.name: Puisseguin-Saint-Émilion
fr-puisseguin-saint-emilion.summary: Puisseguin lies east of Montagne on a hilly limestone plateau, and its wines are often the firmest and most structured of the satellites. Château Guibot-la-Fourvieille and Château Fongaban are reliable names, and the cooperative is important.
fr-puisseguin-saint-emilion.terroir: Clay-limestone plateau and slopes, similar to the côtes of Saint-Émilion.
fr-puisseguin-saint-emilion.nerd_note: The Puisseguin plateau rises to about 90 m, among the highest ground in the Libournais, which tends to delay ripening and keep acidity firmer than on the Saint-Émilion plain.

fr-puligny-montrachet.name: Puligny-Montrachet
fr-puligny-montrachet.summary:
Puligny-Montrachet is the white-wine village par excellence. It added the name of its most famous vineyard, Le Montrachet, in 1879, and it shares Montrachet and Bâtard-Montrachet with Chassagne while holding Chevalier-Montrachet and Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet alone. Its wines are the most precise, finely chiselled whites of the Côte: white flowers, citrus and stone fruit, a steely line and a long mineral finish, less buttery than Meursault.

The premier crus run north from the grand crus: Le Cailleret and Les Pucelles beside them; Les Folatières, Clavaillon and the Champ Canet higher up; Les Combettes, Les Perrières and Les Referts against Meursault. Puligny's water table is high, so cellars are shallow, which is why many growers bottle earlier than in Meursault. Domaine Leflaive, run by Anne-Claude Leflaive from 1990 until her death in 2015, made Puligny's name in biodynamics and is still its reference.
fr-puligny-montrachet.terroir: Limestone with marls and clay; a high water table means few underground cellars. The grand crus sit at 250 to 280 m on thin soil over hard limestone.
fr-puligny-montrachet.nerd_note: Puligny's water table was blamed for its lack of cellars until the 1990s, when growers such as Leflaive found that shallow cellars still allowed slow lees ageing.

fr-quarts-de-chaume.name: Quarts de Chaume
fr-quarts-de-chaume.summary: Quarts de Chaume is a tiny amphitheatre of south-facing slopes above the Layon at Rochefort-sur-Loire, and since 2011 it has been the first and only Loire appellation with 'Grand Cru' in its name. The name comes from the medieval lord's right to a quarter of the harvest from the best plots. The rules ban chaptalisation and require hand harvesting and must of at least 298 g/l of sugar, giving some of the most concentrated sweet Chenins anywhere. Château Pierre-Bise, Domaine des Baumard, Château de Bellerive and Domaine de la Bergerie are references.
fr-quarts-de-chaume.terroir: South-facing schist slopes in a sheltered bowl near the river, warm and well exposed, where botrytis develops reliably.
fr-quarts-de-chaume.nerd_note: In 2011 the INAO also banned cryoextraction (freezing grapes to concentrate sugar) for Quarts de Chaume, after a long dispute with a producer who used it.

fr-quincy.name: Quincy
fr-quincy.summary: Quincy, on the Cher river west of Bourges, was one of the first French AOCs (1936). Its Sauvignon Blanc grows on sand and gravel terraces and is light, citrusy and floral.
fr-quincy.terroir: Sand and gravel terraces over limestone on the left bank of the Cher.
fr-quincy.nerd_note: Quincy was recognised as an AOC in 1936, one of the very first, along with Châteauneuf-du-Pape and Arbois.

fr-rasteau.name: Rasteau
fr-rasteau.grapes: Grenache (min 50%), Syrah, Mourvèdre; Grenache for VDN
fr-rasteau.summary: Rasteau has two appellations. The older is a vin doux naturel, recognised in 1944: fortified Grenache made in red (and amber or rancio) styles, rich and port-like. The newer, since 2010, is a cru for dry red wine, Grenache-led blends that are among the most powerful and ripe of the Southern Rhône, from 861 ha (2025) of south-facing slopes. The village was formerly a Côtes du Rhône Villages.
fr-rasteau.terroir: Marl and clay with some pebbles and sand on south-facing amphitheatre slopes above the Ouvèze; one of the warmest sites in the south.
fr-rasteau.nerd_note: Rasteau vin doux naturel is now tiny (18 ha in 2025) while the dry red is one of the fastest-growing crus.

fr-regnie.name: Régnié
fr-regnie.summary: Régnié became the tenth cru in 1988, the newest of the group. It lies between Morgon and Brouilly on rolling granite hills around Régnié-Durette, whose church has two distinctive towers. The wines are lighter and fruity, with raspberry and red currant, and some growers such as Charly Thévenet and Julien Sunier have shown its potential.
fr-regnie.terroir: Pink granite sand on rounded hills between 300 and 400 m.
fr-regnie.nerd_note: Régnié's promotion in 1988 ended a long campaign; it was previously sold as Beaujolais-Villages.

fr-reuilly.name: Reuilly
fr-reuilly.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc; Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris
fr-reuilly.summary: Reuilly, on the Arnon river near Quincy, makes Sauvignon whites, Pinot Noir reds and a distinctive pale rosé or vin gris from Pinot Gris. Its Kimmeridgian and limestone slopes give wines close to Sancerre in style. Claude Lafond helped revive the area from near abandonment in the 1970s.
fr-reuilly.nerd_note: Reuilly is one of the few places in France that makes a rosé from Pinot Gris.

fr-richebourg.name: Richebourg
fr-richebourg.summary: Richebourg, about 8 ha north of Romanée-Conti, is the most opulent of Vosne's grand crus: rich, velvety and sensuous, with dark fruit, spice and a fleshy weight. It comprises Les Richebourg and Les Véroilles, which faces slightly northeast. Domaine de la Romanée-Conti owns about 3.5 ha; other owners include Leroy, Méo-Camuzet (from Henri Jayer's family vines), Grivot, Anne Gros, Gros Frère et Sœur, Mongeard-Mugneret and Hudelot-Noëllat.
fr-richebourg.terroir: Brown limestone with more clay than Romanée-Conti; the lower part benefits from a slight hollow.
fr-richebourg.nerd_note: The name probably means 'rich town', and the wine was praised as early as the eighteenth century.

fr-rivesaltes.name: Rivesaltes
fr-rivesaltes.grapes: Grenache Noir, Grenache Gris, Grenache Blanc, Macabeu, Malvoisie, Muscat
fr-rivesaltes.summary:
Rivesaltes is the largest VDN appellation, covering much of Roussillon and a few communes of the Aude. Its wines are made by mutage: neutral grape spirit is added to fermenting Grenache, Macabeu or Malvoisie once part of the sugar has turned to alcohol, which keeps natural sweetness and brings the wine to 15 to 18% alcohol. There are four styles. *Grenat* is a young red, bottled after a short reductive ageing to keep its black-cherry fruit. *Tuilé* is red aged oxidatively for years until it turns the colour of old roof tiles. *Ambré* is white aged oxidatively until it turns amber, with notes of orange peel, apricot and toasted almond. *Rosé* is the newest, fresh and fruity.

The oxidative wines are where Rivesaltes becomes extraordinary. Many estates leave young wine in glass bonbonnes in the sun for a year, then age it in large old casks for decades, sometimes topping up old wine with younger wine like a solera. *Hors d'âge* wines must be at least five years old, and *rancio* is a mention for wines that have developed the nutty, maderised, curry-and-walnut character that comes with long oxidation. Sales have fallen sharply since the 1980s, when Rivesaltes was a mass-market aperitif, which means that old vintages are surprisingly affordable. Domaine Cazes, Domaine Sarda-Malet and Domaine des Chênes keep old wines.
fr-rivesaltes.terroir: Schist, limestone, granite and alluvial terraces of the Agly, Têt and Tech valleys.
fr-rivesaltes.nerd_note: Rivesaltes made Marshal Joffre, born in the town in 1852, its most famous son; his statue stands in the main square.

fr-romanee-conti.name: Romanée-Conti
fr-romanee-conti.summary:
Romanée-Conti is the most famous vineyard in the world and its wine the most expensive red. A plot of only 1.81 ha, it is the monopole of Domaine de la Romanée-Conti and produces about 5,000 to 6,000 bottles a year. It was called Cros des Cloux when the monks of Saint-Vivant de Vergy owned it; by 1651 it was La Romanée. In 1760 Louis-François de Bourbon, Prince de Conti, outbid Madame de Pompadour to buy it and added his name. After the Revolution it passed through several owners until Jacques-Marie Duvault-Blochet bought it in 1869; his descendants, the de Villaine family, now share the domaine with the Leroy family heirs.

Romanée-Conti was the last vineyard in the Côte d'Or to be pulled up after phylloxera, in 1945. The wine is not the most powerful in Vosne but the most complete: layered, spicy and ethereal, with roses, oriental spice and a finish that seems to go on forever. Aubert de Villaine co-directed the domaine for nearly five decades from 1974; Perrine Fenal and Bertrand de Villaine now lead it.
fr-romanee-conti.terroir: A gentle 6 percent slope facing east-southeast at about 270 m, on brown limestone soil with clay and some iron, over Bajocian and Bathonian rock; good natural drainage.
fr-romanee-conti.nerd_note: The domaine pulled up the ungrafted vines after the 1945 harvest and replanted from its own cuttings in 1947, so no Romanée-Conti was made from 1946 to 1951.

fr-romanee-saint-vivant.name: Romanée-Saint-Vivant
fr-romanee-saint-vivant.summary: Romanée-Saint-Vivant, about 9.4 ha below Romanée-Conti and Richebourg and just above the village of Vosne, takes its name from the Benedictine priory of Saint-Vivant de Vergy, which owned it for centuries. It gives the most delicate and feminine of Vosne's grand crus: silky, spicy and fragrant, with a gentle tannic touch. Domaine de la Romanée-Conti farms about 5.3 ha, mostly the former Clos des Quatre Journaux of the Marey-Monge family. Leroy, Sylvain Cathiard, Arnoux-Lachaux, Hudelot-Noëllat and Follin-Arbelet also make it.
fr-romanee-saint-vivant.terroir: Deeper soil with more clay on the gentle lower slope near the village.
fr-romanee-saint-vivant.nerd_note: The ruins of the Saint-Vivant abbey are in the Hautes-Côtes above Curtil-Vergy, restored by an association with support from the DRC.

fr-rose-d-anjou.name: Rosé d'Anjou
fr-rose-d-anjou.grapes: Grolleau, Gamay, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Côt, Pineau d'Aunis
fr-rose-d-anjou.summary: Rosé d'Anjou is a medium-sweet rosé, mostly from Grolleau, and one of the best-selling appellation wines in France. Light, fruity and slightly sweet, it is a supermarket staple. Its reputation is modest, but well-made examples are refreshing and cheap.
fr-rose-d-anjou.nerd_note: Grolleau, its main grape, is named for the 'grolle', a local word for crow, because of its dark berries.

fr-rose-de-loire.name: Rosé de Loire
fr-rose-de-loire.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Gamay, Grolleau, Pineau d'Aunis, Pinot Noir
fr-rose-de-loire.summary: Rosé de Loire is a dry rosé appellation covering Anjou, Saumur and Touraine. Created in 1974 to give the region a dry alternative to the off-dry Rosé d'Anjou, it is crisp and light.
fr-rose-de-loire.terroir: The Anjou, Saumur and Touraine areas.
fr-rose-de-loire.nerd_note: Rosé de Loire must contain at least 30% Cabernet, a rule designed to give it more structure than Grolleau alone.

fr-rose-des-riceys.name: Rosé des Riceys
fr-rose-des-riceys.summary: One of the rarest appellations in France: a still, dark rosé made only in the commune of Les Riceys in the Aube, from Pinot Noir. The grapes are macerated in open vats, and the winemaker tastes constantly to stop the maceration when the 'goût des Riceys', a flavour of hazelnut, red fruit and spice, appears. Only a few tens of thousands of bottles are made, and only in good years. Legend says Louis XIV drank it when he visited the area.
fr-rose-des-riceys.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl and limestone on south-facing slopes in Les Riceys.
fr-rose-des-riceys.nerd_note: Les Riceys is the only commune in France with three AOCs: Champagne, Coteaux Champenois and Rosé des Riceys.

fr-rosette.name: Rosette
fr-rosette.summary: One of France's smallest appellations, on the hills just north of Bergerac next to Pécharmant, for semi-sweet (moelleux) whites with delicate, floral sweetness. It was a fashionable aperitif in the early twentieth century. Its sand and gravel soils give light, fragrant wines that are best drunk within a few years.
fr-rosette.terroir: Sand and gravel over clay, similar to Pécharmant.
fr-rosette.nerd_note: Rosette was nearly extinct by the 1990s; a handful of growers keep it alive.

fr-roussette-de-savoie.name: Roussette de Savoie
fr-roussette-de-savoie.summary: Roussette de Savoie is the appellation for Altesse, Savoie's finest white grape, legendarily brought back from Cyprus by a princess of Savoy. The wines are aromatic, with bergamot, quince and honey, and age well. Roussette de Savoie is now made entirely from Altesse. Four crus may add their name: Frangy, Marestel, Monterminod and Monthoux.
fr-roussette-de-savoie.terroir: Limestone and marl slopes; the crus lie on steep sites near the Rhône and above Chambéry.
fr-roussette-de-savoie.nerd_note: Marestel, a very steep slope at Jongieux, is often called the grand cru of Altesse.

fr-roussette-de-savoie-frangy.name: Roussette de Savoie Frangy
fr-roussette-de-savoie-frangy.summary: Frangy in Haute-Savoie, on the Usses river near the Rhône north of Seyssel, is the northernmost Roussette cru. Its molasse and glacial slopes give fresh, floral Altesse with notes of bergamot and almond, lighter than Marestel's. It is one of four crus of Roussette de Savoie.

fr-roussette-de-savoie-marestel.name: Roussette de Savoie Marestel
fr-roussette-de-savoie-marestel.summary: Marestel, a very steep slope at Jongieux above the Rhône, is the most famous Roussette cru, giving rich, long-lived Altesse; Domaine Dupasquier is the reference. It is one of four crus of Roussette de Savoie.

fr-roussette-de-savoie-monterminod.name: Roussette de Savoie Monterminod
fr-roussette-de-savoie-monterminod.summary: Monterminod, on a steep limestone slope above Chambéry at Saint-Alban-Leysse, is the southernmost and smallest Roussette cru, about 16 ha delimited. Its Altesse is rich and honeyed, and suburban housing presses on its edges. It is one of four crus of Roussette de Savoie.

fr-roussette-de-savoie-monthoux.name: Roussette de Savoie Monthoux
fr-roussette-de-savoie-monthoux.summary: Monthoux is a small Roussette cru of about 23 ha on a sheltered limestone slope near the Lac du Bourget. Its Altesse is fine and aromatic, with quince and white flowers, and benefits from the lake's moderating influence. It is one of four crus of Roussette de Savoie.

fr-roussette-du-bugey.name: Roussette du Bugey
fr-roussette-du-bugey.summary: Roussette du Bugey is the Bugey appellation for Altesse whites, with two crus that may add their name, Montagnieu and Virieu-le-Grand. The wines are floral and honeyed, similar to Roussette de Savoie.
fr-roussette-du-bugey.terroir: Limestone scree on slopes along the Rhône.

fr-roussette-du-bugey-montagnieu.name: Roussette du Bugey Montagnieu
fr-roussette-du-bugey-montagnieu.summary: Montagnieu, on the Rhône in the southern Bugey, gives the most prized Roussette du Bugey, a still white from Altesse with a nutty, floral character; Franck Peillot is the reference grower. Bugey became an AOC in 2009; Montagnieu is also a named cru for sparkling Bugey.
fr-roussette-du-bugey-montagnieu.terroir: Steep limestone scree and marl above the Rhône.

fr-roussette-du-bugey-virieu-le-grand.name: Roussette du Bugey Virieu-le-Grand
fr-roussette-du-bugey-virieu-le-grand.summary: A small cru of Roussette du Bugey of about 35 ha around the village of Virieu-le-Grand in the Furans valley, for pure Altesse whites that are floral, honeyed and fresh from limestone scree.

fr-ruchottes-chambertin.name: Ruchottes-Chambertin
fr-ruchottes-chambertin.summary: Ruchottes-Chambertin, about 3.3 ha above Mazis, is the highest and stoniest Gevrey grand cru. Its name may come from rochers, rocks, and its thin soil gives a lean, mineral, finely etched wine that can be austere young. Armand Rousseau's 1.06 ha Clos des Ruchottes monopole, Domaine Georges Roumier (made from the Michel Bonnefond parcel) and Mugneret-Gibourg are the references.
fr-ruchottes-chambertin.terroir: Very thin soil over hard Bathonian limestone, high on the slope.
fr-ruchottes-chambertin.nerd_note: Ruchottes-Chambertin is divided between Ruchottes du Dessus and Ruchottes du Bas.

fr-rully.name: Rully
fr-rully.summary: Rully, the northernmost village of the Côte Chalonnaise, is mostly white and has long been the heart of Burgundy's sparkling wine industry: many crémant houses were founded here in the nineteenth century. Its still Chardonnay is bright and fresh with citrus and apple, and its reds are light and fruity. There are 23 premier crus, such as Grésigny, La Pucelle, Les Cloux and Rabourcé.
fr-rully.terroir: Limestone and marl hills facing east and southeast, around 230 to 350 m, with the twelfth-century Château de Rully on the slope.
fr-rully.nerd_note: The twelfth-century Château de Rully has passed down through the same family line for centuries and overlooks its own vineyards.

fr-sable-de-camargue.name: Sable de Camargue
fr-sable-de-camargue.grapes: Grenache Gris, Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon
fr-sable-de-camargue.summary: Sable de Camargue is France's newest wine AOC, published in the EU Official Journal on 18 October 2023 after twelve years as an IGP. It covers about 3,000 ha of vines on the sands of the Rhône delta in 14 coastal communes of the Hérault, Gard and Bouches-du-Rhône, and is famous for pale 'gris' rosés; 'gris de gris' must come entirely from Grenache Gris. The wines are delicate, salmon-pale, fresh and saline. Domaine Royal de Jarras (Listel) is the best-known name.
fr-sable-de-camargue.terroir: Uniform sands of the delta, at least 80 percent sand, almost free of clay and silt, laid down by the river, the sea and the wind; the sand protected vines from phylloxera, so many are on their own roots.
fr-sable-de-camargue.nerd_note: Benedictine monks of the Abbey of Psalmody, near Aigues-Mortes, were making wine from sand-grown vines in the seventh century; today some 95 percent of the vineyard is organic, in conversion or HVE certified, and sheep graze the cover crops.

fr-saint-amour.name: Saint-Amour
fr-saint-amour.summary: Saint-Amour is the northernmost of the ten crus and the only one lying entirely in Saône-et-Loire, on the border with the Mâconnais. Its name, from a Roman soldier who became a saint, has made it the wine of Valentine's Day, and it sells much of its wine around 14 February. The wines are supple and fruity with red berries and spice, and the mix of granite, schist and limestone soils gives some structure.
fr-saint-amour.terroir: Granite, schist and some limestone and clay on east-facing hills, bordering the Saint-Véran appellation.
fr-saint-amour.nerd_note: Saint-Amour is the only cru lying entirely in Burgundy's Saône-et-Loire department; Moulin-à-Vent (Romanèche-Thorins) and Chénas (La Chapelle-de-Guinchay) straddle it and the Rhône.

fr-saint-aubin.name: Saint-Aubin
fr-saint-aubin.summary: Saint-Aubin is Burgundy's rising white star. Its village and the hamlet of Gamay sit in a side valley behind Puligny and Chassagne, and its best premier crus, En Remilly and Les Murgers des Dents de Chien, touch the Montrachet hill directly. About two thirds of its vineyard is premier cru. The wines are leaner and more mineral than Puligny's, with crisp acidity and a chalky texture, and they have gained from warm vintages.
fr-saint-aubin.terroir: Limestone and marl at 300 to 350 m with steep southeast slopes; cooler than the main côte.
fr-saint-aubin.nerd_note: The hamlet of Gamay is often claimed as the namesake of the Gamay grape.

fr-saint-bris.name: Saint-Bris
fr-saint-bris.summary: Saint-Bris is Burgundy's odd one out: the only appellation in the region for Sauvignon Blanc. Grown around the villages of Saint-Bris-le-Vineux, Chitry, Irancy and Quenne south of Auxerre, it was a VDQS called Sauvignon de Saint-Bris before becoming an AOC in 2003. The wines are crisp and grassy like a Loire Sauvignon but with a chalky, Burgundian texture. Sauvignon Gris may be added for extra weight.
fr-saint-bris.terroir: Kimmeridgian and Portlandian limestones and marls; the village of Saint-Bris sits on a maze of medieval cellars dug into the rock.
fr-saint-bris.nerd_note: The Goisot family, biodynamic since 2002, bottles single-site Saint-Bris such as Exogyra Virgula, named after the fossil oyster in the soil.

fr-saint-chinian.name: Saint-Chinian
fr-saint-chinian.grapes: Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Cinsault, Lledoner Pelut; Grenache Blanc, Marsanne, Roussanne, Vermentino
fr-saint-chinian.summary: Saint-Chinian, north-west of Béziers, is divided by the Vernazobre river: schist in the north and limestone and clay in the south. The northern schist gives fine, fragrant reds; the southern limestone gives more powerful, structured wines. Two villages on the schist, Berlou and Roquebrun, have their own crus (since 2005), and the Roquebrun cooperative is among the best in France. Borie La Vitarèle, Canet-Valette, Mas Champart and Domaine des Jougla are references.
fr-saint-chinian.terroir: Schist in the north (Berlou, Roquebrun), clay-limestone and marl in the south, on hills facing the Mediterranean.
fr-saint-chinian.nerd_note: Roquebrun, on the Orb, is so warm that it is called 'the little Nice of the Hérault' and has a Mediterranean garden of cacti and citrus.

fr-saint-chinian-berlou.name: Saint-Chinian Berlou
fr-saint-chinian-berlou.summary: Berlou is a schist village in the hills of Saint-Chinian whose reds keep a high share of old Carignan, giving dark, spicy wines; the Berlou cooperative makes most of them.
fr-saint-chinian-berlou.terroir: Schist hills with old bush vines.
fr-saint-chinian-berlou.nerd_note: Saint-Chinian's two schist villages have been allowed to add their names since 2005.

fr-saint-chinian-roquebrun.name: Saint-Chinian Roquebrun
fr-saint-chinian-roquebrun.summary: Roquebrun lies on the Orb river in the schist hills of northern Saint-Chinian, a village so sheltered that mimosas and citrus grow in its Mediterranean garden. Its reds, based on Syrah, Grenache and Mourvèdre, are fresh and mineral; the Cave de Roquebrun is central.
fr-saint-chinian-roquebrun.terroir: Schist slopes above the Orb gorge.
fr-saint-chinian-roquebrun.nerd_note: Saint-Chinian's two schist villages have been allowed to add their names since 2005.

fr-saint-emilion.name: Saint-Émilion
fr-saint-emilion.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec
fr-saint-emilion.summary: Saint-Émilion AOC is the basic appellation of the medieval hill town and its eight neighbouring communes, which together form the old Jurisdiction of Saint-Émilion, listed by UNESCO in 1999 as the first vineyard landscape on the World Heritage list. The zone is the same as Saint-Émilion Grand Cru; the difference lies in rules (yields, ageing, tasting) and in what growers choose to declare. Most serious estates use the Grand Cru appellation, so plain Saint-Émilion is mostly the softer, earlier-drinking wine of the sandy plain toward the Dordogne and from cooperatives such as the Union des Producteurs de Saint-Émilion.
fr-saint-emilion.terroir: The same mosaic as the Grand Cru: limestone plateau, clay-limestone slopes, sands and gravel. Plain Saint-Émilion comes largely from the sandy and alluvial lower land.
fr-saint-emilion.nerd_note: The word 'Grand Cru' in Saint-Émilion is an appellation, not a ranking; only the separate classification (Grand Cru Classé, Premier Grand Cru Classé) ranks estates.

fr-saint-emilion-grand-cru.name: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru
fr-saint-emilion-grand-cru.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec
fr-saint-emilion-grand-cru.summary:
Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is the heart of the right bank: about 5,400 ha shared by the Saint-Émilion and Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellations in nine communes around a limestone hill town honeycombed with quarries, catacombs and a monolithic church carved from the rock in the twelfth century. More than 800 estates share it, most of them small family holdings, and the wines range from juicy Merlot to some of the most expensive bottles on earth.

The classification, created in 1955, applies only to this appellation and is revised about every ten years, which makes it the only Bordeaux ranking where estates can be promoted or demoted. That flexibility made it litigious. The 2006 list was annulled by the courts; the 2012 list was challenged for a decade by demoted owners until the Conseil d'État finally upheld it in March 2024; and in late 2021 a Bordeaux criminal court found Hubert de Boüard, co-owner of Angélus, guilty of illegal taking of interest (*prise illégale d'intérêts*) over his role in the 2012 process. Partly in protest at criteria that weighed wine tourism, reputation and social media presence alongside tasting, Cheval Blanc and Ausone announced in mid-2021 that they would not apply for 2022, and Angélus followed in January 2022. They still use the Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellation, simply without a classification mention.

The 2022 classification, published in September 2022 and valid until 2032, names 85 estates: two Premiers Grands Crus Classés A (Pavie and Figeac, the latter promoted after decades of campaigning), twelve Premiers Grands Crus Classés B (Beau-Séjour Bécot, Beauséjour, Bélair-Monange, Canon, Canon-la-Gaffelière, Clos Fourtet, Larcis Ducasse, La Mondotte, Pavie Macquin, Troplong Mondot, Trottevieille, Valandraud) and 71 Grands Crus Classés. La Gaffelière, a former B, also withdrew.

Styles follow the soils. Wines from the limestone plateau and its slopes (Ausone, Canon, Bélair-Monange, Pavie) are taut, mineral and slow to evolve. The gravel island beside Pomerol (Cheval Blanc, Figeac) gives Cabernet-rich, fragrant wines. The sandy plain makes soft, early wines. The 1990s 'garagiste' movement (Valandraud, La Mondotte) showed that tiny plots and extreme ripeness could command cult prices, and its excesses later gave way to fresher, less oaky wines.
fr-saint-emilion-grand-cru.terroir: A limestone plateau of *calcaire à astéries* at 60 to 100 m, edged by steep clay-limestone slopes (*côtes*) facing south toward the Dordogne. Below are sandy-clay *pieds de côte* and the sandy, alluvial plain. In the north-west, toward Pomerol, a band of gravel and sand carries Cheval Blanc and Figeac. Clay and limestone keep vines supplied in drought and give the wines freshness.
fr-saint-emilion-grand-cru.nerd_note: Saint-Émilion's quarries supplied stone for Bordeaux for centuries; the resulting 200 km of tunnels under the plateau now age wine, and roots of old vines can be seen piercing the ceilings.

fr-saint-estephe.name: Saint-Estèphe
fr-saint-estephe.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
fr-saint-estephe.summary:
Saint-Estèphe is the northernmost of the great Médoc communes, separated from Pauillac by the Jalle du Breuil stream, which also separates Lafite from Cos d'Estournel. Its wines have a reputation for sturdiness: deep colour, firm tannin and acidity, and a savoury, earthy core that needs ten or more years to relax. That reputation has softened since the 2000s as estates picked riper and used more Merlot, but the structure remains.

There are five classed growths: Cos d'Estournel and Montrose (seconds), Calon-Ségur (third), Lafon-Rochet (fourth) and Cos Labory (fifth). The appellation is also unusually strong below the classed level.
