Phélan Ségur, Les Ormes de Pez, de Pez, Haut-Marbuzet and Meyney make some of the best value in the Médoc, and two 2025 Crus Bourgeois Exceptionnels (Le Crock and Lafitte Carcasset) are here.
fr-saint-estephe.terroir: More clay sits under the gravel than in Pauillac, and the soils are cooler and slower to drain, which preserves acidity and gives a slightly later harvest. The gravel croupes of Montrose and Cos face the estuary; the plateau around Saint-Estèphe village and Pez is heavier. Merlot often makes up 30 to 50% of blends.
fr-saint-estephe.nerd_note: The name Cos is thought to come from the Gascon *caux*, 'pebbly hill'; Montrose takes its name from the pink heather that covered its gravel mound before vines were planted in the early nineteenth century.

fr-saint-georges-saint-emilion.name: Saint-Georges-Saint-Émilion
fr-saint-georges-saint-emilion.summary: Saint-Georges is the smallest satellite, a single hill in the commune of Montagne whose growers can use either name. Its south-facing limestone slopes give some of the best satellite wines. The eighteenth-century Château Saint-Georges, attributed to Victor Louis, architect of Bordeaux's Grand Théâtre, dominates it.
fr-saint-georges-saint-emilion.terroir: A limestone hill facing south toward Saint-Émilion across the Barbanne.
fr-saint-georges-saint-emilion.nerd_note: Saint-Georges is part of the commune of Montagne, so it is an appellation without its own town hall, and its growers may choose to label their wine Montagne-Saint-Émilion instead.

fr-saint-joseph.name: Saint-Joseph
fr-saint-joseph.grapes: Syrah (up to 10% Marsanne and Roussanne); Marsanne and Roussanne for white
fr-saint-joseph.summary: Saint-Joseph is the long, thin appellation of the right bank, running about 60 km from Chavanay to Guilherand-Granges opposite Valence across 26 communes in the Ardèche and Loire. It began in 1956 around Tournon and Mauves, where the slopes facing Hermitage were known as the Côte de Saint-Joseph after a Jesuit vineyard, and was expanded in 1969 to include flat land; a 1992 revision moved much of it back to the slopes. With 1,504 ha (2025), its reds range from light and peppery to dense and age-worthy. The best come from the original heart around Mauves, Tournon and Saint-Jean-de-Muzols, and from growers such as Jean-Louis Chave, Gonon, Coursodon and Faury. White Saint-Joseph from Marsanne and Roussanne is rich and nutty.
fr-saint-joseph.terroir: Granite and gneiss terraces, with some loess and sandy soils in the north; the best sites face southeast over the Rhône.
fr-saint-joseph.nerd_note: Chave's Saint-Joseph Clos Florentin, a walled parcel replanted on the terraces above Mauves, is one of the appellation's flagship wines.

fr-saint-julien.name: Saint-Julien
fr-saint-julien.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot, Malbec, Carmenère
fr-saint-julien.summary:
Saint-Julien is the smallest of the big four Médoc communes and the most consistent. There is no first growth, but eleven classed growths farm most of its 900-odd hectares: the three Léovilles (Las Cases, Poyferré and Barton), Gruaud Larose and Ducru-Beaucaillou as seconds; Lagrange and Langoa Barton as thirds; Saint-Pierre, Talbot, Branaire-Ducru and Beychevelle as fourths. Almost all the land is in the hands of classified estates or of Gloria, the domain Henri Martin assembled from classed-growth parcels in the twentieth century.

The style sits between Pauillac's power and Margaux's perfume: dense, cedar-scented Cabernet with polished tannins and a recognisable balance. Léoville Las Cases, with its walled Grand Clos running up to Latour, is often called a 'super second' and priced close to the firsts. Ducru-Beaucaillou, whose name refers to its 'beautiful stones', sits on the gravel nearest the river.
fr-saint-julien.terroir: A compact block of deep gravel ridges facing the estuary, bordered by the Juillac stream to the north and the Jalle de Saint-Julien to the south. The riverside estates (Las Cases, Ducru, Beychevelle) are on the finest gravel; Gruaud Larose, Talbot and Lagrange lie on higher, more clay-rich gravel inland and give broader wines.
fr-saint-julien.nerd_note: Beychevelle's name is said to come from *baisse-voile*, 'lower the sail': ships passing on the Gironde lowered their sails in salute to the Duc d'Épernon, admiral of France, who owned the estate in the seventeenth century. The ship on the label remembers it.

fr-saint-mont.name: Saint-Mont
fr-saint-mont.grapes: Tannat, Pinenc (Fer Servadou), Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon; Gros Manseng, Petit Courbu, Arrufiac, Petit Manseng
fr-saint-mont.summary: Saint-Mont, in the Gers, is almost entirely the work of the Plaimont cooperative, founded in 1979 by André Dubosc, whose campaign to save local grapes and old vineyards earned it the AOC in 2011. In Sarragachies, Plaimont protects a pre-phylloxera vineyard of under a hectare with about 20 varieties, some found nowhere else; in 2012 it became the first vineyard in France listed as a Monument Historique. The reds are Tannat blends, less tannic than Madiran; the whites are fresh and floral.
fr-saint-mont.terroir: Clay-limestone, sandy and boulbènes soils on Gers hillsides.
fr-saint-mont.nerd_note: The Sarragachies vineyard is planted 'en foule', haphazardly, with vines layered (provignés) from older vines, a method used before rows were the norm.

fr-saint-nicolas-de-bourgueil.name: Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil
fr-saint-nicolas-de-bourgueil.grapes: Cabernet Franc, up to 10% Cabernet Sauvignon
fr-saint-nicolas-de-bourgueil.summary: Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil is a single commune west of Bourgueil with its own appellation. Its vines sit mostly on sand and gravel, giving lighter, more fragrant, earlier-drinking Cabernet Franc than Bourgueil, though the slopes at the north make serious wines. Yannick Amirault and Frédéric Mabileau are leading names.
fr-saint-nicolas-de-bourgueil.terroir: Mostly sand and gravel terraces; tuffeau slopes in the north.
fr-saint-nicolas-de-bourgueil.nerd_note: Because most of its vines grow on sand and gravel, Saint-Nicolas is often the first Loire red ready to drink, best served cool within a few years of release.

fr-saint-peray.name: Saint-Péray
fr-saint-peray.summary: Saint-Péray, at the southern end of the Northern Rhône opposite Valence, is a white-only appellation of 128 ha (2025) that was once famous for sparkling wine: in the nineteenth century its traditional-method Marsanne was compared with Champagne, and Wagner is said to have ordered it. Sparkling Saint-Péray is now rare, and growers concentrate on still whites from Marsanne and Roussanne with surprising freshness from the area's limestone. Domaine Alain Voge, Chapoutier, Bernard Gripa and Vincent Paris are among the producers.
fr-saint-peray.terroir: Granite in the west and a limestone outcrop around the ruined Château de Crussol, which gives Saint-Péray its distinctive freshness.
fr-saint-peray.nerd_note: Sparkling Saint-Péray dates to 1829, when the Faure family applied the Champagne method to Marsanne.

fr-saint-pourcain.name: Saint-Pourçain
fr-saint-pourcain.grapes: Gamay, Pinot Noir; Chardonnay, Tressallier, Sauvignon Blanc
fr-saint-pourcain.summary: Saint-Pourçain, on the Sioule and Allier rivers in the Allier department, claims to be one of the oldest vineyards in France. In the Middle Ages its wine was served at the court of Saint Louis and the papal court of Avignon. It became AOC in 2009. Whites must include the local Tressallier grape; reds blend Gamay and Pinot Noir.
fr-saint-pourcain.terroir: Limestone, sand and granite on terraces and slopes along the Sioule.
fr-saint-pourcain.nerd_note: Tressallier, Saint-Pourçain's own white grape, turns out to be Sacy, an old Yonne variety.

fr-saint-romain.name: Saint-Romain
fr-saint-romain.summary: Saint-Romain is the highest village of the Côte de Beaune, set among cliffs and woods 400 m up where the Auxey valley meets the Hautes-Côtes. Long considered too cool for great wine, it makes crisp, mineral whites and light reds that have gained from warmer summers. It has no premier crus. The village is also the home of the tonnellerie François Frères, one of Burgundy's most famous barrel makers, and of Domaine d'Auvenay, Lalou Bize-Leroy's private estate.
fr-saint-romain.terroir: Marl and limestone at 300 to 400 m below limestone cliffs; late ripening and cool nights.
fr-saint-romain.nerd_note: François Frères, founded in 1910 in Saint-Romain, supplies barrels to many of Burgundy's top domaines, including the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti.

fr-saint-sardos.name: Saint-Sardos
fr-saint-sardos.grapes: Syrah (at least 40%), Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Merlot
fr-saint-sardos.summary: A small appellation on the left bank of the Garonne west of Montauban, promoted to AOC in 2011 and dominated by the Saint-Sardos cooperative. Syrah is the main grape, blended with Tannat, giving dark, peppery reds and rosés that suit the region's cassoulet and confit.
fr-saint-sardos.nerd_note: One of the few Southwest appellations where Syrah is the main grape.

fr-saint-veran.name: Saint-Véran
fr-saint-veran.summary: Saint-Véran, created in 1971, wraps around Pouilly-Fuissé in two separate parts: Davayé and Prissé to the north, and Chânes, Chasselas, Leynes and Saint-Vérand to the south, on the border with the Beaujolais. It was created partly to give the white wines of Beaujolais villages a proper Burgundian name. The wines are fresh and fruity in the south on granite and clay, and more mineral in the north on limestone. They are some of the best-value whites in Burgundy.
fr-saint-veran.terroir: Limestone and marl in Davayé and Prissé; granite, sandy clay and limestone patches in the southern villages near the Beaujolais.
fr-saint-veran.nerd_note: Saint-Véran is spelled without the final d of the village of Saint-Vérand, a quirk of its 1971 creation.

fr-sainte-croix-du-mont.name: Sainte-Croix-du-Mont
fr-sainte-croix-du-mont.summary: Sainte-Croix-du-Mont is the best of the right-bank sweet appellations, a hilltop village facing Sauternes across the Garonne. Its steep south-facing slopes and limestone give wines with real botrytis character and the freshness to age 20 years, at a fraction of Sauternes prices. Château Loubens, La Rame and Crabitan-Bellevue lead.
fr-sainte-croix-du-mont.terroir: The hill is built on a bank of giant fossil oysters from the Miocene sea, visible in a cliff face below the church, over limestone and clay.
fr-sainte-croix-du-mont.nerd_note: The fossil oyster bank of Sainte-Croix-du-Mont is so thick that a cave carved into it serves as a tasting room.

fr-sainte-foy-bordeaux.name: Sainte-Foy-Bordeaux
fr-sainte-foy-bordeaux.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon, Muscadelle
fr-sainte-foy-bordeaux.summary: Sainte-Foy-Bordeaux sits at the eastern tip of the Gironde, next to Bergerac, around the Protestant bastide of Sainte-Foy-la-Grande. Reds, dry and sweet whites are made; since 2016 growers can also use Sainte-Foy Côtes de Bordeaux. The appellation is small and many growers farm organically.
fr-sainte-foy-bordeaux.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes along the Dordogne, similar to neighbouring Bergerac.
fr-sainte-foy-bordeaux.nerd_note: Sainte-Foy-la-Grande was a Huguenot stronghold, and its growers' links with Protestant merchants in Holland and England shaped the area's early export trade.

fr-sainte-foy-cotes-de-bordeaux.name: Sainte-Foy Côtes de Bordeaux
fr-sainte-foy-cotes-de-bordeaux.grapes: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc; Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon
fr-sainte-foy-cotes-de-bordeaux.summary: Sainte-Foy Côtes de Bordeaux is the newest member of the Côtes family, added in 2016, covering the same zone as Sainte-Foy-Bordeaux at the eastern edge of the Gironde. Growers can choose either name.
fr-sainte-foy-cotes-de-bordeaux.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes on the left bank of the Dordogne bordering Bergerac.
fr-sainte-foy-cotes-de-bordeaux.nerd_note: It is the only Côtes appellation on the left bank of the Dordogne.

fr-sancerre.name: Sancerre
fr-sancerre.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc; Pinot Noir for red and rosé
fr-sancerre.summary:
Sancerre is the world's reference for Sauvignon Blanc: a hilltop town above the Loire, surrounded by 14 communes of steep chalky hills that make a crisp, minerally white with notes of citrus, gooseberry, cut grass and flint. It became France's most popular bistro white in the 1960s and 1970s. About 80% of the production is white; the rest is Pinot Noir red and rosé, which has improved greatly since the 1990s.

Three soils define it. The *terres blanches*, Kimmeridgian marl with fossil oysters, as in Chablis, on the western hills (Chavignol, Bué, Verdigny), give the fullest, longest-lived wines. The *caillottes*, small stones of Oxfordian limestone, give aromatic, early-drinking wines. And *silex*, flint on clay near the town and the Loire, gives smoky, tight wines. The Monts Damnés above Chavignol (a slope so steep it was 'damned' to work) is the most famous lieu-dit. Producers such as Vacheron, Cotat, Alphonse Mellot, Gérard Boulay, Henri Bourgeois, Lucien Crochet and Edmond Vatan made Sancerre a wine of place. Chavignol is also the home of the Crottin de Chavignol goat cheese, Sancerre's classic partner.
fr-sancerre.terroir: Kimmeridgian marl (terres blanches), Oxfordian limestone (caillottes) and flint (silex), on steep hills rising to 400 m. A semi-continental climate, cooler and frostier than western Loire.
fr-sancerre.nerd_note: Sancerre was a Protestant stronghold that resisted a royal siege for eight months in 1572 and 1573; the town's inhabitants were reduced to eating leather and parchment.

fr-santenay.name: Santenay
fr-santenay.summary: Santenay is the last major village of the Côte de Beaune and makes mostly red wine: sturdy, dark-fruited and earthy, more structured than Volnay and less polished than Pommard. Premier crus such as Les Gravières, La Comme, Clos Rousseau and Clos de Tavannes lie on varied soils, and a few whites, such as the premier cru Clos des Mouches, are excellent. Santenay is also a spa town with hot springs and a casino, and its castle once belonged to Philip the Bold.
fr-santenay.terroir: Complex geology with faults; limestone and marl with gravel; the slope turns southwest toward the Maranges.
fr-santenay.nerd_note: The Château de Santenay, also called Château Philippe le Hardi, is famous for its roof of glazed tiles and its large vineyard estate.

fr-saumur.name: Saumur
fr-saumur.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc; Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pineau d'Aunis
fr-saumur.summary:
Saumur, on the tuffeau cliffs of the south bank of the Loire, makes red, white and especially sparkling wine. It is the Loire's sparkling-wine capital: Jean Ackerman founded the first house in 1811 after working in Champagne, and Bouvet-Ladubay, Gratien & Meyer, Langlois-Chateau and Veuve Amiot followed, ageing their bottles in kilometres of tuffeau galleries. Saumur Brut is mostly Chenin Blanc, often with Chardonnay and Cabernet Franc.

The still whites, pure Chenin, have become some of the Loire's best since Clos Rougeard, Domaine Guiberteau, Arnaud Lambert and Romain Guiberteau's Brézé hill showed what the tuffeau can do. Saumur Rouge is fresh Cabernet Franc. Saumur Puy-Notre-Dame, a named sub-zone in the south recognised in 2009, makes reds with stricter rules (Cabernet Franc with at most 15% Cabernet Sauvignon and lower yields).
fr-saumur.terroir: Turonian tuffeau chalk covered by clay, sand and flint. The tuffeau stores water and regulates temperature, and the slopes facing the Loire and the Thouet are the best sites.
fr-saumur.nerd_note: The hill of Brézé produced one of the most famous white wines of eighteenth-century France, said to be sold at the price of Montrachet; growers today are trying to reclaim that status.

fr-saumur-champigny.name: Saumur-Champigny
fr-saumur-champigny.grapes: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pineau d'Aunis
fr-saumur-champigny.summary: Saumur-Champigny is red-only, from nine communes east of Saumur, and in the 1980s it was the fashionable Paris bistro wine: juicy, fragrant Cabernet Franc with red fruit and violet, served lightly chilled. Its serious side came from the Foucault brothers of Clos Rougeard in Chacé, whose old-vine, barrel-aged Le Bourg and Les Poyeux became among the most sought-after wines of France. Domaine Filliatreau, Château du Hureau, Domaine des Roches Neuves (Thierry Germain) and Château de Villeneuve continue the line.
fr-saumur-champigny.terroir: Tuffeau chalk with clay and sand on top; the 'Champigny' name may come from Latin *campus igni*, 'field of fire', for its warm slopes.
fr-saumur-champigny.nerd_note: Clos Rougeard's Charly and Nady Foucault refused to use new technology for decades; after Charly's death in 2015 the estate was sold to Martin Bouygues in 2017.

fr-saussignac.name: Saussignac
fr-saussignac.grapes: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Muscadelle, Chenin Blanc
fr-saussignac.summary: Saussignac is a tiny sweet-wine appellation west of Monbazillac with some of the strictest rules in France: hand picking by tries, no chaptalisation, and high minimum must weight. Growers such as Château Les Miaudoux, Château Richard and Château Le Payral make intense, botrytised wines that rival Sauternes.
fr-saussignac.terroir: Clay-limestone slopes south of the Dordogne.
fr-saussignac.nerd_note: Rabelais mentions Saussignac in *Gargantua*, as one of the great sweet wines of his day.

fr-sauternes.name: Sauternes
fr-sauternes.grapes: Sémillon (about 80%), Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris, Muscadelle
fr-sauternes.summary:
Sauternes is the most famous sweet wine in the world, and its making is a gamble against the weather. The appellation covers four communes on the south side of the Ciron (Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac) plus Barsac, whose wines may be sold as either Barsac or Sauternes. In 2010 the zone had over 2,200 ha of vines and around 190 estates producing about 41,000 hl a year; both figures have since fallen as estates switched land to dry white or red.

Everything depends on noble rot. *Botrytis cinerea* thrives when the cold Ciron meets the warmer Garonne and autumn nights produce fog, followed by dry, sunny afternoons. The fungus perforates the skins of ripe Sémillon, water evaporates, and the berries shrivel into brown, sticky raisins whose juice can exceed 350 g/l of sugar. Rot does not arrive evenly, so pickers go through the vineyard several times, sometimes berry by berry, over six to ten weeks: these passes are the *tries successives*. The rules demand hand harvesting by successive tries, must of at least 221 g/l of sugar (15% potential alcohol), at least 12% actual alcohol and 45 g/l residual sugar, and a maximum yield of 25 hl/ha. In practice the best estates make far less: Yquem's often-quoted rule of thumb is one glass of wine per vine.

Fermentation in barrel is slow and stops naturally, or is stopped, around 13.5 to 14% alcohol with 100 to 150 g/l of sugar left. The wines then age 18 to 36 months in oak. Young Sauternes tastes of apricot, peach, pineapple, honey, saffron and botrytis's signature notes of orange marmalade and beeswax; with decades in bottle the colour turns amber and the flavours move to crème brûlée, dried fig, tea and spice. The high sugar and acidity let great vintages live a century.

The 1855 list classed Sauternes and Barsac separately from the Médoc: Yquem alone as Premier Cru Supérieur, then Premiers and Deuxièmes Crus (27 châteaux today). Sales have struggled for decades as diners moved away from sweet wine, and many estates now also make dry whites (Y, R de Rieussec, G de Guiraud, S de Suduiraut) and promote Sauternes young, chilled or with tonic as an aperitif.
fr-sauternes.terroir: Gravel and sand over clay in Sauternes and Bommes, with clay-limestone at Fargues and on the slopes around Yquem's hill, the highest point at about 75 m. The Ciron's cold water and the gallery forest along it are essential; so is the sunshine that follows the fog. Wet autumns bring grey rot instead, and some vintages (1992, 2012 at Yquem) yield no grand vin at all.
fr-sauternes.nerd_note: Botrytis produces the enzyme laccase and compounds such as sotolon (also found in fenugreek and vin jaune), which is why old Sauternes can smell of curry spice and walnuts.

fr-savennieres.name: Savennières
fr-savennieres.summary:
Savennières is a tiny appellation on the north bank of the Loire just west of Angers, and the most uncompromising dry Chenin Blanc on earth. Its south-facing slopes on volcanic rock and schist give wines of searing acidity and intense minerality, notes of quince, chamomile, beeswax and wet stone, and a reputation for being closed for years after release; the best need a decade or more and last half a century.

Three names share it: Savennières itself and two Grand Cru enclaves with their own appellations, La Roche aux Moines and La Coulée de Serrant. In the nineteenth century the sweet and dry wines of Savennières were among the most valuable in France. Today the style is mostly dry, sometimes demi-sec in warm years. Domaine des Baumard, Domaine du Closel (Évelyne de Pontbriand), Damien Laureau, Eric Morgat and Thibaud Boudignon are leading producers.
fr-savennieres.terroir: Steep south-facing slopes over violet schist, sandstone and volcanic rhyolite, with thin soil and little water. The river reflects heat and keeps frost away.
fr-savennieres.nerd_note: Chenin in Savennières often shows a slightly bitter, phenolic grip because growers tolerate some botrytis and skin contact; that grip is part of why the wines need time.

fr-savennieres-roche-aux-moines.name: Savennières Roche aux Moines
fr-savennieres-roche-aux-moines.summary: La Roche aux Moines, 'the monks' rock', is a set of south-facing slopes east of the Coulée de Serrant, once owned by the monks of Saint-Nicolas in Angers. In 1214 the French Prince Louis defeated King John of England here, in a battle that led to the loss of Anjou by the Plantagenets. The wines are powerful, dense dry Chenin; Domaine aux Moines (Tessa Laroche) and Pierre Soulez's Château de Chamboureau are the references. A 2011 decree gave it its own appellation status, with stricter yields.
fr-savennieres-roche-aux-moines.terroir: Schist and volcanic rock on steep slopes facing the river.
fr-savennieres-roche-aux-moines.nerd_note: The 1214 Battle of La Roche-aux-Moines was fought the same summer as Bouvines; together they ended England's hold on Anjou.

fr-savigny-les-beaune.name: Savigny-lès-Beaune
fr-savigny-les-beaune.summary: Savigny-lès-Beaune lies where the valley of the Rhoin opens onto the plain just north of Beaune, and it is one of the Côte de Beaune's largest red-wine villages. The valley creates two slopes: the north side, facing south and southeast, has premier crus such as Les Lavières, Aux Serpentières, Aux Guettes and Les Vergelesses next to Pernand, while the south side, facing northeast toward Beaune, includes Les Marconnets, Les Narbantons, Les Peuillets and La Dominode. The reds are fresh, light to medium-bodied and fragrant, with red berry fruit and a gentle tannic grip.
fr-savigny-les-beaune.terroir: Limestone and gravelly scree brought down by the Rhoin; sandier soils near the valley floor.
fr-savigny-les-beaune.nerd_note: The Château de Savigny-lès-Beaune houses a museum of motorcycles, racing cars and fighter jets in its grounds.

fr-seyssel.name: Seyssel
fr-seyssel.summary: Seyssel, on both banks of the Rhône at Seyssel (Ain and Haute-Savoie), was one of the first appellations of the Alps, recognised in 1942. It makes still Altesse whites and a traditional-method sparkling wine based on the local Molette grape with Altesse, a speciality made famous by the house of Varichon et Clerc.
fr-seyssel.terroir: Molasse, sand and glacial deposits on slopes above the Rhône gorge.
fr-seyssel.nerd_note: Seyssel's sparkling wine was a nineteenth-century speciality of the Savoie and still uses the rare Molette grape.

fr-tavel.name: Tavel
fr-tavel.grapes: Grenache (max 60%), Cinsault, Clairette, Syrah, Mourvèdre, Bourboulenc, Picpoul, Calitor, Carignan
fr-tavel.summary: Tavel is the only Rhône appellation and one of the few in France devoted entirely to rosé, made since the Middle Ages and loved by the popes of Avignon, Louis XIV and Ernest Hemingway. Its 781 ha (2025) in Tavel and Roquemaure make a deeply coloured, structured rosé, more like a light red, with red fruit, spice and a vinous texture, which pairs with food and even ages. It was among the first AOCs in 1936. Tavel has suffered as fashion turned to pale Provence rosé; some producers now make paler versions, and its area fell by about a fifth between 2020 and 2024.
fr-tavel.terroir: Three terroirs: galets roulés over red clay, sand and pebbles, and limestone slabs (lauzes) on the plateau.
fr-tavel.nerd_note: Tavel's colour comes from several days of maceration, longer than most rosés, which is why it has tannin and ages.

fr-terrasses-du-larzac.name: Terrasses du Larzac
fr-terrasses-du-larzac.summary: Terrasses du Larzac covers 32 communes on the foothills of the Larzac plateau north-west of Montpellier, around Aniane, Saint-Jean-de-Fos, Jonquières and Saint-Saturnin. Its great asset is the big difference between day and night temperatures (often 20°C), because cold air flows down from the plateau. The reds are fresh, dark and mineral. AOC since 2014, it is home to the Languedoc's most famous estates: Mas de Daumas Gassac, Grange des Pères and Mas Jullien, as well as Domaine de Montcalmès and Clos du Serres.
fr-terrasses-du-larzac.terroir: Very varied: limestone scree, red ruffe (iron-rich sandstone and clay, especially near the Lac du Salagou), schist, basalt and glacial deposits; altitudes up to 400 m.
producers: Domaine de la Grange des Pères
fr-terrasses-du-larzac.nerd_note: Mas de Daumas Gassac and Grange des Pères, the two most famous estates in the area, sell their wines as IGP, outside the appellation, because their grape blends do not fit the rules.

fr-touraine.name: Touraine
fr-touraine.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Orbois; Gamay, Côt, Cabernet Franc, Pineau d'Aunis, Grolleau
fr-touraine.summary: Touraine is the regional appellation of the Tours area, and its volume is mostly crisp, affordable Sauvignon Blanc from the Cher valley, plus Gamay, Côt (Malbec) and Cabernet Franc reds. It has five named sub-areas: Amboise and Mesland (Chenin, Gamay, Côt), Azay-le-Rideau (Chenin and Grolleau rosé), Chenonceaux (Sauvignon and Côt-based reds, created 2011) and Oisly (Sauvignon Blanc, created 2011). The Cher valley, with its flint and clay soils, is also home to natural wine pioneers such as Thierry Puzelat and Noëlla Morantin.
fr-touraine.terroir: Clay-flint, sandy clay and tuffeau around the Cher and the Loire.
fr-touraine.nerd_note: Henry Marionnet grows ungrafted vines of Romorantin dating from before phylloxera, as well as ungrafted Gamay planted in 1992 to see how wines tasted before grafting.

fr-touraine-amboise.name: Touraine Amboise
fr-touraine-amboise.grapes: Chenin Blanc, Côt, Cabernet Franc, Gamay
fr-touraine-amboise.summary: Touraine-Amboise surrounds the royal château of Amboise on both banks of the Loire, giving Chenin Blanc whites (dry to sweet), Côt-based reds and rosés. Leonardo da Vinci spent his last years at the nearby Clos Lucé.
fr-touraine-amboise.terroir: Tuffeau limestone and clay-flint (perruches) on slopes above the Loire.
fr-touraine-amboise.nerd_note: Touraine allows a handful of villages or areas to add their name to the regional appellation for their own styles.

fr-touraine-azay-le-rideau.name: Touraine Azay-le-Rideau
fr-touraine-azay-le-rideau.summary: Touraine Azay-le-Rideau, around the Renaissance château on the Indre, gives dry and off-dry Chenin Blanc and rosé based on Grolleau.
fr-touraine-azay-le-rideau.terroir: Tuffeau, clay-limestone and sand above the Indre.
fr-touraine-azay-le-rideau.nerd_note: Touraine allows a handful of villages or areas to add their name to the regional appellation for their own styles.

fr-touraine-chenonceaux.name: Touraine Chenonceaux
fr-touraine-chenonceaux.summary: Touraine Chenonceaux (2011) follows the Cher valley around the famous château spanning the river, giving Sauvignon Blanc whites and Côt and Cabernet Franc reds, both with stricter rules than plain Touraine.
fr-touraine-chenonceaux.terroir: Clay-flint and limestone on the Cher slopes.
fr-touraine-chenonceaux.nerd_note: Touraine allows a handful of villages or areas to add their name to the regional appellation for their own styles.

fr-touraine-mesland.name: Touraine Mesland
fr-touraine-mesland.grapes: Gamay, Côt, Cabernet Franc, Chenin Blanc
fr-touraine-mesland.summary: Touraine-Mesland lies on the north bank of the Loire between Amboise and Blois, giving Gamay-based reds and rosés, plus Chenin whites.
fr-touraine-mesland.terroir: Clay-flint and sandy soils on the plateau edge.
fr-touraine-mesland.nerd_note: Touraine allows a handful of villages or areas to add their name to the regional appellation for their own styles.

fr-touraine-noble-joue.name: Touraine Noble Joué
fr-touraine-noble-joue.grapes: Pinot Meunier, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir
fr-touraine-noble-joue.summary: A rare vin gris (very pale rosé) from five communes south of Tours, from Pinot Meunier, Pinot Gris and Pinot Noir. Popular at the court of Louis XI in the fifteenth century, it nearly vanished in the twentieth century as Tours expanded and was revived by a few growers and recognised in 2001.
fr-touraine-noble-joue.terroir: Clay-flint and sand south of Tours.
fr-touraine-noble-joue.nerd_note: Its mix of Meunier, Pinot Gris and Pinot Noir echoes the grapes of Champagne, but it is made as a still, very pale vin gris.

fr-touraine-oisly.name: Touraine Oisly
fr-touraine-oisly.summary: Touraine Oisly (2011) is a white-only name for Sauvignon Blanc from sandy clay soils on the edge of the Sologne, long promoted by the Oisly-Thésée cooperative.
fr-touraine-oisly.terroir: Sand and clay over flint, cooler than the Cher valley.
fr-touraine-oisly.nerd_note: Touraine allows a handful of villages or areas to add their name to the regional appellation for their own styles.

fr-tursan.name: Tursan
fr-tursan.grapes: Baroque, Gros Manseng, Sauvignon Blanc; Tannat, Cabernet Franc
fr-tursan.summary: Tursan, in the Landes south of the Adour, is the home of Baroque, a white grape found almost nowhere else, giving round, nutty wines. The chef Michel Guérard of Eugénie-les-Bains revived the appellation's image with his Château de Bachen.
fr-tursan.nerd_note: Baroque's high natural sugar made it popular in Armagnac before phylloxera; Tursan is now almost its last refuge.

fr-vacqueyras.name: Vacqueyras
fr-vacqueyras.grapes: Grenache with Syrah and/or Mourvèdre; whites from Clairette, Grenache Blanc, Bourboulenc, Roussanne
fr-vacqueyras.summary: Vacqueyras, between Gigondas and Beaumes-de-Venise, became a cru in 1990. Its 1,421 ha (2025) spread over Vacqueyras and Sarrians on flatter terraces below the Dentelles, and its reds are generous, spicy and dark, slightly softer than Gigondas and good value. A little white and rosé is made. The twelfth-century troubadour Raimbaut de Vaqueiras was born here.
fr-vacqueyras.terroir: Pebbly terraces with red clay (like Châteauneuf) and sandy-limestone soils toward the Dentelles.
fr-vacqueyras.nerd_note: Vacqueyras is the only Rhône cru whose name is also that of a medieval troubadour; the Le Sang des Cailloux domaine names its cuvées after local saints and family members.

fr-valencay.name: Valençay
fr-valencay.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Orbois; Gamay, Pinot Noir, Côt, Cabernet Franc
fr-valencay.summary: Valençay, south of Cheverny near the château Talleyrand owned, makes fresh Sauvignon whites and light blended reds. It is also the name of a pyramid-shaped goat cheese coated in ash, whose flat top is said to have been cut off at Talleyrand's table to avoid reminding Napoleon of Egypt.
fr-valencay.nerd_note: Talleyrand, who owned Château de Valençay, used it to host diplomatic feasts prepared by the chef Antonin Carême.

fr-ventoux.name: Ventoux
fr-ventoux.grapes: Grenache, Syrah, Cinsault, Mourvèdre, Carignan; whites from Clairette, Bourboulenc, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne
fr-ventoux.summary: Ventoux (Côtes du Ventoux until 2009) spreads across the foothills of Mont Ventoux, the 1,910 m giant of Provence, from Vaison-la-Romaine to Apt. Its 4,987 ha (2025) make fresh, fruity reds and rosés with a cooler character than the Rhône plain, thanks to altitude and cold air from the mountain. Château Pesquié, Domaine de Fondrèche and Perrin's La Vieille Ferme are well-known names.
fr-ventoux.terroir: Limestone, sandy and clay foothills at 200 to 500 m; big day-night temperature swings.
fr-ventoux.nerd_note: Ventoux lost about 12 percent of its area between 2020 and 2025.

fr-vezelay.name: Vézelay
fr-vezelay.summary: Vézelay is Burgundy's newest village appellation, promoted from Bourgogne Vézelay to its own AOC in 2017. Its Chardonnay vineyards climb the hills around the hilltop basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine, a UNESCO World Heritage site and the starting point of a pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela. The wines are light, floral and racy, closer to Chablis than to the Côte d'Or, and the vineyard was largely replanted from the 1970s after a century of abandonment.
fr-vezelay.terroir: Limestone and marl slopes at 200 to 300 m in the Cure valley; cool, late-ripening sites.
fr-vezelay.nerd_note: Vézelay grows on four communes: Vézelay, Saint-Père, Asquins and Tharoiseau.

fr-vin-de-corse.name: Vin de Corse
fr-vin-de-corse.grapes: Nielluccio, Sciaccarellu, Grenache, Carcajolu Neru, Minustellu, Aleatico; Vermentinu, Biancu Gentile, Codivarta, Genovese
fr-vin-de-corse.summary: Vin de Corse, now often labelled simply Corse, is the island's regional AOP, and it has five named sub-areas. Calvi, in the north-west Balagne, makes elegant wines on granite (Clos Culombu, Domaine d'Alzipratu). Coteaux du Cap Corse, on the schist of the northern peninsula, makes mineral Vermentinu (Clos Nicrosi). Figari, the southernmost and windiest, uses granite and gives intense wines (Clos Canarelli, which revived the old Carcajolu Neru and Biancu Gentile grapes). Porto-Vecchio, on the south-east coast, has granitic soils and cooling sea breezes (Domaine de Torraccia). Sartène, in the south-west, is a land of granite and old family estates. Rosé is the largest category, and many estates make serious reds from Nielluccio and Sciaccarellu.
fr-vin-de-corse.terroir: Granite in the west and south, schist in Cap Corse, alluvial plain in the east; altitude and sea breezes.
fr-vin-de-corse.nerd_note: Clos Canarelli in Figari replanted Carcajolu Neru, a nearly forgotten Corsican grape that DNA work has matched to Parraleta, a variety of Aragon in Spain.

fr-vin-de-corse-calvi.name: Vin de Corse Calvi
fr-vin-de-corse-calvi.summary: Calvi, in the Balagne of north-west Corsica, gives reds, rosés and whites from Niellucciu, Sciaccarellu and Vermentinu on granite; Clos Culombu and Domaine Alzipratu are leading estates.
fr-vin-de-corse-calvi.nerd_note: Vin de Corse allows five areas to add their names.

fr-vin-de-corse-coteaux-du-cap-corse.name: Vin de Corse Coteaux du Cap Corse
fr-vin-de-corse-coteaux-du-cap-corse.summary: Coteaux du Cap Corse covers the schist slopes of Corsica's northern peninsula, best known for its Vermentinu whites; the same area also produces Muscat du Cap Corse.
fr-vin-de-corse-coteaux-du-cap-corse.nerd_note: Vin de Corse allows five areas to add their names.

fr-vin-de-corse-figari.name: Vin de Corse Figari
fr-vin-de-corse-figari.summary: Figari, in the far south of Corsica, is the island's windiest wine area; Clos Canarelli made it famous with wines from rare local grapes such as Carcajolu Neru.
fr-vin-de-corse-figari.nerd_note: Vin de Corse allows five areas to add their names.

fr-vin-de-corse-porto-vecchio.name: Vin de Corse Porto-Vecchio
fr-vin-de-corse-porto-vecchio.summary: Porto-Vecchio, on the south-east coast, gives fresh rosés and whites and supple reds on granite; Domaine de Torraccia was a pioneer of quality here. The granite massif of the Ospedale rises behind the vineyards and shelters them from western weather.
fr-vin-de-corse-porto-vecchio.nerd_note: Vin de Corse allows five areas to add their names.

fr-vin-de-corse-sartene.name: Vin de Corse Sartène
fr-vin-de-corse-sartene.summary: Sartène, in the south-west of Corsica, follows the valleys of the Rizzanese and Ortolo rivers and is a stronghold of Sciaccarellu, the island's fragrant, peppery red grape. Domaine Saparale and Domaine Fiumicicoli are key estates.
fr-vin-de-corse-sartene.terroir: Granite and its sandy weathering on terraces near the sea.
fr-vin-de-corse-sartene.nerd_note: Vin de Corse allows five areas to add their names.

fr-vin-de-savoie.name: Vin de Savoie
fr-vin-de-savoie.grapes: Jacquère, Altesse, Roussanne (Bergeron), Chasselas, Gringet, Chardonnay; Mondeuse, Gamay, Pinot Noir, Persan
fr-vin-de-savoie.summary: Vin de Savoie (or Savoie) covers the whole Savoie vineyard across 56 communes and makes mostly crisp, light whites from Jacquère, plus reds from Mondeuse, Gamay and Pinot Noir. Recognised in 1957 and confirmed as an AOC in 1973, it may add one of 16 cru names: Abymes, Apremont, Arbin, Ayze, Chautagne, Chignin, Chignin-Bergeron, Cruet, Crépy, Jongieux, Marignan, Marin, Montmélian, Ripaille, Saint-Jean-de-la-Porte and Saint-Jeoire-Prieuré. Since 2015 its traditional-method sparkling wines may be labelled Crémant de Savoie, with at least 40 percent Jacquère and Altesse.
fr-vin-de-savoie.terroir: Glacial moraines, limestone scree and molasse on south and southeast-facing Alpine slopes at 250 to 500 m.
fr-vin-de-savoie.nerd_note: Mondeuse from Arbin was so valued in the nineteenth century that it was shipped to Paris and Lyon as a rival to Burgundy.

fr-vin-de-savoie-abymes.name: Vin de Savoie Abymes
fr-vin-de-savoie-abymes.summary: Les Abymes (the abysses) is the chaotic field of limestone boulders left by the collapse of Mont Granier in November 1248, now planted with Jacquère that gives light, flinty whites. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-apremont.name: Vin de Savoie Apremont
fr-vin-de-savoie-apremont.summary: Apremont lies on the same Mont Granier landslide as Les Abymes, at Apremont and neighbouring communes; its Jacquère whites are crisp, floral and mineral, the best-known wine of Savoie. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-arbin.name: Vin de Savoie Arbin
fr-vin-de-savoie-arbin.summary: Arbin, on the steep slopes of the Combe de Savoie near Montmélian, is the home of Mondeuse, whose red here is dark, peppery and able to age. Louis Magnin made it famous. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-ayze.name: Vin de Savoie Ayze
fr-vin-de-savoie-ayze.summary: Ayze in the Arve valley of Haute-Savoie makes still and sparkling wine from Gringet, a grape found only here; Domaine Belluard rescued it. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-chautagne.name: Vin de Savoie Chautagne
fr-vin-de-savoie-chautagne.summary: Chautagne, on the slopes north of the Lac du Bourget, is known for light reds from Gamay, Pinot Noir and Mondeuse. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-chignin.name: Vin de Savoie Chignin
fr-vin-de-savoie-chignin.summary: Chignin, below the ruined towers of Chignin southeast of Chambéry, makes Jacquère whites and Mondeuse reds on limestone scree. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-chignin-bergeron.name: Vin de Savoie Chignin-Bergeron
fr-vin-de-savoie-chignin-bergeron.summary: Chignin-Bergeron is Savoie's richest white, made from Roussanne (locally Bergeron) on the warm, stony slopes of Chignin, Francin and Montmélian; apricot and honey with Alpine freshness. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-crepy.name: Vin de Savoie Crépy
fr-vin-de-savoie-crepy.summary: Crépy, near Lake Geneva at Ballaison, makes Chasselas whites, light and often slightly sparkling; it was a separate AOC (1948) before becoming a Vin de Savoie cru. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-cruet.name: Vin de Savoie Cruet
fr-vin-de-savoie-cruet.summary: Cruet, in the Combe de Savoie, makes fresh Jacquère and Mondeuse from south-facing scree slopes. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-jongieux.name: Vin de Savoie Jongieux
fr-vin-de-savoie-jongieux.summary: Jongieux, on the steep slopes above the Rhône west of the Lac du Bourget, makes whites and reds; the Marestel Roussette cru is in the same village. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-marignan.name: Vin de Savoie Marignan
fr-vin-de-savoie-marignan.summary: Marignan, on the shores of Lake Geneva at Sciez, makes light Chasselas whites. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-marin.name: Vin de Savoie Marin
fr-vin-de-savoie-marin.summary: Marin, near Thonon-les-Bains on Lake Geneva, makes Chasselas whites from glacial soils. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-montmelian.name: Vin de Savoie Montmélian
fr-vin-de-savoie-montmelian.summary: Montmélian, below the site of a great Savoyard fortress demolished by Louis XIV, makes Jacquère and Mondeuse. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-ripaille.name: Vin de Savoie Ripaille
fr-vin-de-savoie-ripaille.summary: Ripaille is the vineyard of the Château de Ripaille near Thonon-les-Bains on Lake Geneva, a single-estate cru of Chasselas. Its château belonged to Amadeus VIII of Savoy, who became antipope Felix V. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-saint-jean-de-la-porte.name: Vin de Savoie Saint-Jean-de-la-Porte
fr-vin-de-savoie-saint-jean-de-la-porte.summary: Saint-Jean-de-la-Porte, in the Combe de Savoie, is a cru for Mondeuse reds. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vin-de-savoie-saint-jeoire-prieure.name: Vin de Savoie Saint-Jeoire-Prieuré
fr-vin-de-savoie-saint-jeoire-prieure.summary: Saint-Jeoire-Prieuré, on the slopes southeast of Chambéry toward the Combe de Savoie, makes crisp Jacquère whites on limestone scree around an old Benedictine priory. It is one of the 16 crus (dénominations géographiques complémentaires) of the Vin de Savoie AOC.

fr-vinsobres.name: Vinsobres
fr-vinsobres.summary: Vinsobres, in the Drôme near Nyons, became the first cru of the Drôme provençale in 2006. Its 559 ha (2025) lie at 200 to 500 m among olive groves, and its reds, mostly Grenache with plenty of Syrah, are fresher and more structured than those of lower crus. The name is often traced to Vinum Sobrium, and a seventeenth-century bishop of Vaison is said to have advised drinking it soberly.
fr-vinsobres.terroir: Limestone, marl and pebble terraces on hillsides at altitude, with cooler nights.
fr-vinsobres.nerd_note: Vinsobres was the first cru of the Drôme department's southern Rhône vineyards.

fr-vire-clesse.name: Viré-Clessé
fr-vire-clesse.summary: Viré-Clessé, created in 1999 from two former Mâcon village appellations, covers Viré, Clessé, Laizé and Montbellet in the northern Mâconnais. Its whites are rich and ripe, sometimes with a touch of residual sugar from botrytis-affected grapes, a style championed by Jean Thévenet of Domaine de la Bongran, whose late-harvested wines were initially refused the appellation. The rules were later changed to allow them.
fr-vire-clesse.terroir: Limestone and clay with white marl, on gentle slopes at 200 to 300 m.
fr-vire-clesse.nerd_note: The rules now provide for late-harvested wines with residual sugar, which may carry the traditional local mention levroutée.

fr-volnay.name: Volnay
fr-volnay.summary:
Volnay is the most delicate and perfumed red wine of the Côte de Beaune, often called the Chambolle-Musigny of the south. Its vineyards climb to a village perched high on the slope, and more than half the appellation is premier cru. The reds are bright, silky and floral, with red cherry and violet and fine tannin, yet the best age for decades.

The great premier crus include Les Caillerets, Clos des Chênes, Taillepieds, Champans and Les Santenots (which lie in Meursault but are sold as Volnay when red). Several walled clos are monopoles of historic domaines: Marquis d'Angerville's Clos des Ducs, which belonged to the dukes of Burgundy, and Domaine de la Pousse d'Or's Clos de la Bousse d'Or. The Marquis d'Angerville was a pioneer of estate bottling in the 1920s and fought fraud with Henri Gouges, and Volnay's reputation owes much to that independence.
fr-volnay.terroir: Thin soils on hard limestone with less clay than Pommard; the higher slope has whiter, stonier soil, and the slope turns southeast.
fr-volnay.nerd_note: Red wines from the Santenots climats in Meursault are sold as Volnay premier cru Santenots, while white wines from the same plots are sold as Meursault.

fr-vosne-romanee.name: Vosne-Romanée
fr-vosne-romanee.summary:
Vosne-Romanée is the most famous wine village in the world. Its grand crus (Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Richebourg, La Romanée, Romanée-Saint-Vivant and La Grande Rue) together cover only about 27 ha, yet they make the most expensive red wines anywhere. Next door, Échezeaux and Grands-Échezeaux in the commune of Flagey-Échezeaux are worked largely by Vosne growers, and Flagey's village and premier cru land is sold as Vosne-Romanée.

The style is rich and exotic: dark cherry, spice, rose and orange peel over silky, velvety tannins, with a density that sets it apart from Chambolle's lightness and Nuits's firmness. The premier crus are worth their own pilgrimage: Cros Parantoux, made famous by Henri Jayer; Aux Malconsorts, which touches La Tâche; Les Suchots and Aux Brûlées, close to Richebourg and Romanée-Saint-Vivant; Les Beaux Monts high on the slope. The village is home to Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, Domaine Leroy, Méo-Camuzet, Grivot, Cathiard, Liger-Belair, Arnoux-Lachaux and the Gros family.
fr-vosne-romanee.terroir: Brown limestone soils with clay over Bathonian and Bajocian rock; the grand crus sit on a smooth, gently sloping band at 260 to 300 m facing east.
fr-vosne-romanee.nerd_note: Dr Morelot wrote in 1831 that there were no common wines in Vosne, a line still quoted by every grower in the village.

fr-vougeot.name: Vougeot
fr-vougeot.summary: Vougeot is Burgundy's smallest village appellation once you take away its grand cru: the 50 ha Clos de Vougeot fills most of the commune's vineyard, leaving only about 16 ha for village and premier cru wine. The premier crus Les Petits Vougeots, Les Cras, Clos de la Perrière and Le Clos Blanc lie just above and north of the Clos, against Chambolle-Musigny. Le Clos Blanc de Vougeot, a Chardonnay vineyard planted by the Cistercians in 1110 and now a monopole of Domaine de la Vougeraie, is one of the Côte de Nuits' rare great whites.
fr-vougeot.terroir: Limestone slopes north of the Clos with the brown soils of the Combe d'Orveau fan.
fr-vougeot.nerd_note: The village premier crus are among the least known in Burgundy because almost all attention goes to the Clos.

fr-vouvray.name: Vouvray
fr-vouvray.grapes: Chenin Blanc (a little Orbois/Menu Pineau tolerated)
fr-vouvray.summary:
Vouvray is Chenin Blanc's spiritual home, on the tuffeau cliffs on the north bank of the Loire just east of Tours. Its range is unmatched: sparkling (mousseux and pétillant, more than half the production), dry (sec), off-dry (tendre, demi-sec), and in hot, botrytis-rich years sweet (moelleux, liquoreux). The style is chosen each year based on the vintage, which makes Vouvray hard to market and endlessly fascinating.

The great Vouvrays age for a century: honey, quince, chamomile, and a mineral, chalky backbone held together by Chenin's acidity. The plateau above the cliffs is covered in clay and flint (*perruches*) and clay-limestone (*aubuis*). Domaine Huet, with its Le Haut-Lieu, Clos du Bourg and Le Mont vineyards, is the reference; Gaston Huet, mayor of Vouvray and former prisoner of war, ran it from 1947 and converted to biodynamics with his son-in-law Noël Pinguet in the 1990s. Philippe Foreau's Clos Naudin, Domaine des Aubuisières, Vincent Carême and François Pinon are other leaders. The cellars in the tuffeau cliffs along the river road hold bottles from the nineteenth century.
fr-vouvray.terroir: Tuffeau cliffs and slopes, with clay-flint (perruches) and clay-limestone (aubuis) on the plateau; the best sites are on the edges of the plateau above the Loire and the small Brenne and Cisse valleys.
producers: Domaine de la Taille aux Loups
fr-vouvray.nerd_note: Huet's Le Haut-Lieu was the first vineyard bought by Victor Huet in 1928, and Gaston Huet's 1947 moelleux is one of the legendary sweet wines of France.

sites.name: Château Lafite Rothschild
sites.text: Listed first among the first growths in 1855, Lafite sits on the northern edge of Pauillac, its vines running down to the Jalle du Breuil stream that separates it from Cos d'Estournel in Saint-Estèphe. The Marquis Nicolas-Alexandre de Ségur made it famous in the eighteenth century; Baron James de Rothschild bought it in 1868 and died three months later, and his descendants still own it. The style is the most perfumed of the Pauillac firsts: cedar, graphite and violets over a fine-grained frame. Its second wine is Carruades de Lafite.

sites.name: Château Latour
sites.text: Latour takes its name from a fourteenth-century fort that guarded the estuary; the domed tower in the vines is a later dovecote. The heart of the estate is the 47-ha Enclos around the château, deep gravel sloping to the riverside meadows that blunt frost and cool hot nights. Latour is the most powerful and slowest-maturing of the first growths, famous for consistency in poor vintages. François Pinault's Artémis group has owned it since 1993, and in 2012 Latour left the en primeur system to release wines only when it judges them ready.

sites.name: Château Margaux
sites.text: The only first growth in the Margaux appellation, and the only one whose château is a true neoclassical palace: Louis Combes built it between 1810 and 1816, columns and all. The Mentzelopoulos family bought the estate in 1977 and, with director Paul Pontallier, restored its reputation after a weak spell. The wine is the archetype of Margaux perfume, violets and red fruit over silky tannins. Its Pavillon Blanc, pure Sauvignon Blanc, is sold as Bordeaux because the appellation is red-only. Norman Foster designed the new cellars, opened in 2015.

sites.name: Château Haut-Brion
sites.class: Premier Cru Classé (1855); Cru Classé de Graves (red, and white from 1960)
sites.text: The only red outside the Médoc ranked in 1855, and arguably the first estate wine sold by name: Arnaud III de Pontac shipped 'Ho Bryan' to London, where Samuel Pepys drank it in 1663. The vineyard sits on a deep gravel ridge in Pessac, now surrounded by the city. American banker Clarence Dillon bought it in 1935; his descendant Prince Robert of Luxembourg runs it. The red is smoky and tobacco-scented; the white, rare and expensive, ages for decades.

sites.name: Château Mouton Rothschild
sites.class: Premier Cru Classé (1973; Deuxième Cru in 1855)
sites.text: The only estate ever promoted in the 1855 classification. Ranked first among the seconds in 1855, two years after Baron Nathaniel de Rothschild bought it, Mouton was raised to first growth in 1973 after half a century of lobbying by Baron Philippe de Rothschild, who also pioneered château bottling in 1924. Its motto changed from 'Premier ne puis, second ne daigne, Mouton suis' to 'Premier je suis, second je fus, Mouton ne change'. Every vintage since 1945 carries a label by an artist, from Braque and Picasso to Bacon and Warhol.

sites.name: Château Rauzan-Ségla
sites.text: Pierre de Rauzan created this estate in 1661, and it was split in the eighteenth century into Rauzan-Ségla and Rauzan-Gassies. In 1855 Rauzan-Ségla headed the second growths, just behind Mouton. After a long slump, the Wertheimer family (owners of Chanel) bought it in 1994 and invested heavily in drainage and replanting; it is now one of the finest Margaux, perfumed and silky with real depth.

sites.name: Château Rauzan-Gassies
sites.text: The other half of Pierre de Rauzan's seventeenth-century estate, owned by the Quié family since 1946. Its parcels interlock with Rauzan-Ségla on the gravel around Margaux village. The wine has improved markedly since the 2000s, with more precision and freshness than its old reputation suggests.

sites.name: Château Léoville Las Cases
sites.text: The largest share of the old Léoville estate, which was divided after the Revolution into Las Cases, Poyferré and Barton. Its walled Grand Clos, entered through a stone gateway with a lion on top (the label's emblem), runs right up to Latour's vineyards. Under the Delon family, especially Michel Delon from the 1970s, it became the archetypal 'super second', with Pauillac-like density and prices to match. Clos du Marquis is a separate wine, not a second wine.

sites.name: Château Léoville Poyferré
sites.text: Named after Baron Jean-Marie de Poyferré, who inherited this third of the Léoville estate in the early nineteenth century. The Cuvelier family has owned it since 1920; Didier Cuvelier's modernisation from 1979 made it one of Saint-Julien's richest, most plush wines. Its château faces Las Cases across the road in the village of Saint-Julien.

sites.name: Château Léoville Barton
sites.text: Hugh Barton, of an Irish family of Bordeaux merchants, bought a third of the Léoville vineyard in 1826, five years after buying Langoa. There is no Léoville Barton château: the wine is made in the cellars of Langoa. Anthony Barton, who ran both estates from 1983 until his death in 2022, kept prices fair through the boom years, and his daughter Lilian Barton Sartorius continues the line. The wine is classic, firm, cedary Saint-Julien that rewards patience.

sites.name: Château Durfort-Vivens
sites.text: Named after the Durfort de Duras family, who owned it from the fourteenth century. The Lurton family took it over in 1961, and Gonzague Lurton converted it to biodynamics in the 2010s; it now experiments with amphorae and bottlings of single Cabernet parcels. The wine is one of the more Cabernet-driven, mineral Margaux.

sites.name: Château Gruaud Larose
sites.text: Founded in the 1720s by the abbé Gruaud and later passed to his heir, Monsieur de La Rose, it is one of the largest estates in Saint-Julien, set inland on a broad gravel plateau. The Merlaut family has owned it since 1997. Gruaud makes dense, long-lived wine, a little more rustic and broad-shouldered than the riverside Saint-Juliens.

sites.name: Château Lascombes
sites.text: Named after Antoine de Lascombes, a seventeenth-century owner. The American writer and merchant Alexis Lichine bought it in 1952 and expanded it to over 100 ha, making it one of the largest Margaux estates. A large share of Merlot on clay-rich parcels gives it a riper, rounder style than most Margaux.

sites.name: Château Brane-Cantenac
sites.text: Baron Hector de Brane, nicknamed the 'Napoleon of the vines', sold Brane-Mouton (now Mouton Rothschild) in 1830 to concentrate on his estate in Cantenac. The Lurton family has owned it since 1925, and Henri Lurton has run it since 1992. Its central gravel plateau gives one of the most fragrant and refined Margaux.

sites.name: Château Pichon Baron
sites.text: In 1850 the Pichon-Longueville estate was divided between Baron Raoul de Pichon-Longueville and his sisters; the baron kept this half and built the turreted fairytale château in 1851. AXA Millésimes bought it in 1987 and, under Christian Seely, restored its reputation. The wine is dense, structured Pauillac, the vineyard facing Latour across the D2 road.

sites.name: Château Pichon Longueville Comtesse de Lalande
sites.text: The sisters' share of the 1850 Pichon division, named after Virginie, Comtesse de Lalande. May-Eliane de Lencquesaing ran it from 1978 to 2007, when she sold it to Champagne Louis Roederer. Some of its vines lie across the border in Saint-Julien, and a relatively high share of Merlot gives a famously silky, perfumed style for Pauillac.

sites.name: Château Ducru-Beaucaillou
sites.text: The name means Ducru (a nineteenth-century owner) plus 'beaux cailloux', beautiful stones, for the large gravel that covers its riverside vineyard. The Borie family has owned it since 1941; Bruno Borie runs it. The château, with its Victorian towers, faces the Gironde, and the wine is the most refined and polished of the Saint-Julien seconds.

sites.name: Château Cos d'Estournel
sites.text: Louis-Gaspard d'Estournel, who traded horses and wine with India, built the extraordinary chai with pagoda towers and a carved door from Zanzibar in the 1830s. Nicknamed the 'Maharajah of Saint-Estèphe', he died in debt. Cos faces Lafite across the Jalle du Breuil, on a gravel ridge facing south-east. Owned by Michel Reybier since 2000, it makes rich, exotic, spicy Saint-Estèphe from gravity-fed cellars rebuilt in 2008.

sites.name: Château Montrose
sites.text: Montrose did not exist as a vineyard until the early nineteenth century, when Étienne Théodore Dumoulin cleared a heath of pink heather on a gravel mound above the estuary. Fifty years later it was a second growth. The estuary breeze and gravel over clay give one of the most powerful, long-lived wines of the Médoc. Martin and Olivier Bouygues bought it in 2006 and rebuilt it with a strong environmental focus, including solar panels and geothermal energy.

sites.name: Château Kirwan
sites.text: Named after Mark Kirwan, an Irishman from Galway who married into the estate in the eighteenth century. The Schÿler family, Bordeaux négociants of German origin, have owned it since 1925, and their botanical gardens around the château are listed. Kirwan was named first of the third growths in 1855; its Cantenac vineyard gives supple, aromatic wine.

sites.name: Château d'Issan
sites.text: A moated seventeenth-century château built on the foundations of the medieval Château de la Mothe-Cantenac, beside the estuary meadows. Its motto, 'Regum mensis arisque deorum' (for the tables of kings and the altars of the gods), appears on the gate. The Cruse family has owned it since 1945 and was joined by Jacques Thienpont in 2013. The wine is classic, elegant Margaux.

sites.name: Château Lagrange
sites.text: The largest estate in Saint-Julien, inland on two gravel hills behind Gruaud Larose, with an Italianate tower. Japan's Suntory bought it in 1983, the first Japanese investment in a classed growth, and replanted most of the vineyard. It makes firm, good-value Saint-Julien and a white wine, Les Arums de Lagrange, sold as Bordeaux.

sites.name: Château Langoa Barton
sites.text: Bought by Hugh Barton in 1821, Langoa is the oldest classed growth to have remained with the same family, now the seventh and eighth Barton generations. Its eighteenth-century chartreuse houses the family and the cellars for both Langoa and Léoville Barton. The wine is a slightly softer, earlier-drinking cousin of Léoville.

sites.name: Château Giscours
sites.text: A large estate in Labarde with a grand Second Empire château and a park landscaped by Eugène Bühler. The Dutch Albada Jelgersma family has owned it since 1995 and also owns du Tertre. Giscours made famous wines in the 1970s, then slipped; it has steadily regained form with generous, dark-fruited Margaux.

sites.name: Château Malescot Saint-Exupéry
sites.text: Simon Malescot, counsellor to King Louis XIV, bought the estate in 1697; Count Jean-Baptiste de Saint-Exupéry, an ancestor of the author of *The Little Prince*, owned it in the nineteenth century. The Zuger family has run it since 1955. Its château stands in the middle of Margaux village, and the wine is deep and spicy, among the most concentrated in the appellation.

sites.name: Château Boyd-Cantenac
sites.text: Named after Jacques Boyd, of an Irish family, who bought vines in Cantenac in the 1750s. Owned by the Guillemet family, who also make Château Pouget in the same cellars. A small estate making traditional, firm Margaux with a good share of Cabernet.

sites.name: Château Cantenac Brown
sites.text: John Lewis Brown, of a Scottish family and father of the animal painter of the same name, built the château in the 1830s in an English Tudor style that looks nothing like any other building in the Médoc. Its vineyard lies on gravel in Cantenac, giving firm, deep-coloured wine. A new low-carbon winery, built with traditional materials such as rammed earth, opened in the 2020s.

sites.name: Château Palmer
sites.text: Major-General Charles Palmer, a British officer who fought under Wellington, bought the estate in 1814 and ruined himself on it; the Pereire banking brothers took it over in 1853. Today owned by the Sichel and Mähler-Besse families, Palmer consistently sells above many second growths. Farmed biodynamically since 2014, it uses a high share of Merlot (often 40% or more), which gives a sensual, velvety style. Its *Historical XIXth Century Wine* blends Margaux with northern Rhône Syrah, as merchants did when 'hermitaging' claret.

sites.name: Château La Lagune
sites.text: The first classed growth heading north from Bordeaux, in Ludon on sandy gravel close to the estuary. Its eighteenth-century chartreuse is attributed to the architect Victor Louis. The Frey family (also owners of Paul Jaboulet Aîné and Château Corton C) has owned it since 2000, with Caroline Frey making the wine and converting to biodynamics. The style is supple and perfumed.

sites.name: Château Desmirail
sites.text: Named after Jean Desmirail, who married into the Rauzan family in the eighteenth century. Its vines were absorbed into Palmer and other estates in the twentieth century, and the name survived only as a brand until Lucien Lurton revived it in 1981. His son Denis Lurton now runs a small estate making elegant Margaux.

sites.name: Château Calon-Ségur
sites.text: The most northerly classed growth, once owned by the Marquis de Ségur, who also owned Lafite and Latour but said his heart was at Calon: hence the heart on the label, a favourite Valentine's Day wine. The vineyard is largely walled. Since 2012, new owners have replanted and rebuilt the cellars, and the wine has become one of Saint-Estèphe's best, with a high share of Cabernet Sauvignon.

sites.name: Château Ferrière
sites.text: One of the smallest classed growths, at under 25 ha, named after Gabriel Ferrière, a royal shipbroker. Leased to Château Lascombes for decades, it was revived by the Villars-Merlaut family in 1992 and is now run by Claire Villars-Lurton, who converted it to biodynamics. The wine is fine-boned and floral.

sites.name: Château Marquis d'Alesme
sites.text: Formerly Marquis d'Alesme Becker, this small estate in Margaux village was bought by the Perrodo family (also owners of Labégorce) in 2006. They dropped 'Becker' from the name in 2009 and built a new winery with Chinese-inspired gardens, a nod to Hubert Perrodo's Asian business links.

sites.name: Château Saint-Pierre
sites.text: A small Saint-Julien estate bought in 1982 by Henri Martin, mayor of Saint-Julien and creator of Château Gloria, and now run by his descendants, the Triaud family. Its vines are scattered parcels of excellent gravel in the village, and the wine is plush and generous for Saint-Julien.

sites.name: Château Talbot
sites.text: Named after John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, the English commander killed at Castillon in 1453, though there is no proof he ever owned it. The Cordier family has owned Talbot since 1917 and now runs it with the Rustmann and Bignon families. A large inland estate, it makes sturdy, savoury red and a well-known white, Caillou Blanc, sold as Bordeaux.

sites.name: Château Branaire-Ducru
sites.text: Facing Beychevelle across the road, Branaire takes its name from Jean-Baptiste Braneyre, who bought it in 1680, and from the Ducru family of the nineteenth century. The Maroteaux family has owned it since 1988 and built one of the first gravity-flow cellars in the Médoc in 1991. The wine is elegant, mid-weight Saint-Julien of real charm.

sites.name: Château Duhart-Milon
sites.text: Bought by the Rothschilds of Lafite in 1962, Duhart-Milon's vines lie on the slopes of the Carruades plateau west of Lafite, next to the hamlet of Milon. The name recalls a legendary eighteenth-century pirate, Monsieur Duhart, said to have lived in Pauillac; it is a story more than a fact. The wine is a firmer, more affordable sibling of Lafite.

sites.name: Château Pouget
sites.text: One of the smallest classed growths, about 10 ha in Cantenac, owned by the Guillemet family and made alongside Boyd-Cantenac. It makes traditional, firm Margaux at modest prices.

sites.name: Château La Tour Carnet
sites.text: A genuine medieval castle with a moat and a thirteenth-century keep, in Saint-Laurent-Médoc. Bernard Magrez bought it in 2000 and changed it radically, with heavy investment in the vineyard and a ripe, modern style. Its name comes from Jean de Foix's squire, Carnet, who won it by defending it in the Hundred Years War, according to tradition.

sites.name: Château Lafon-Rochet
sites.text: Instantly recognisable by its yellow château and label, painted that colour by the Tesseron family, who owned it from 1960 until 2021, when Jacky Lorenzetti (owner of Pédesclaux) bought it. The vineyard is next to Cos d'Estournel and Lafite, and the wine is firm, fresh Saint-Estèphe.

sites.name: Château Beychevelle
sites.text: Its name is said to derive from *baisse-voile*, lower the sail: ships on the Gironde dipped their sails to salute the Duc d'Épernon, admiral of France, who owned the estate in the seventeenth century. Hence the ship on the label. The eighteenth-century château is among the most elegant in the Médoc. Owned since the 1980s by a partnership led by Castel and Suntory, Beychevelle makes supple, aromatic Saint-Julien that often outperforms its rank.

sites.name: Château Prieuré-Lichine
sites.text: Once the priory of the Benedictine monks of Cantenac, it was bought in 1951 by Alexis Lichine, the Russian-born wine writer and merchant, who added his name and opened it to visitors when such hospitality was unheard of in the Médoc. The vineyard is a patchwork of parcels across Margaux's five communes, giving a blended picture of the appellation.

sites.name: Château Marquis de Terme
sites.text: Named after the Marquis de Terme, who acquired it by marriage in 1762. The Sénéclauze family has owned it since 1935. A mid-sized estate in Margaux village whose wine has gained finesse since the 2010s.

sites.name: Château Pontet-Canet
sites.text: Owned by the Tesseron family since 1975, Pontet-Canet became the most talked-about fifth growth of the 2000s. Alfred Tesseron converted to biodynamics, certified in 2010, brought back horses for ploughing, and introduced concrete amphorae made from the estate's own gravel. The wines, from vineyards next to Mouton, are now priced and scored like seconds.

sites.name: Château Batailley
sites.text: Its name recalls a battle of the Hundred Years War said to have been fought on the site. Owned by the Castéja family (of Borie-Manoux), it sits inland in a wooded park in south-western Pauillac. Batailley makes classic, firm, fairly priced Pauillac.

sites.name: Château Haut-Batailley
sites.text: Split off from Batailley in 1942 when the Borie family divided its holdings, Haut-Batailley was run by the Bories of Ducru-Beaucaillou until the Cazes family of Lynch-Bages bought it in 2017. Its vines border Pichon Baron and Latour inland, and the wine is lighter-bodied and graceful.

sites.name: Château Grand-Puy-Lacoste
sites.text: 'Puy' means hill: the estate sits on a high gravel mound on the Bages plateau. The Borie family bought it in 1978, and Xavier Borie and now his daughter Emeline have made it a byword for classic, cassis-and-cedar Pauillac at a fair price.

sites.name: Château Grand-Puy Ducasse
sites.text: Unusually, its château stands on the waterfront quay of Pauillac town, while its vines are scattered across three parts of the appellation. Named after Pierre Ducasse, an eighteenth-century lawyer. It makes approachable, mid-weight Pauillac.

sites.name: Château Lynch-Bages
sites.text: Named after Thomas Lynch, of an Irish family, whose son Jean-Baptiste became mayor of Bordeaux. The Cazes family has owned it since 1939; Jean-Michel Cazes made it a 'poor man's Latour' famous for rich, cassis-laden wine, and restored the hamlet of Bages with a bakery and café. A new cellar designed by Chien Chung Pei opened in 2020.

sites.name: Château Lynch-Moussas
sites.text: The westernmost classed growth of Pauillac, on gravel at the edge of the forest. Like Lynch-Bages it was once owned by the Lynch family. The Castéja family has run it since 1919, replanting and expanding it from the 1970s.

sites.name: Château Dauzac
sites.text: In Labarde, close to the estuary, Dauzac has a famous place in wine science. In the early 1880s its manager Ernest David and the botanist Alexis Millardet noticed that vines sprayed with copper sulphate and lime, to deter grape thieves along the road, had escaped downy mildew. The result was *bouillie bordelaise*, the Bordeaux mixture that saved Europe's vineyards.

sites.name: Château d'Armailhac
sites.text: Baron Philippe de Rothschild bought this neighbour of Mouton in 1933 and renamed it several times (Mouton Baron Philippe, then Mouton Baronne Philippe) before reverting in 1989 to the name of the eighteenth-century d'Armailhacq family. The wine has a relatively high share of Cabernet Franc and is softer than Mouton.

sites.name: Château du Tertre
sites.text: 'Tertre' means a small hill, and this estate in Arsac sits on one of the highest gravel ridges in the Margaux appellation. Owned by the Albada Jelgersma family since 1997, it uses a striking share of Cabernet Franc and some Petit Verdot, giving fragrant, fresh wines.

sites.name: Château Haut-Bages Libéral
sites.text: Named after the Libéral family, eighteenth-century merchants. Part of its vineyard borders Latour. Claire Villars-Lurton has converted it to biodynamics and agroforestry, planting hedges and trees among the vines.

sites.name: Château Pédesclaux
sites.text: Founded by Pierre Urbain Pédesclaux, a Bordeaux wine broker of the early nineteenth century, when brokers (courtiers) were the men who drew up the 1855 ranking. Long underperforming, it was transformed after Jacky Lorenzetti bought it in 2009, with a glass-walled, gravity-fed cellar by architect Jean-Michel Wilmotte and replanted vineyards near Mouton and Pontet-Canet.

sites.name: Château Belgrave
sites.text: An inland estate in Saint-Laurent-Médoc, just behind Lagrange and the Saint-Julien border. Part of the Dourthe group since 1979, it makes firm, good-value Haut-Médoc from gravel over clay.

sites.name: Château de Camensac
sites.text: An eighteenth-century chartreuse in Saint-Laurent-Médoc. The Merlaut family and associates have owned it since 2005 and worked to restore its gravel vineyard. The wine is supple and approachable for a classed growth.

sites.name: Château Cos Labory
sites.text: A small estate next door to Cos d'Estournel, owned by the Audoy family. Its wine is firm, honest Saint-Estèphe at a price well below its famous neighbour's.

sites.name: Château Clerc Milon
sites.text: Bought by Baron Philippe de Rothschild in 1970, its vines lie next to Lafite and Mouton close to the estuary, around the hamlet of Milon. A new winery opened in 2011. The wine is richer and more Mouton-like than its rank suggests.

sites.name: Château Croizet-Bages
sites.text: On the Bages plateau next to Lynch-Bages, owned by the Quié family (also of Rauzan-Gassies) since 1942. Long considered an underachiever, it has improved with recent investment.

sites.name: Château Cantemerle
sites.text: Missing from the original list of April 1855, Cantemerle was added a few months later at the bottom of the fifth growths after its owner, the widow Villeneuve-Durfort, produced records proving its prices. The château stands in a wooded park in Macau, at the southern end of the Médoc. The wine is perfumed and supple, from sandy gravel.

sites.name: Château d'Yquem
sites.text: The only wine given the rank of Premier Cru Supérieur in 1855, a title no red wine received. Yquem sits on the highest hill of Sauternes, about 75 m, with a fortified manor dating back to the fifteenth century. The Sauvage family owned it from 1593; in 1785 Françoise-Joséphine de Sauvage d'Yquem married Count Louis-Amédée de Lur-Saluces, and their descendants ran it until LVMH took control at the end of the 1990s, with Alexandre de Lur-Saluces leaving in 2004. Thomas Jefferson ordered it in the 1780s. About 100 ha are in production, roughly three quarters Sémillon. Pickers make up to ten or more tries, and in poor years (1992, 2012 among them) no Yquem is released. Its dry white, Ygrec (Y), first made in 1959, is now produced every year.

sites.name: Château La Tour Blanche
sites.text: Ranked first of the Premiers Crus after Yquem in 1855. In 1907 its owner, the philanthropist Daniel Iffla Osiris, left it to the French state on condition that it house a school of viticulture, and it still runs a wine college today. Its wines, from Bommes, are rich and barrel-fermented.

sites.name: Château Lafaurie-Peyraguey
sites.text: A thirteenth-century fortified manor in Bommes with crenellated walls. Swiss businessman Silvio Denz, owner of the glassmaker Lalique, bought it in 2014 and opened a hotel and restaurant, Lalique, where crystal and Sauternes meet. The wines are among the most consistent of the Premiers Crus.

sites.name: Clos Haut-Peyraguey
sites.text: Created when the Peyraguey estate was divided in 1879, this small vineyard on the summit of the Bommes hill was owned by the Pauly family for a century before Bernard Magrez bought it in 2012. The wines are fine and lifted rather than heavy.

sites.name: Château de Rayne Vigneau
sites.text: On a hill in Bommes famous for its soil studded with semi-precious stones, agate, onyx and quartz brought by the Garonne, which a nineteenth-century owner had catalogued. The wine is fragrant and finely balanced.

sites.name: Château Suduiraut
sites.text: A grand seventeenth-century château in Preignac with gardens attributed to André Le Nôtre's school, bordering Yquem's vines. AXA Millésimes has owned it since 1992. Suduiraut is one of the richest, most opulent Sauternes; it also makes dry whites (Lions de Suduiraut and S de Suduiraut).

sites.name: Château Coutet
sites.text: The largest of the Barsac first growths, with a thirteenth-century tower that once served as an English fort. Owned by the Baly family since 1977, distributed with Baron Philippe de Rothschild SA. Its rare Cuvée Madame, made only in great years from the oldest vines, is one of the most sought-after Barsacs.

sites.name: Château Climens
sites.text: Often called the Lord of Barsac, Climens farms about 30 ha in one block on the highest point of the Barsac limestone plateau, planted entirely with Sémillon. Bérénice Lurton ran it from 1992 and converted it to biodynamics in 2010, the first Sauternais classed growth to do so. In 2022 she sold a majority stake to the Moitry family and stayed on as a consultant. The wine is a model of Barsac freshness and finesse.

sites.name: Château Guiraud
sites.text: One of the largest estates of Sauternes, on gravel next to Yquem. Since 2006 it has belonged to a group including Robert Peugeot, Xavier Planty, Olivier Bernard of Domaine de Chevalier and Stephan von Neipperg, and it was the first Sauternes classed growth certified organic (2011). It runs a conservatory of old vine selections.

sites.name: Château Rieussec
sites.text: In Fargues, on high gravel next to Yquem. The Rothschilds of Lafite (Domaines Barons de Rothschild) bought it in 1984. Rieussec is known for its deep golden colour and rich, honeyed style. Its dry wine is R de Rieussec.

sites.name: Château Rabaud-Promis
sites.text: The old Rabaud estate in Bommes was ranked as one in 1855, divided in 1903 into Rabaud-Promis and Sigalas-Rabaud, reunited in 1929 and divided again in 1952. Rabaud-Promis has been owned by the Déjean family since 1981.

sites.name: Château Sigalas Rabaud
sites.text: The smaller half of the old Rabaud estate, on a gravel slope in Bommes facing north-west. Owned by the de Lambert des Granges family, descendants of the Marquis de Sigalas, it makes delicate, pure Sauternes and was among the first to make a sulphite-free sweet wine.

sites.name: Château de Myrat
sites.text: The de Pontac family, owners since the nineteenth century, pulled up the vines in 1976 when Sauternes could not be sold. Two of the family sons replanted in 1988, and the estate returned to production in the 1990s.

sites.name: Château Doisy-Daëne
sites.text: Part of the original Doisy estate, owned by the Dubourdieu family since 1924. Denis Dubourdieu, the great white-wine scientist of the University of Bordeaux, worked here; his sons now run it. Its L'Extravagant, made in tiny quantities from the richest berries, is one of the most concentrated sweet wines of Bordeaux.

sites.name: Château Doisy-Dubroca
sites.text: The smallest of the three Doisy estates, a few hectares of old Sémillon. For many years it was owned by the Lurton family and made by the team at Climens.

sites.name: Château Doisy-Védrines
sites.text: The largest of the three Doisy estates and the original seat of the family, owned by the Castéja family since 1840. It makes rich, long-lived Barsac.

sites.name: Château d'Arche
sites.text: A seventeenth-century château on a gravel hill in Sauternes, named after the Comte d'Arche, an eighteenth-century owner who built up the estate. It makes rich, classic Sauternes with a high share of Sémillon and now hosts a small hotel among the vines, a rare chance to sleep in the heart of the Sauternais.

sites.name: Château Filhot
sites.text: A large estate in the south of Sauternes with an elegant château built in the early nineteenth century and a park. Owned by the Lur-Saluces family for a long time, it now belongs to the Vaucelles family. The wines are lighter than most, with a good share of Sauvignon Blanc.

sites.name: Château Broustet
sites.text: A small Barsac estate on the limestone plateau beside the road to Langon, with vineyards on red sand and clay over limestone. Its wines are lighter and more citrus-toned than the Sauternes heavyweights, a good introduction to the Barsac style.

sites.name: Château Nairac
